Specifies that the partition is carried out by the Collector of the district where the estate is located, or by a Collector specially ordered by the Commissioner or Board of Revenue if the estate spans multiple districts or divisions.

main_sections.section_title: Assessment and levy of costs incurred in making partition
main_sections.description: Covers the assessment and recovery of costs associated with the partition process, including measurement, survey, paper preparation, and other charges. These costs can be realized similarly to arrears of rent or revenue.

main_sections.section_title: Partition may be stayed, and proceedings quashed, by Commissioner
main_sections.description: Empowers the Commissioner to stay partition proceedings and quash them if, after partition is ordered, new information suggests it should not proceed. Decisions by Revenue authorities under this section are not subject to civil court revision.

main_sections.section_title: Procedure after lapse of period mentioned in notification under section XII
main_sections.description: Describes the Collector's actions after the period mentioned in the Section XII notification expires, which may include land measurement and rent-roll preparation.

important_rules: Future partitions must be conducted under the provisions of this Act.
Every recorded proprietor of a joint undivided estate paying Government revenue is entitled to claim partition.
Applications for partition must be in writing, signed by the applicant(s), and include specific details about the estate and co-sharers.
Applications lacking the specified particulars may be rejected.
When a partition is ordered, a notification must be published, and objections from non-joining proprietors must be invited.
The Collector may refuse partition if valid objections are raised for good and sufficient reasons.
If questions of title or proprietary right arise, the Collector may refer them to a competent court or conduct an inquiry and potentially refer issues to arbitration.
Decisions by the Collector on proprietary rights are appealable to higher civil courts.
Civil courts are generally restricted from entertaining partition suits except on appeal from a Collector's decision.
After partition is ordered, a notification must be published, and the partition process will commence after a specified period.
Costs incurred in partition, including measurement and survey, are to be assessed and levied from the parties.
The Commissioner has the power to stay or quash partition proceedings under certain circumstances.
After a partition is ordered, if necessary, the Collector will cause a measurement of lands and prepare a rent-roll.
Lands held in common are to be divided.
The Collector may refuse to separate lands in certain specified cases.
Where no lands are held in common, lands held in severalty may be declared separate estates, subject to provisos regarding transfers.
Sharers failing to attend after proclamation may forfeit their right to object.
Partition may be stayed if parties agree to it.
Estates formed during partition should be as compact as possible.
Revenue is to be assessed on each divided estate.
Circumstances must be considered when making partitions.
Specific rules apply when a dwelling house belonging to one sharer is situated on ground allotted to another.
Specific rules govern the division of tanks, wells, water-courses, and embankments.
Specific rules apply to places of worship during partition.
The paper of partition and accompanying map submitted by the officer making the partition must contain specific particulars.
The Collector will review the submitted partition papers.
The Commissioner can confirm or modify the partition, with potential appeal to the Board of Revenue, and may direct division by lot.
The Collector will act on orders received from the Commissioner or the Board of Revenue.
The Government may order a new allotment of public revenue in cases of fraud or error in the original allotment.
Failure to affirm or establish an interest in an estate under attachment for partition can have consequences.
Holders of civil court decrees awarding rights to a portion of an estate can apply for partition.
Union of severed portions of originally undivided estates is possible under certain circumstances.
Provisions of the Act apply to the partition of estates held free from revenue payment.
Collector's proceedings under the Act are subject to control by superior revenue authorities.
Certain other officers may exercise powers vested in the Collector.
Officers exercising jurisdiction under the Act have powers regarding false evidence.

penalties: Consequence to a party having an interest in an estate if he neglects to affirm or establish such interest while the estate is under attachment with a view to partition (Section 46).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector, Commissioner, Board of Revenue, Civil Courts (on appeal).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through application to the Collector, inquiry, arbitration, appeals to higher revenue and civil authorities, and by officers charged with making the partition. Costs can be realized under rules for arrears of rent or revenue. Powers regarding false evidence are also outlined.

rights: Right of recorded proprietors to claim partition.
Right to object to a partition application within a specified time.
Right to appeal decisions of the Collector.
Right to present evidence and have interests determined.
Right to have partition proceedings stayed.
Right to have the partition process conducted impartially and according to established rules.
Right to have estates formed during partition be as compact as possible.
Right to have revenue assessed on each divided estate.
duties: Duty of proprietors to apply in writing for partition, specifying required particulars.
Duty to serve notice to non-joining proprietors.
Duty to appear before the Collector or be represented by an agent when required.
Duty to abide by decisions of the Collector and appellate authorities.
Duty to cooperate with officers carrying out the partition, including measurement and survey.
Duty to pay costs incurred in making the partition.
Duty to respond to proclamations and attend proceedings.
Duty to provide accurate information and papers.
Duty to not neglect to affirm or establish interest in an estate under attachment for partition.
obligations: Obligation to adhere to the Act's provisions for partition.
Obligation to pay partition costs.
Obligation to comply with orders of the Collector, Commissioner, and Board of Revenue.
Obligation for sharers to attend proceedings after proclamation, or risk forfeiting objection rights.

key_procedures: Initiating partition by written application to the Collector, specifying details of the estate and co-sharers.
Collector's review of the application, publication of notification, and invitation of objections.
Collector's inquiry into objections, determination of title/proprietary rights, and potential reference to arbitration.
Decision of the Collector on rights, which is appealable to higher courts.
Notification of partition being ordered and a waiting period before commencement.
Execution of partition by the Collector or appointed officer, potentially involving measurement, survey, and preparation of papers.
Review and confirmation/modification of the partition by the Commissioner or Board of Revenue.
Finalization of partition and assessment of revenue on divided estates.
Application for union of severed portions of estates.
Process for partition of estates held free from revenue payment.
administration: Collector, Commissioner, Board of Revenue, Local Government.
important_notes: Sections 1 and 50 are repealed.
The Act has been affected by subsequent Acts (XIV of 1870, XIX of 1873, and XVIII of 1876).
The Act was originally applicable to the North-Western Provinces of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal, with some provisions repealed concerning those provinces and Oudh.
Decisions of Revenue authorities regarding staying or quashing partitions are not open to revision by civil courts.
Civil courts' jurisdiction for partition suits is limited to appeals from Collector's decisions.
In cases of fraud or error in revenue allotment during partition, the Government may order a new allotment.
The Board of Revenue is guided by instructions from the Local Government.

title: The Religious Endowments Act, 1863
purpose: To enable the Government to divest itself of the management of Religious Endowments, specifically by relieving the Boards of Revenue and local Agents from duties related to the appropriation of rents and produce of lands granted for religious purposes, maintenance of public buildings, and custody of escheats, as previously mandated by Bengal Regulation XIX, 1810, and Madras Regulation VII, 1817.
scope: The Act applies to mosques, Hindu temples, colleges, and other religious establishments in the Presidencies of Fort William in Bengal and Fort Saint George. It also extends to certain scheduled districts and has been extended to Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The Act's application has been modified or repealed in specific regions and for particular types of endowments (e.g., Madras Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments, Bengal Wakf Act, Bihar Act, Wakf Act, 1954). Section 22 applies to the whole of India except Part B States.

key_definitions.Civil Court and Court: The principal Court of original civil jurisdiction in the district where the mosque, temple, or religious establishment is situated, or any other Court empowered by the State Government within whose local jurisdiction it lies. This definition is subject to the provisions in section 10.

main_sections.description: This section, concerning the repeal of parts of Bengal Regulation 19 of 1810 and Madras Regulation 7 of 1817, has been repealed by the Repealing Act, 1870.
Defines 'Civil Court' and 'Court'.

main_sections.section_title: Government to make special provision respecting mosques, etc.
main_sections.description: Mandates the State Government to make special provisions for religious establishments where the nomination of trustees, managers, or superintendents is vested in or subject to confirmation by the Government or a public officer.

main_sections.section_title: Transfer to trustees, etc., of trust-property in charge of Revenue Board.
main_sections.description: Directs the State Government to transfer all landed or other property belonging to religious establishments, which is under the superintendence or possession of the Board of Revenue or local agents, to the existing trustees, managers, or superintendents. It also stipulates the cessation of the Board's and local agents' powers and responsibilities regarding such property, except for acts done and liabilities incurred prior to the transfer.

main_sections.section_title: Procedure in case of dispute as to right of succession to vacated trusteeship.
main_sections.description: Outlines the procedure when a vacancy occurs in the office of a trustee, manager, or superintendent to whom property has been transferred under section 4, and a dispute arises regarding succession. Any interested person can apply to the Civil Court to appoint a manager until a successor is established by suit. The manager appointed by the Court has the same powers as the former trustee.

main_sections.section_title: Rights, etc., of trustees to whom property is transferred under section 4.
main_sections.description: States that the rights, powers, responsibilities, and conditions of appointment, election, and removal of trustees to whom property is transferred under section 4 remain the same as if the Act had not been passed, except for the liability to be sued under this Act and the authority of the Board of Revenue and local agents, which is determined and repealed. Powers for rent recovery can be exercised by the trustee after transfer.

Requires the State Government to appoint one or more committees in every division or district to replace the Board of Revenue and local agents in cases described in section 3. Such committees will consist of three or more persons and will perform the duties of the Board, except concerning property covered by section 21.

Specifies that committee members must profess the religion for which the establishment was founded and be appointed according to the general wishes of interested persons. The State Government may hold elections to ascertain these wishes. Rules framed for elections must be laid before the State Legislature.
Members of the committee hold office for life unless removed for misconduct or unfitness. Removal requires an order from the Civil Court.

Details the procedure for filling vacancies in committees. The remaining members must give public notice and fix a date for an election by interested persons within three months. If the vacancy is not filled within three months by election, the Civil Court may appoint a person or order the remaining members to fill the vacancy.

main_sections.section_title: No member of Committee to be also trustee, etc., of mosque,
main_sections.description: Prohibits members of a committee from simultaneously being a trustee, manager, or superintendent of the same mosque, temple, or religious establishment.

main_sections.section_title: On appointment of Committee, Board and local agents to transfer property.
main_sections.description: When a committee is appointed, the Board and local agents must transfer property to the committee. The powers and responsibilities of the Board and agents cease upon transfer, and the committee's powers commence.

main_sections.section_title: Duty of trustee, etc., as to accounts.
main_sections.description: Requires trustees, managers, superintendents, and committees to maintain accounts for the trust.

main_sections.section_title: Persons interested may singly sue in case of breach of trust, etc.
main_sections.description: Grants any person interested the right to sue in the Civil Court for a breach of trust or mismanagement of a religious establishment or its property. The Civil Court has powers to make orders regarding such matters.

main_sections.section_title: Nature of interest entitling person to sue.
main_sections.description: Defines the nature of interest that entitles a person to sue under the Act.
States that Act 10 of 1940 is applied for reference to arbitrators.
Details the process of reference under Act 10 of 1940.

main_sections.section_title: Application for leave to institute suits.
main_sections.description: Governs the application for leave to institute suits and costs associated with them.

main_sections.section_title: Court may require accounts of trust to be filed.
main_sections.description: Empowers the Court to require the filing of accounts of the trust.

main_sections.section_title: Proceedings for criminal breach of trust.
main_sections.description: Pertains to proceedings for criminal breach of trust.

main_sections.section_title: Cases in which endowments are partly for religious and partly for secular purposes.
main_sections.description: Addresses endowments that serve both religious and secular purposes.

main_sections.section_title: Government not to hold charge henceforth of property for support of any mosque, temple, etc.
main_sections.description: Declares that the Government will no longer hold charge of property dedicated to the support of any mosque, temple, or other religious establishment from the commencement of the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Effect of Act in respect of Regulations therein mentioned, and of buildings of antiquity, etc.
main_sections.description: Specifies the effect of the Act concerning the mentioned Regulations and buildings of antiquity.
This section has been repealed.

important_rules: Rule 1: In cases where Government or a public officer has the power to nominate or confirm trustees/managers of religious establishments, the State Government must make special provisions for their management.

Rule 2: For religious establishments whose property is under the management of trustees not nominated or confirmed by the Government, the State Government must transfer such property from the Board of Revenue or local agents to the existing trustees.

Rule 3: When a vacancy occurs in a trusteeship that was transferred under section 4, and a dispute arises over succession, any interested person can apply to the Civil Court to appoint a manager until the succession is legally determined.

Rule 4: The State Government shall appoint committees of three or more persons to manage religious establishments where the Government previously held management responsibilities, as outlined in section 3.

Rule 5: Members of the appointed committees must profess the religion of the establishment and be chosen based on the general wishes of interested persons. Elections may be held to ascertain these wishes.
Rule 6: Committee members hold office for life unless removed by a Civil Court order for misconduct or unfitness.
Rule 7: Vacancies in committees must be filled by election within three months. If not filled, the Civil Court can appoint a member or order the remaining members to do so.
Rule 8: No committee member can simultaneously be a trustee, manager, or superintendent of the same religious establishment.
Rule 9: Trustees, managers, superintendents, and committees are responsible for maintaining proper accounts.
Rule 10: Any person interested in a religious establishment can sue in the Civil Court for breach of trust or mismanagement.

penalties: Proceedings for criminal breach of trust are mentioned, but specific penalties are not detailed in the provided text.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Civil Courts and the State Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through court orders, appointment of managers, requiring accounts, and facilitating elections for committee members. The State Government is responsible for making special provisions and appointing committees.

rights: Right for interested persons to apply to the Civil Court for the appointment of a manager in case of succession disputes.
Right for interested persons to sue in the Civil Court for breach of trust or mismanagement of religious endowments.
Right of trustees to exercise powers for rent recovery after property transfer.
Right for persons interested in the maintenance of an establishment to have their wishes considered in committee appointments and to participate in elections.
duties: Duty of the State Government to make special provisions for certain religious establishments.
Duty of the State Government to transfer trust property from revenue boards to trustees.
Duty of the State Government to appoint committees.
Duty of committee members to perform their duties as successors to the Board of Revenue and local agents.
Duty of trustees, managers, superintendents, and committees to maintain accounts.
Duty of remaining committee members to give public notice of vacancies and fix dates for elections.
Duty of remaining committee members to comply with Civil Court orders to fill vacancies.
obligations: Obligation for committees to perform all duties imposed on the Board of Revenue and local agents, except for specially provided property.
Obligation for committee members to be removed only by Civil Court order.
Obligation for remaining committee members to fill vacancies as per Court orders if elections fail.
Obligation for persons to obtain leave from the Court to institute suits.
Obligation for the Government to divest itself of the management of religious endowments.

key_procedures: Procedure for transferring trust property from revenue boards to existing trustees.
Procedure for appointing a manager by the Civil Court in case of succession disputes.
Procedure for appointing committees by the State Government.
Procedure for ascertaining the wishes of interested persons for committee appointments, including potential elections.
Procedure for filling vacancies in committees through election or by Civil Court appointment.
Procedure for applying for leave to institute suits.
Procedure for the Court to require the filing of trust accounts.
Procedure for Civil Courts to make orders in cases of breach of trust or mismanagement.
administration: The administration of religious endowments is transferred from the Government (Boards of Revenue and local agents) to appointed trustees, managers, superintendents, or committees, with oversight and intervention capabilities by the Civil Courts and the State Government.
important_notes: The Act repealed provisions of Bengal Regulation XIX, 1810, and Madras Regulation VII, 1817, concerning the management of religious endowments.
The Act does not apply to certain religious trusts or wakfs as specified in later legislation (e.g., Bihar Act 1 of 1951, Wakf Act, 1954).
Section 5 has been modified by the Wakf Act, 1954.
The Act has been extended to various scheduled districts and union territories over time.
The Act ceased to be in force in the State of Madras by Madras Act 22 of 1959.
Section 1 of the Act has been repealed.

title: THE WASTE LANDS (CLAIMS) ACT, 1863
purpose: To provide for the speedy adjudication of claims to waste lands proposed to be sold or otherwise dealt with on account of the Provincial Government, and of objections taken to the sale or other disposition of such lands.
scope: Applies to claims preferred to waste lands proposed to be sold or otherwise dealt with by the State Government, and objections to such sales or dispositions. The geographical scope is limited to areas where the Act is in force, as indicated by notifications and extensions to various provinces and scheduled districts in India. The subject matter scope is specific to claims and objections related to 'waste lands'.

main_sections.section_title: Provision for inquiry into claims to land, or objections to sale of same
main_sections.description: Empowers the Collector or equivalent officer to inquire into claims or objections regarding waste land proposed for sale or other disposition, provided the claim or objection is preferred within the period specified in the advertisement, which must be at least three months.

Details the procedure for the Collector to call for evidence from claimants/objectors, conduct further inquiries, and dispose of the case by admitting or rejecting the claim/objection. If the land is to be sold, it can be subject to conditions or reservations notified to purchasers.

main_sections.section_title: Pending enquiry, sale &c., to be postponed
main_sections.description: Mandates the postponement of sale or other disposition of land during an inquiry into a claim or objection. If the claim/objection is rejected, the sale is further postponed to allow the claimant/objector to contest the order.

main_sections.section_title: Sale to be stopped if claim appear to be established, but may afterwards be proceeded with
main_sections.description: Instructs the Collector to stop the sale or disposition if a claim appears established. However, the sale can resume if the claimant fails to establish their claim in a subsequent suit ordered by the Local Government.

main_sections.section_title: Procedure after passing of order in the case, Report to Revenue Board, Decision of Board
main_sections.description: Outlines the process after the Collector issues an order. If the claimant/objector does not contest within a specified time, the order is final. If contested, a report is made to the superior Revenue Authority, which may confirm, modify, or reverse the Collector's order. If the Board's order is adverse to the claimant, a suit must be instituted within thirty days to establish the claim.

main_sections.section_title: Local Government may, with in Twelve months, order suit to be brought to try claim admitted by Collector
main_sections.description: Allows the Local Government to direct a suit to be brought within twelve months to try a claim or objection admitted by the Collector.

Mandates the Local Government to constitute a Special Court of at least three members (including the District Judge or presiding officer of the principal Civil Court) for investigating and trying claims under this Act. The officer who held the original inquiry cannot be a member if they also preside over the principal Civil Court.

main_sections.section_title: Notice of constitution of Special Courts. Claims not cognizable in other Courts
main_sections.description: Requires public notice of the constitution of Special Courts. From the date of proclamation, no other court can entertain claims or objections for which the Special Court is constituted.

main_sections.section_title: Special Courts where to be held
main_sections.description: States that Special Courts will be held at the most convenient place within their respective jurisdictions.

main_sections.section_title: Plaintiff and defendant in suit under section V, Plaintiff and defendant in suits under section VI
main_sections.description: Defines the plaintiff and defendant in suits instituted under Sections V and VI. In Section V suits, the claimant is the plaintiff and the Collector is the defendant. In Section VI suits, the State Government (represented by an appointed officer) is the plaintiff, and the claimant is the defendant. Either party can appear by pleader or agent.
States that proceedings in suits instituted under this Act will be regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, as far as applicable.

Details the procedure before the hearing, including fixing a date for appearance, issuing notices, parties bringing witnesses and documents, and the court's power to require personal attendance of the claimant or objector.
Describes the procedure on the day of the hearing, involving examination of parties and witnesses, inspection of documents, and making further inquiries before passing an order.

important_rules: Claims or objections must be preferred within the period mentioned in the advertisement for sale or disposition of waste land, which must be at least three months.
If a claim or objection is rejected by the Collector, the claimant/objector has a specified time (initially one week, extendable by the Collector) to give notice of intent to contest.

If a claimant or objector decides to contest the Collector's order, they must institute a suit in the Special Court within thirty days of receiving notice from the Court, if the Board's order is adverse.
The Local Government can order a suit to be brought within twelve months to try a claim admitted by the Collector.

Special Courts for trying claims are constituted by the Local Government, consisting of an uneven number of persons (not less than three), including the District Judge or presiding officer of the principal Civil Court.
Once a Special Court is constituted, no other Court is competent to entertain claims or objections falling under its jurisdiction.
Proceedings in suits under this Act are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, where applicable.
Parties must bring their witnesses and documents on the day fixed for hearing or apply to the Court for assistance to procure witnesses in advance.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector, Revenue Authorities, Local Government, and Special Courts constituted under the Act.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through inquiries, orders, reports, decisions by Revenue Authorities, and trials in Special Courts. Failure to establish claims in suits can lead to finality of adverse orders. Enforcement of orders and judgments of the Special Courts would be through established legal processes.

rights: Right to prefer a claim to waste land proposed for sale or disposition.
Right to raise objections to the sale or disposition of waste land.
Right to present evidence and documents in support of a claim or objection.
Right to contest the Collector's order of rejection in the manner provided.
Right to institute a suit in a Special Court to establish a claim or objection after an adverse order from the Revenue Board.
Right to appear by pleader or agent in suits.
Right to have assistance from the Court to procure witness attendance.
Right to receive notice of hearings and court proceedings.
duties: Duty to prefer claims or objections within the stipulated time period.
Duty to produce evidence and documents upon which reliance is placed.
Duty to appear in court and present cases.
Duty of the Collector to conduct inquiries and issue orders.
Duty of Revenue Authorities to report and decide on appeals.
Duty of the Local Government to constitute Special Courts and order suits.
Duty of the Special Court to conduct trials and pass orders.
obligations: Obligation to comply with the orders of the Collector, Revenue Authorities, and Special Courts.
Obligation to institute a suit within the specified time if contesting an adverse order.
Obligation to follow the procedural rules laid down in the Act and the Code of Civil Procedure.

key_procedures: Claim/Objection Filing: A claim or objection must be preferred to the Collector or equivalent officer within the period specified in the sale/disposition advertisement (minimum three months).
Collector's Inquiry: The Collector inquires into the claim/objection, calls for evidence, and makes an order (admission/rejection, or sale with conditions).
Postponement of Sale: Sale or disposition is postponed during inquiry and potentially after rejection to allow for contest.
Contesting Collector's Order: If the claimant/objector wishes to contest, they must give notice within a specified time. If not, the order is final.
Report to Revenue Board: If contested, the Collector reports to the superior Revenue Authority, who may confirm, modify, or reverse the order.
Institution of Suit: If the Revenue Board's order is adverse, the claimant must institute a suit in a Special Court within thirty days.
Constitution of Special Court: Local Government constitutes a Special Court for trials.
Court Proceedings: Procedures in Special Courts follow the Code of Civil Procedure, including hearing of evidence, examination of witnesses, and passing orders.
administration: The Act is administered at different stages by the Collector, the superior Revenue Authority (e.g., Board of Revenue), the Local Government, and the Special Courts constituted under the Act.
important_notes: The Act has been extended to various Scheduled Districts and has been repealed in Bombay by the Waste Lands (Claims) (Bombay Repeal) Act, 1943.
The Act has been extended to new Provinces and Merged States.

The time limit for instituting a suit after notice from the Court (Section V) was originally thirty days but was repealed by Act 9 of 1871. Limitation is now governed by the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
The Act is designated as an old Indian law and its applicability and interpretation may be subject to subsequent legislative changes and judicial precedents.
Section 24 was repealed.

title: THE DIVORCE ACT, 1869
purpose: To amend the law relating to Divorce and Matrimonial Causes for persons professing the Christian religion, and to confer upon certain Courts jurisdiction in matters matrimonial.
scope: This Act extends to the whole of India. It applies to marriages where at least one party professes the Christian religion.  For dissolution of marriage, parties must be domiciled in India. For nullity of marriage, the marriage must be solemnized in India and the petitioner must be resident in India. Other reliefs under the Act are available to petitioners resident in India.

key_definitions.High Court: With reference to any area, it means the High Court for that State, or specific High Courts for Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, and Chandigarh. For petitions, it means the High Court for the area where the husband and wife reside or last resided together.
key_definitions.District Judge: A Judge of a principal civil court of original jurisdiction.
key_definitions.District Court: The court of the District Judge within whose ordinary jurisdiction or jurisdiction under this Act, the marriage was solemnized or the husband and wife reside or last resided together.
key_definitions.Court: Means the High Court or the District Court, as the case may be.
key_definitions.minor children: For sons of Native fathers, boys under sixteen; for daughters of Native fathers, girls under thirteen. In other cases, unmarried children under eighteen.
key_definitions.marriage with another woman: Marriage of any person, being married, to another person during the life of the former wife, whether the second marriage took place within India or elsewhere.
key_definitions.desertion: Implies an abandonment against the wish of the person charging it.
key_definitions.property: Includes, in the case of a wife, any property to which she is entitled for an estate in remainder or reversion or as a trustee, executrix, or administratrix.

main_sections.description: Establishes the short title as the Divorce Act and states its commencement date as April 1, 1869.
Defines the geographical and personal extent of the Act's application, including conditions for granting relief, dissolution, and nullity decrees.
Provides definitions for key terms used in the Act, including High Court, District Judge, District Court, Court, minor children, marriage with another woman, desertion, and property.

main_sections.section_title: Matrimonial jurisdiction of High Courts to be exercised subject to Act. Exception.
main_sections.description: Specifies that the matrimonial jurisdiction of High Courts and District Courts shall be exercised subject to the provisions of this Act, with an exception for marriage licenses.

Outlines the grounds on which a marriage can be dissolved, including adultery, conversion to another religion, unsound mind, communicable venereal disease, seven years of no news, wilful refusal to consummate, failure to comply with a decree for restitution of conjugal rights, desertion for two years, and cruelty causing reasonable apprehension of harm.

important_rules: A marriage solemnized may be dissolved on petition by husband or wife if the respondent has committed adultery.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has ceased to be Christian by conversion to another religion.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has been incurably of unsound mind for at least two years.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has been suffering from a communicable venereal disease for at least two years.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has not been heard of as alive for seven years or more.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has wilfully refused to consummate the marriage.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has failed to comply with a decree for restitution of conjugal rights for two years or more.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has deserted the petitioner for at least two years.
A marriage may be dissolved if the respondent has treated the petitioner with such cruelty as to cause a reasonable apprehension of harm to the petitioner to live with the respondent.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: High Courts and District Courts are vested with jurisdiction and enforcement powers.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the exercise of matrimonial jurisdiction, enforcement of decrees and orders, and the procedures outlined in the Code of Civil Procedure as applied by this Act.

rights: Right to petition for dissolution of marriage on specified grounds.
Right to seek nullity of marriage.
Right to seek judicial separation.
Right to apply for protection orders for deserted wives.
Right to petition for restitution of conjugal rights.
Right to claim alimony pendente lite and permanent alimony.
Right to make orders as to the custody of children.
Right of parties to marry again after a decree of dissolution or nullity.
Right of a separated wife to be deemed a spinster with respect to after-acquired property and for purposes of contract and suing.
duties: Duty to abide by decrees and orders of the Court.
Duty to attend Court proceedings when summoned.
obligations: Husband's obligation to provide restitution of conjugal rights where applicable.
Obligation to disclose absence of collusion in petitions.
Obligations related to settlements in cases of dissolution or nullity.

key_procedures: Petitions for divorce, nullity, judicial separation, restitution of conjugal rights, protection orders, and alimony are presented to the District Court.
The Code of Civil Procedure applies to proceedings under this Act.
Statements in petitions and answers must be verified.
Suits on behalf of lunatics and minors are provided for.
Service of petitions must be carried out as prescribed.
Evidence is taken in accordance with prescribed modes.
Husband and wife are competent witnesses regarding cruelty or desertion.
Courts have powers to close doors, adjourn proceedings, and make orders as to custody of children.
Appeals from orders and decrees lie to higher courts, with an exception for costs.
References to the High Court can be made on questions of law or usage.
administration: High Courts and District Courts administer this Act. The Preamble also suggests the intention to confer jurisdiction upon certain Courts.
important_notes: The Act is primarily applicable to persons professing the Christian religion.
Specific conditions regarding domicile and residence are required for granting decrees of dissolution and nullity.
Certain sections (7, 17A, 20, 34, 35, 39) have been omitted by subsequent amendments.
The Act's application to Jammu and Kashmir has been modified by subsequent notifications.

title: THE OUDH ESTATES ACT, 1869
purpose: To define the rights of Taluqdárs and others in certain estates in Oudh, and to regulate the succession thereto.
scope: This Act applies only to certain estates in Oudh, specifically those held by Taluqdárs and Grantees as defined within the Act.

key_definitions.Transfer: An alienation inter vivos (between living persons).
key_definitions.Will: The legal declaration of the intentions of the testator with respect to his property affected by this Act, which he desires to be carried into effect after his death.
key_definitions.Codicil: An instrument made in relation to a Will, and explaining, altering, or adding to its dispositions; considered as forming an additional part of the Will.
key_definitions.Signed: Applies to the affixing of a mark.
key_definitions.Registered: Registered according to the provisions of the rules relating to the registration of assurances for the time being in force in Oudh.
key_definitions.Minor: Any person who shall not have completed the age of eighteen years, and minority means the status of such person.
key_definitions.Taluqdár: Any person whose name is entered in the first of the lists mentioned in section eight.
key_definitions.Grantee: Any person upon whom the proprietary right in an estate has been conferred by a special grant of the British Government, and whose name is entered in the fifth or sixth of the lists mentioned in section eight.
key_definitions.Estate: The taluqa or immovable property acquired or held by a Taluqdár or Grantee in the manner mentioned in section three, section four, or section five, or the immovable property conferred by a special grant of the British Government upon a Grantee.
key_definitions.Heir: A person who inherits property otherwise than as a widow, under the special provisions of this Act.
key_definitions.Legatee: A person to whom property is bequeathed under the same provisions.
key_definitions.Words expressing relationship: Denote only legitimate relatives, but apply to children in the womb who are afterwards born alive.

main_sections.description: Covers the short title of the Act, its extent, and interpretation clauses.

main_sections.section_title: Rights and liabilities of Taluqdárs and Grantees
main_sections.description: Defines the heritable and transferable rights of Taluqdárs and Grantees in their estates, subject to specific conditions, and outlines the rights and liabilities of persons named in the second schedule and Grantees.
Details the preparation and publication of six lists that identify Taluqdárs and Grantees for the purposes of the Act, and establishes that only persons named in these lists are considered as such.

main_sections.section_title: Powers of Taluqdárs and Grantees to transfer and bequeath
main_sections.description: Grants Taluqdárs and Grantees, and their heirs and legatees, the power to transfer and bequeath their estates, subject to the Act's provisions and government conditions. It also addresses conditions for sound mind, minors, and the voiding of transfers due to fraud or coercion.

Governs the specifics of transfers and bequests to Taluqdárs or heirs, to persons out of the line of succession, and sets requirements for transfers to be in writing, signed, and attested, with further requisites for gifts inter vivos.
Applies sections of the Succession Act to wills of Taluqdárs and addresses bequests to religious and charitable uses.
Defines terms like 'son,' 'descendants,' 'daughter,' 'brother,' and 'widow,' and lays out special and general rules of succession for intestate Taluqdárs and Grantees.

Details provisions for the maintenance of surviving relatives of Taluqdárs and Grantees, including grandparents, parents, widows, brothers, minor sons, nephews, unmarried daughters, and widows of sons and brothers.

Includes provisions for Muhammadan Taluqdárs and Grantees to adopt, alteration of intestate succession rules for specific lists, reverter to ordinary law of succession, saving of creditors' rights, and awards for compensation and maintenance.

important_rules: Taluqdárs to have permanent, heritable, and transferable rights in their estates, subject to conditions in the orders of the Governor General and their sanads (Section 3).
Persons named in the second schedule possess rights and titles similar to those acquired under Section 3, subject to Taluqdár conditions (Section 4).
Grantees have the same rights and are subject to the same conditions as Taluqdárs regarding their grants (Section 5).
Transfers and bequests must adhere to the rule against perpetuity, not delaying vesting beyond a defined period (Section 12).

Gifts or bequests of estates or portions thereof are restricted to persons who would have succeeded intestate or to a younger son (under specific conditions), and require specific execution and registration timelines (Section 13).
Transfers and bequests must be in writing, signed, and attested (Section 16).
Gifts inter vivos have further requisites for validity (Section 17).

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Act does not explicitly detail penalties for violations, but enforcement of its provisions, including the validity of transfers and succession rules, would likely fall under the jurisdiction of the courts and administrative authorities in Oudh.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: The Act relies on judicial notice of its lists (Section 10) and established legal processes for disputes concerning transfers, succession, and maintenance. Publication in the Gazette of India serves as a key enforcement and notification mechanism.

rights: Taluqdárs and Grantees have permanent, heritable, and transferable rights in their estates (Section 3, 5).
Persons named in the second schedule have specific rights in their lands (Section 4).
Taluqdárs and Grantees have the power to transfer and bequeath their estates, subject to conditions (Section 11).
Married women can bequeath property they could alienate during their lifetime (Section 11).
Deaf, dumb, or blind individuals are not incapacitated if they understand their actions; ordinarily insane individuals can transfer/bequeath during lucid intervals (Section 11).
Surviving relatives are entitled to maintenance (Section 24-27).
Creditors' rights are saved (Section 32).
duties: Taluqdárs and Grantees are subject to conditions affecting their estates (Section 3, 4, 5).
Taluqdárs and Grantees must take an inventory of heirlooms they wish to devolve with their estate, signed and deposited with the Deputy Commissioner (Section 7).
Transfers and bequests must be in writing, signed, and attested, with specific requirements for gifts inter vivos and wills (Section 13, 16, 17).
Gifts or bequests to non-heirs or non-younger sons require specific execution, attestation, and registration timelines (Section 13).
obligations: Taluqdárs and Grantees are obligated to comply with the conditions specified in their sanads and the orders of the Governor General of India (Section 3, 5).
Taluqdárs and Grantees must ensure their transfers and bequests do not violate the rule against perpetuity (Section 12).
Specific procedures and timelines must be followed for certain transfers and bequests, including registration (Section 13).

key_procedures: Preparation and publication of six lists identifying Taluqdárs and Grantees (Section 8, 9).
Judicial notice of the lists by courts as conclusive evidence of Taluqdár/Grantee status (Section 10).
Transfer or bequest of estates by Taluqdárs/Grantees requires them to be of sound mind and not a minor, with specific conditions for those with disabilities or intervals of sanity (Section 11).
Procedure for including heirlooms with an estate: inventory, signing, and deposit with the Deputy Commissioner (Section 7).

Procedure for restricted transfers/bequests (to non-heirs or younger sons): execution and attestation not less than three months before death, and registration within one month of execution (Section 13).
administration: The Chief Commissioner of Oudh is responsible for the preparation of the lists (Section 8), and the Governor General of India in Council has oversight and the power to order supplementary lists (Section 9). The administration of estates and adherence to succession and transfer rules would involve the courts and relevant administrative bodies in Oudh.
important_notes: The Act does not bar suits for redemption of mortgages executed on or after February 13, 1844, under specific conditions related to fixed terms for redemption (Section 6).
Muhammadan Taluqdárs and Grantees are empowered to adopt (Section 29).
The Act allows for the reverter to the ordinary law of succession in specific cases (Section 31).
The rights of creditors are saved (Section 32).
The lists prepared under Section 8 are critical for determining who is considered a Taluqdár or Grantee for the purposes of the Act (Section 10).

title: The Pensions’ Act, 1871
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to pensions and grants by Government of money or land-revenue.
scope: In so far as it relates to Union pensions, it extends to the whole of India. In so far as it relates to other pensions, it extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. The Act has state amendments that may restrict or broaden its scope within specific states (e.g., Karnataka).

key_definitions.grant of money or land-revenue: Anything payable on the part of Government in respect of any right, privilege, perquisite or office.
key_definitions.the appropriate Government: In relation to Union pensions, the Central Government, and in relation to other pensions, the State Government.

main_sections.section_title: Short title and Extent of Act
main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act as the 'Pensions’ Act, 1871' and outlines its territorial applicability.
Defines the term 'grant of money or land-revenue'.
Defines 'the appropriate Government' in relation to Union and other pensions.

main_sections.section_title: Bar of suits relating to pensions
main_sections.description: Prohibits Civil Courts from entertaining suits relating to pensions or grants of money or land-revenue conferred by the Government, with certain exceptions.

main_sections.section_title: Claims to be made to Collector, Deputy Commissioner, or other authorized officer
main_sections.description: Specifies that claims relating to pensions or grants should be preferred to the Collector, Deputy Commissioner, or other authorized officer, who shall dispose of them according to prescribed rules.

main_sections.section_title: Civil Court empowered to take cognizance of such claims
main_sections.description: Allows Civil Courts to take cognizance of pension claims upon a certificate from the authorized officer, but prohibits orders or decrees that directly or indirectly affect the Government's liability to pay such pensions or grants.

main_sections.section_title: Pensions for lands held under grants in perpetuity
main_sections.description: Exempts certain types of inams and pensions granted as indemnity for loss from the provisions of sections 4 and 6, making them alienable and recoverable like other property.

main_sections.section_title: Payment to be made by Collector, Deputy Commissioner or other authorized officer
main_sections.description: Mandates that all pensions or grants by the Government be paid by the Collector, Deputy Commissioner, or other authorized officer, subject to prescribed rules.

main_sections.section_title: Saving of rights in respect of the recovery of land-revenue
main_sections.description: Preserves the right of a grantee of land-revenue to recover such revenue from liable persons, notwithstanding sections 4 and 8.
Empowers the appropriate Government to commute the whole or any part of a pension or grant for a lump sum with the consent of the holder.

Exempts pensions granted for political considerations, past services, infirmities, or as compassionate allowances, and money due on account thereof, from attachment by any Court at the instance of a creditor.

main_sections.section_title: Assignments, &c., in anticipation of pension, to be void
main_sections.description: Declares all assignments, agreements, and securities made in anticipation of pension or allowance as null and void.

main_sections.section_title: Nomination by pensioner to receive moneys outstanding on account of pension
main_sections.description: Allows pensioners to nominate a person to receive outstanding pension moneys after their death, with provisions for nominee predeceasing the pensioner.
Entitles informers to a reward equivalent to six months' pension if they prove that a pension is fraudulently or unduly received.

Grants power to the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority (or the appropriate Government in Karnataka) to make rules consistent with the Act regarding payment, inquiries, records, and other matters concerning pensions.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government to make rules
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to make rules regarding nominations under section 12A, including cancellation, variation, and provisions for nominee predeceasing the pensioner.
Requires rules made by the Central Government or Chief Controlling Revenue Authority to be laid before each House of Parliament.

important_rules: Claims relating to pensions or grants must be made to the Collector, Deputy Commissioner, or other authorized officer (Section 5).
Civil Courts can take cognizance of pension claims only upon a certificate from the authorized officer and cannot make orders affecting the Government's liability (Section 6).
Pensions granted for specific reasons (political, past services, infirmities, compassionate allowance) are exempt from attachment by creditors (Section 11).
Assignments or agreements made in anticipation of future pension payments are void (Section 12).
Pensioners can nominate individuals to receive outstanding pension payments after their death (Section 12A).
Fraudulent or undue receipt of pensions can lead to the informer receiving a reward and the recipient potentially forfeiting the pension (Section 13).

penalties: While not explicitly detailed as criminal penalties, Section 13 offers a reward to informers proving fraudulent or undue receipt of pensions, implying potential forfeiture or recovery for the fraudulent recipient.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Appropriate Government (Central or State), Collectors, Deputy Commissioners, or other authorized officers.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the established administrative and judicial channels. Claims are processed by designated officers, and civil courts can be involved under specific conditions. Rules prescribed under the Act further govern enforcement.

rights: Right to claim pensions or grants from the Government.
Right to receive pensions or grants through authorized officers.
Right to have certain pensions (e.g., for lands held under grants in perpetuity) be alienable and descendible.
Right of a grantee of land-revenue to recover revenue from liable persons.
Right of a nominated person to receive outstanding pension moneys after the pensioner's death.
Right to a reward for informing about fraudulent pension claims.
duties: Duty to prefer claims related to pensions or grants to the designated administrative officers.
Duty to abide by rules made under the Act for the payment and management of pensions.
Duty to ensure that assignments or agreements are not made in anticipation of pension.
Duty for the Government to pay pensions or grants as per the Act and prescribed rules.
obligations: Government's obligation to pay pensions and grants appropriately.
Obligation for authorized officers to dispose of pension claims according to rules.
Obligation for pensioners to follow nomination procedures if they wish to designate beneficiaries for outstanding payments.

key_procedures: Claiming a pension or grant: A person with a claim must prefer it to the Collector, Deputy Commissioner, or other authorized officer. The officer disposes of the claim based on rules prescribed by the Chief Revenue Authority, subject to the appropriate Government's control (Section 5).

Civil Court cognizance of claims: A Civil Court can only take cognizance of a claim if it receives a certificate from the authorized officer stating the case can be tried. The court cannot make orders affecting the Government's liability (Section 6).
Commutation of pension: The appropriate Government, with the holder's consent, may order the commutation of a pension or grant for a lump sum (Section 10).

Nomination for outstanding pension moneys: A pensioner can nominate a person to receive unpaid pension moneys after their death. The nomination must be made in the prescribed manner and form (Section 12A).

Reporting fraudulent pensions: An informer proving fraudulent or undue receipt of a pension is entitled to a reward. This implies a procedure for reporting and substantiating such claims to the appropriate Government (Section 13).
administration: Primarily administered by the 'appropriate Government' (Central Government for Union pensions, State Government for other pensions), Collectors, Deputy Commissioners, and other authorized officers. Chief Revenue Authorities and the Central Government are empowered to make rules.
important_notes: The Act has undergone several amendments and extensions to various territories over time.
State Amendments, such as the one for Karnataka, can alter the application or interpretation of sections within that state.
Section 2, concerning repealed enactments, is itself repealed.
Certain historical land grants and specific types of pensions are explicitly exempted from some of the Act's provisions.

title: The Punjab Laws Act, 1872
purpose: To declare which of certain existing rules, laws, and regulations had the force of law in the Punjab, and to amend, consolidate, or repeal others. It also aimed to establish various legal provisions and administrative mechanisms within the Punjab region.
scope: Geographically, it extended to the territories comprising the States of Punjab and Delhi. Subject matter scope covered civil and criminal judicature, descent of Jaghirs, pre-emption, decrees concerning land, insolvency, minors and the Court of Wards, criminal matters, honorary police officers, track law, slaughter of kine, armed men and foreign vagrants, and miscellaneous provisions. However, many sections have been repealed by subsequent acts.

key_definitions.Native law: Refers to the applicable customs of parties concerned, Muhammadan law for Muhammadans, and Hindu law for Hindus, provided these are not contrary to justice, equity, or good conscience, and have not been altered or abolished by legislative enactment or declared void by a competent authority.
key_definitions.Justice, equity and good conscience: A principle guiding decisions in cases not specifically provided for by law or custom, ensuring fair and equitable outcomes.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act as 'The Punjab Laws Act, 1872'.
Defines the territorial extent of the Act to the territories of Punjab and Delhi, and specifies its commencement date as June 1, 1872.
States that the Regulations, Acts, and orders specified in the First Schedule are in force within the Act's territorial jurisdiction.

main_sections.section_title: Decisions in certain cases to be according to Native law.
main_sections.description: Specifies that in matters of succession, special property of females, betrothal, marriage, divorce, dower, adoption, guardianship, minority, bastardy, family relations, wills, legacies, gifts, partitions, or any religious usage or institution, decisions shall be based on applicable custom or relevant religious law (Muhammadan or Hindu), subject to certain conditions.

main_sections.section_title: Decisions in cases not specially provided for.
main_sections.description: Mandates that in cases not specifically covered by other provisions, Judges shall decide according to justice, equity, and good conscience.

main_sections.section_title: Local customs and mercantile usages when valid.
main_sections.description: Declares that local customs and mercantile usages are valid unless they contravene justice, equity, or good conscience, or have been previously declared void by a competent authority.

main_sections.section_title: Indian Penal Code to apply to offences committed previous to 1st January, 1862.
main_sections.description: Makes the Indian Penal Code (except Chapter VI) applicable to offences committed before January 1, 1862, in Punjab territory. It includes a saving clause for privileges of certain Chiefs and pardons.

main_sections.section_title: Power to establish system of village-watchmen and municipal-watchmen, and to make rules.
main_sections.description: Empowers the State Government to establish village and municipal watchmen systems and make rules for their organization, powers, duties, and funding.

main_sections.section_title: Obligation to assist watchmen and headmen.
main_sections.description: Establishes an obligation for all persons to assist watchmen and headmen discharging police duties and allows for the arrest without warrant of those who obstruct them.

main_sections.section_title: Power to direct local taxation for payment of police enrolled under Act 5 of 1861.
main_sections.description: Grants the State Government the power to impose local taxation for the payment of police officers performing watch-and-ward and internal police services in towns or villages not covered by municipalities or village-watchman beats.

main_sections.section_title: Trackers may call for assistance in carrying on tracks.
main_sections.description: Empowers trackers to seek assistance in pursuing tracks.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for withholding assistance or conniving at offence or escape.
main_sections.description: Prescribes penalties for withholding assistance from trackers or conniving at offences or escapes. It also mentions appeal to the High Court and awarding fines to injured parties and fees to trackers.

main_sections.section_title: Control of slaughter of kine and sale of beef.
main_sections.description: Provides for the control of the slaughter of kine (cows) and the sale of beef.

main_sections.section_title: Control of entry into towns of bands of armed men.
main_sections.description: Allows for the control of the entry of bands of armed men into towns.

main_sections.section_title: Powers of Magistrate of district as to foreign vagrants.
main_sections.description: Confers powers on the District Magistrate regarding foreign vagrants.

main_sections.section_title: Power to make rules as to matters mentioned in sections 43 to 48.
main_sections.description: Grants the power to make rules concerning matters detailed in sections 43 to 48.

main_sections.section_title: Conditions of validity of rules hereafter made under this Act.
main_sections.description: Outlines the conditions under which rules made after the enactment of this Act would be valid.

main_sections.section_title: Penalties for breach of such rules.
main_sections.description: Specifies penalties for violating rules made under the Act.

important_rules: Rule 1: Decisions in certain civil cases (succession, marriage, family relations, etc.) must be based on applicable custom or religious law, provided they are not contrary to justice, equity, or good conscience and are not altered or abolished by law. (Section 5)
Rule 2: In cases not specifically provided for, decisions must be made according to justice, equity, and good conscience. (Section 6)
Rule 3: Local customs and mercantile usages are valid unless they contradict justice, equity, or good conscience or have been declared void by a competent authority. (Section 7)
Rule 4: The Indian Penal Code, with exceptions, applies to offences committed before January 1, 1862, in Punjab territory. (Section 39)
Rule 5: State Government can establish village and municipal watchmen systems and make rules for their operation. (Section 39A)
Rule 6: All persons must assist watchmen and headmen in their duties; obstruction can lead to arrest without warrant. (Section 39B)
Rule 7: Local taxation can be imposed for police services in specific areas. (Section 39C)
Rule 8: Trackers can demand assistance in their work, and penalties apply for refusal or connivance. (Section 41, 42)
Rule 9: The slaughter of kine and sale of beef are subject to control. (Section 43)
Rule 10: Entry of armed men into towns can be controlled. (Section 44)
Rule 11: District Magistrates have powers concerning foreign vagrants. (Section 45)
Rule 12: Rules made under sections 43 to 48 will govern specific matters, with conditions for their validity and penalties for breach. (Sections 50, 50A, 50B)

penalties: Penalty for withholding assistance or conniving at offence or escape in track law cases (Section 42).
Penalties for breach of rules made under the Act (Section 50B).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: State Government, District Magistrate, Judges, Police officers, Village-watchmen, Municipal-watchmen, Headmen.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through judicial decisions based on applicable laws and customs, administrative orders, establishment of police and watchmen systems, and imposition of taxes. Enforcement of rules is through prescribed penalties and arrest powers.

rights: Right to decisions based on justice, equity, and good conscience in unprovided cases (Section 6).
Right to have local customs and mercantile usages considered valid if not contrary to justice, equity, or good conscience (Section 7).
Privileges conferred on certain Chiefs are saved (Section 39).
Potential for fines to be awarded to injured parties (Section 42).
duties: Duty to have civil decisions conform to Native law or justice, equity, and good conscience (Sections 5, 6).
Duty to provide assistance to watchmen and headmen (Section 39B).
Duty to comply with rules and regulations made under the Act.
obligations: Obligation to assist village-watchmen, municipal-watchmen, or village-headmen discharging police duties (Section 39B).
Obligation to pay taxes imposed for police services (Sections 39D, 39E, 39F).

key_procedures: Procedure for deciding civil cases based on custom or religious law, or justice, equity, and good conscience (Sections 5, 6).
Procedure for establishing and regulating village and municipal watchmen systems, including making rules for their appointment, discipline, and funding (Section 39A).
Procedure for local taxation for police services, including notice, objections, and determination of rates (Sections 39C, 39D, 39E, 39F).
Procedure for the control of slaughter of kine and sale of beef (Section 43).
Procedure for controlling the entry of armed men into towns (Section 44).
Procedure for the District Magistrate's actions concerning foreign vagrants (Section 45).
Procedure for making and validating rules under sections 43 to 48, and enforcing penalties for breaches (Sections 50, 50A, 50B).
administration: The Act's administration falls under the purview of the State Government. Specific responsibilities are assigned to the District Magistrate and potentially other authorities for implementing various provisions, such as establishing watchmen systems, imposing taxes, and managing certain types of individuals.
important_notes: Numerous sections of the Act have been repealed by subsequent legislation, indicating that much of its original scope is no longer in effect.
The Act explicitly preserves privileges conferred on certain Chiefs and any pardons granted by competent authority (Section 39).
The application of Native law (Section 5) is subject to the condition that it is not contrary to justice, equity, or good conscience and has not been altered or abolished by legislation.
The Act's commencement date is June 1, 1872.
The territorial extent has been amended to reflect subsequent re-organizations of states, specifically mentioning the States of Punjab and Delhi as they were before November 1, 1956.

title: The Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to the solemnization of the marriages of Christians in India.
scope: Applies to the whole of India, with specific exclusions for certain territories. It governs marriages where one or both parties are Christians. The term 'Indian Christians' includes Christian descendants of natives of India converted to Christianity, as well as such converts.

key_definitions.Church of England and Anglican: The Church of England as by law established.
key_definitions.Church of Scotland: The Church of Scotland as by law established.
key_definitions.Church of Rome and Roman Catholic: The Church that regards the Pope of Rome as its spiritual head.
key_definitions.Church: Includes any chapel or other building generally used for public Christian worship.
key_definitions.India: The territories to which this Act extends.
key_definitions.minor: A person who has not completed the age of twenty-one years and who is not a widower or a widow.
key_definitions.Indian Christians: Includes the Christian descendants of natives of India converted to Christianity, as well as such converts.
key_definitions.Registrar General of Births, Deaths and: A Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages appointed under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act, 1886.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act as 'The Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872' and defines its territorial extent.

Defines various terms used in the Act, such as 'Church of England', 'Church of Scotland', 'Church of Rome', 'Church', 'India', 'minor', 'Christians', 'Indian Christians', and 'Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages'.

main_sections.section_title: Marriages to be solemnized according to Act
main_sections.description: States that every marriage between persons, one or both of whom is a Christian, must be solemnized in accordance with the provisions of the Act; any marriage solemnized otherwise is void.

main_sections.section_title: Persons by whom marriages may be solemnized
main_sections.description: Lists the categories of individuals who are authorized to solemnize marriages in India, including episcopal ordained persons, Clergymen of the Church of Scotland, Ministers licensed under the Act, Marriage Registrars, and persons licensed to grant certificates of marriage between Indian Christians.

main_sections.section_title: Grant and revocation of licenses to solemnize marriages
main_sections.description: Empowers the State Government to grant and revoke licenses to Ministers of Religion to solemnize marriages.
Details the appointment of Marriage Registrars by the State Government, the role of a Senior Marriage Registrar, and the circumstances under which a Magistrate acts as a Marriage Registrar.

Specifies that marriages must be solemnized between 6 AM and 7 PM, with exceptions for Clergymen of the Church of England, Church of Rome, and Church of Scotland under specific conditions and licenses.
Outlines the requirement for giving notice of an intended marriage, which includes details about the parties and the solemnizing minister.
Describes the process of solemnizing a marriage after a certificate has been issued.

main_sections.section_title: Notice of intended marriage before Marriage Registrar
main_sections.description: Details the procedure for giving notice of an intended marriage when it is to be solemnized before a Marriage Registrar.

main_sections.section_title: False oath, declaration, notice or certificate for procuring marriage
main_sections.description: Specifies penalties for making false oaths, declarations, notices, or certificates to procure a marriage.

important_rules: Marriages between Christians must be solemnized according to the provisions of this Act, otherwise they are void (Section 4).
Marriages must be solemnized between 6 AM and 7 PM, with specific exceptions for certain clergy under special licenses (Section 10).
Notice of an intended marriage must be given to the relevant minister or Marriage Registrar (Section 12, 38).
A certificate of notice given and declaration made must be issued before a marriage can be solemnized (Section 17, 41).
A marriage must be solemnized within two months of the notice, or a new notice is required (Section 26, 52).
Certain marriages must be registered in duplicate and signed by attesting witnesses (Section 32, 33).

penalties: False oath, declaration, notice, or certificate for procuring marriage (Section 66).
Forbidding the issue of a certificate by false personation (Section 67).
Solemnizing marriage without due authority (Section 68).
Solemnizing marriage out of proper time or without witnesses (Section 69).
Solemnizing marriage with a minor without notice or within fourteen days after notice (Section 70).
Issuing certificate or marrying without proper notice or publication (Section 71, 72, 73).
Issuing a certificate or solemnizing a marriage authorizedly forbidden (Section 71, 73).
Unlicensed person granting a certificate pretending to be licensed (Section 74).
Destroying or falsifying register-books (Section 75).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Enforcement involves the application of penalties for violations. Specific authorities for day-to-day enforcement are implied through the roles of Marriage Registrars, State Governments, and Magistrates.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Enforcement is primarily through legal proceedings initiated upon detection of violations, leading to penalties and the invalidation of marriages solemnized contrary to the Act's provisions.

rights: Right to solemnize marriage if a person falls under the categories listed in Section 5.
Right to obtain a certificate of notice for marriage, subject to meeting the Act's requirements.
Right to have a marriage registered.
Right to access marriage registers for searches and copies of entries.
Right to petition the High Court to order the issue of a certificate in certain circumstances (e.g., less than fourteen days notice, or if consent is refused).
duties: Duty to solemnize marriages in accordance with the Act.
Duty to give notice of an intended marriage.
Duty to register marriages solemnized.
Duty to maintain register-books accurately.
Duty of Marriage Registrars to file notices and enter copies in the Marriage Notice Book.
Duty of Marriage Registrars to ascertain that notices and declarations are understood by Indian Christians.
Duty of Clergy to solemnize marriages according to their church's rites and ceremonies.
Duty to comply with the time and place restrictions for solemnizing marriages, unless exceptions apply.
obligations: Obligation to ensure that a marriage is not solemnized unless the prescribed notices have been given and certificates issued.
Obligation to obtain consent of father or guardian if a party is a minor.
Obligation to adhere to the age requirements for marriage (minimum age of 21 for a 'minor' to marry).
Obligation to register marriages and forward certificates to the Registrar General.
Obligation to avoid solemnizing marriages if a valid prohibition notice has been issued.

key_procedures: Giving notice of an intended marriage, publication of the notice, and issuance of a certificate of notice (Sections 12-17, 38-41).
Obtaining consent for marriage when a party is a minor, or petitioning the court if consent is withheld or the person is insane (Sections 19, 44, 45).
Solemnization of marriage after the certificate is issued (Sections 25, 51).
Registration of marriages, including quarterly or monthly returns to the Registrar General (Sections 27-37, 54-55).
Procedures for petitioning the High Court in cases of refusal of certificate, protest against issue of certificate, or when a Marriage Registrar doubts authority (Sections 43, 46, 48).
Procedures for obtaining a license to solemnize marriages (Section 6).
administration: State Governments are responsible for granting licenses, appointing Marriage Registrars, and other administrative aspects as per the Act. The Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages oversees the registration aspect.
important_notes: The Act does not apply to marriages within prohibited degrees (Section 88).
Consular marriages are saved (Section 87).
The Act's provisions regarding marriage registration do not apply to Roman Catholics (Section 65).
The State Government has the power to prescribe fees (Section 82) and make rules (Section 83).

title: The Married Women's Property Act, 1874
purpose: To explain and amend the law relating to certain married women, specifically for the enjoyment of wages and earnings by women married before January 1, 1866, and for insurances on lives by married persons.
scope: Extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir (as of the provided text, though a later note indicates applicability to Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh). It does not apply to married women professing Hindu, Muhammadan, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jain religions, or whose husbands profess these religions at the time of marriage. State Governments can exempt specific races, sects, or tribes. The Act also has specific applicability dates for insurance provisions related to different religious groups and territories.

main_sections.description: Names the Act as the Married Women's Property Act, 1874.
Specifies the territorial extent of the Act and outlines exemptions based on religion and potential exemptions by State Government orders for specific groups.
This section was repealed.

main_sections.section_title: Married women’s earnings to be their separate property
main_sections.description: Declares that wages and earnings of a married woman, acquired after the Act's passing through her employment, occupation, or trade, and any property acquired through literary, artistic, or scientific skill, along with savings and investments thereof, shall be her separate property.

main_sections.section_title: Married woman may effect policy of insurance
main_sections.description: Allows a married woman to effect a policy of insurance on her own behalf, independently of her husband. Such policies, if expressed on their face to be so effected, will ensure as her separate property and be as valid as if made with an unmarried woman.

main_sections.section_title: Insurance by husband for benefit of wife
main_sections.description: Establishes that a policy of insurance effected by a married man on his own life for the benefit of his wife or wife and children shall be a trust for them and not subject to the husband's control or creditors, nor part of his estate, as long as the trust object remains. It specifies payment to the Official Trustee in absence of special trustees and notes that this provision applies under certain conditions to Hindus, Muhammadans, Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists based on territory and date of policy effect. It also states it does not affect the rights of creditors if the policy was intended to defraud them.

main_sections.section_title: Married woman may take legal proceedings
main_sections.description: Grants married women the right to sue in their own name for the recovery of property that is their separate property under the Indian Succession Act, 1865, or this Act. They have the same civil and criminal remedies as if unmarried for the protection and security of such property and are liable to suits, processes, and orders concerning it as if unmarried.

States that if a married woman possesses separate property, any person contracting with her concerning such property or on the faith that her obligations will be satisfied from it, can sue her. Recovery is limited to the extent of her separate property, as if she were unmarried at the time of contract and decree execution. Exclusions include property transferred on condition of no power to transfer or charge, and the husband's liability for debts contracted through his wife's agency.

main_sections.section_title: Husband not liable for wife’s antenuptial debts
main_sections.description: Releases husbands, married after December 31, 1865, from liability for their wife's pre-marriage debts solely by reason of the marriage. The wife remains liable to the extent of her separate property. Proviso notes this doesn't invalidate contracts a husband made before the Act in consideration of his wife's antenuptial debts.

main_sections.section_title: Extent of husband’s liability for wife’s breach of trust or devastation
main_sections.description: States that a husband is not liable for his wife's breach of trust, misapplication, loss, or damage to an estate as a trustee, executrix, or administratrix, unless he actively participates in the trust or administration.

important_rules: Married women's wages and earnings acquired after the Act's passing are their separate property.
Married women can effect insurance policies on their own lives, which become their separate property if expressed as such.
Life insurance policies taken by a husband for his wife's or children's benefit are considered a trust and protected from the husband and his creditors.
Married women can sue and be sued in their own name for their separate property, with the same rights and liabilities as if unmarried.
A wife's separate property is liable for her postnuptial debts contracted with reference to that property.
Husbands are not liable for their wife's antenuptial debts, but the wife is liable to the extent of her separate property.
Husbands are generally not liable for their wife's breaches of trust or devastations as a trustee unless they participate in the actions.
