penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Implied to be civil and criminal courts for legal proceedings and enforcement of contracts and trusts.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through legal proceedings (civil and criminal), attachment and sale of separate property for debts, and by Official Trustees for insurance benefits.

rights: Right to own and control wages and earnings as separate property.
Right to effect life insurance policies for their own benefit.
Right to sue and be sued in their own name for their separate property.
Right to have life insurance benefits protected from husband and creditors.
Right to recover debts from wife's separate property if contracted with reference to it.
duties: Duty to satisfy debts from separate property if contracted with reference to it.
Duty to act as trustee/executrix/administratrix responsibly.
obligations: Obligation to repay antenuptial debts from separate property.
Obligation to fulfill contracts made with reference to separate property.
Obligation to avoid fraudulent intent when effecting life insurance policies.

key_procedures: A married woman may sue in her own name for recovery of her separate property.
A person can sue a married woman for debts contracted with reference to her separate property, to the extent of that property.
Insurance policies for the benefit of wife/children are managed by the Official Trustee if no special trustees are appointed.
A husband's liability for wife's breach of trust is limited to instances where he actively participates.
administration: The administration appears to be handled through the general legal and judicial system of India, with State Governments having powers to issue orders regarding exemptions, and Official Trustees managing insurance benefits.
important_notes: The Act does not apply to women professing Hindu, Muhammadan, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jain religions, or whose husbands profess these religions at the time of marriage.
State Governments have the authority to exempt specific races, sects, or tribes from the Act's provisions.
The application of Section 6 (insurance by husband) has specific temporal and geographical conditions tied to different religious groups and territories.
Nothing in the Act affects a creditor's right to be paid from insurance proceeds if the policy was effected with intent to defraud creditors.
The Act's provisions on insurance by husbands for the benefit of wives and children have specific commencement dates and applicability based on the religion of the policyholder and the territory.

title: The Majority Act, 1875
purpose: To specify the age of majority for persons domiciled in India and amend the law respecting the age of majority.
scope: This Act extends to the whole of India, except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It applies to persons domiciled in India.

main_sections.section_title: Short title. Local extent. Commencement and operation.
main_sections.description: This section provides the short title of the Act as the Majority Act, 1875. It defines the local extent of the Act, stating it extends to the whole of India except Jammu and Kashmir. It also specifies that the Act comes into force and has effect only after the expiration of three months from its passing.

This section outlines the exceptions to the Act. It states that the Act does not affect the capacity of any persons in matters of marriage, dower, divorce, and adoption. It also does not affect the religion or religious rites and usages of any class of citizens of India, nor does it affect the capacity of any person who had already attained majority under the applicable law before this Act came into force.

main_sections.section_title: Age of majority of persons domiciled in India.
main_sections.description: This section stipulates that every person domiciled in India shall attain the age of majority on completing eighteen years of age and not before. It also specifies that in computing the age, the day of birth is included as a whole day, and majority is attained at the beginning of the eighteenth anniversary of that day.

important_rules: Rule 1: A person domiciled in India attains the age of majority upon completing eighteen years of age.
Rule 2: The day of birth is to be included as a whole day in computing the age of majority.
Rule 3: Majority is deemed to be attained at the beginning of the eighteenth anniversary of the day of birth.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Not explicitly mentioned in the provided text.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Not explicitly mentioned in the provided text.

administration: Not explicitly mentioned in the provided text.
important_notes: The Act was extended to Dadra and Nagar Haveli and the Union territory of Lakshadweep.
The Act was extended to Pondicherry with a modification that it shall not apply to the Renoncants of the Union territory of Pondicherry.
The original wording of Section 1, concerning local extent, and Section 3 and 4 were substituted by later amendments.

title: The Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876
purpose: To limit the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts throughout the Bombay Presidency in matters relating to the Land-revenue, and for other purposes.
scope: Applies to all territories now within the State of Maharashtra, with specific exclusions for lands in the City of Bombay regarding assessment and collection of revenue. Also excludes certain provisions of other Bombay Acts and a Central Act. Certain sections have a delayed commencement.

key_definitions.Land: Includes village, town, and city sites, trees, growing crops and grass, fruit and juice in trees, rights-of-way, ferries, fisheries, and all other benefits arising from land, as well as things attached to or permanently fastened to things attached to the earth.
key_definitions.Land-revenue: All sums and payments, in money or kind, received or claimable by the Government from any person on account of any land held under the provisions of any law.
key_definitions.Revenue officer: Any officer employed in or about the business of the land-revenue, or of surveys, assessment, accounts, or records connected therewith.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act. Specifies the commencement date for different parts of the Act, with some sections coming into force on a date directed by the Governor General in Council. Defines the territorial extent of the Act and its specific exclusions.
Defines key terms used in the Act, including 'Land', 'Land-revenue', and 'Revenue officer'.

Lists various categories of claims and suits that Civil Courts are barred from exercising jurisdiction over. These include claims relating to hereditary and village officers' property or duties, objections to land-revenue assessment, claims arising from land-revenue realization, claims to be entered or have entries made/amended in revenue records, matters of land distribution/allotment on partition, claims for exemption from land-revenue or to receive payments charged on land-revenue, and claims regarding boundaries fixed under specific Acts.

Outlines exceptions to Section 4, allowing Civil Courts to entertain certain suits. These include suits against the Government to contest claimed/paid land-revenue amounts, suits between private parties to establish private rights affected by revenue records, suits between superior holders/occupants and inferior holders/tenants regarding dues, and suits for possession of whole survey numbers or recognized shares of survey numbers (excluding suits against the Government). It also includes provisions for certain districts listed in the Second Schedule regarding pre-1876 jurisdiction over specific claims against the Government.

main_sections.section_title: Bar of certain suits against Revenue officers
main_sections.description: States that Revenue officers are not liable to be sued for damages in Civil Courts for acts bona fide done or ordered to be done in pursuance of law. It also provides protection to Collectors from damages for actions taken against absconding Revenue officers or their sureties for public money, papers, or property.

main_sections.section_title: Punishment or prosecution of Revenue officers not a bar to civil remedies
main_sections.description: Clarifies that departmental punishment or criminal prosecution of a Revenue officer for an offence or breach of duty does not prevent civil remedies against such an officer.

main_sections.section_title: Suits not to be entertained unless plaintiff has exhausted right of appeal
main_sections.description: Prohibits Civil Courts from entertaining suits unless the plaintiff has exhausted their right of appeal.

main_sections.section_title: Power of State Government to refer questions for decision of High Court
main_sections.description: Empowers the State Government to refer questions of law or jurisdiction to the High Court for its decision.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Civil Judge to refer questions of jurisdiction to High Court
main_sections.description: Allows a Civil Judge to refer questions of jurisdiction to the High Court for decision.

main_sections.section_title: Privileges of Government in suits in which it is concerned
main_sections.description: Grants certain privileges to the Government in suits in which it is involved.

important_rules: No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over claims against the Government relating to hereditary/village officers' property or duties, or claims to perform such duties, or in respect of exclusion from such office/service, or to set aside orders passed by the State Government or authorized officers concerning these matters.
No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over claims against Government relating to lands held under treaty, saranjam, or other political tenure, or lands declared to be held for service.

No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over objections to the amount or incidence of land-revenue assessment authorized by the State Government, or to the mode or principle of assessment, or to the validity of survey/settlement notifications.

No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over claims connected with land-revenue realization or assistance provided by the State Government or officers to superior holders for recovery of dues from inferior holders/tenants.
No Civil Court shall entertain claims to set aside sales for arrears of land-revenue on grounds of irregularity, mistake, or any other ground except fraud.

No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over claims against Government to be entered in revenue survey/settlement records or village papers as liable for land-revenue or as superior holder, inferior holder, occupant, or tenant, or to have any entry made, omitted, or amended in such records.
No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over the distribution of land or allotment of land-revenue on partition of an estate.

No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over claims against Government to hold land free from land-revenue, or to receive payments charged on land-revenue, or to set aside cesses/rates authorized by the State Government, or respecting the occupation of vacant land belonging to the Government.

No Civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over claims regarding boundaries fixed under specific Acts or to set aside orders passed by competent officers with regard to boundary-marks, unless specific exemptions apply.
Suits to contest the amount claimed, paid under protest, or recovered as land-revenue, on the ground of excess, prior satisfaction, or incorrect liability, are permissible.
Suits between private parties for establishing private rights, even if affected by revenue records, are permissible.
Suits between superior holders/occupants and inferior holders/tenants regarding dues are permissible.
Suits for possession of land being a whole survey number or a recognized share of a survey number (other than against the Government) are permissible.
Revenue officers are protected from civil suits for damages for bona fide acts done or ordered in pursuance of law.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The text implies enforcement through the Civil Courts, Revenue officers, and the State Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Jurisdiction is limited for Civil Courts in matters concerning land-revenue. Enforcement of the Act's provisions would occur through the stipulated procedures and by the authorities involved in revenue administration and civil justice.

rights: Right to seek relief in Civil Court for over-assessment if an exemption not before existing is expressly created by enactment.

Right to have claims to hold land exempt from land-revenue recognized if such exemption is expressly confirmed by enactment on the ground of being shown in a public record or having existed for a specified term.
Right to establish private rights through suits between private parties, even if affected by revenue records.
Right to pursue possession of land being a whole survey number or a recognized share of a survey number (excluding against the Government).
duties: Revenue officers have a duty to act bona fide in pursuance of the provisions of any law.
Revenue officers have a duty to be available when called upon by their official superiors.
Individuals may have a duty to pay land-revenue as assessed.
obligations: Obligation to exhaust rights of appeal before filing a suit in certain cases.
Obligation for superior holders or occupants to potentially recover dues from inferior holders or tenants, with Civil Courts entertaining disputes between them.

key_procedures: Referral of questions of law or jurisdiction by the State Government or a Civil Judge to the High Court for decision.
Civil Courts entertaining suits to contest land-revenue amounts paid under protest or recovered, if the amount is in excess, previously satisfied, or wrongly claimed.
Civil Courts entertaining suits between private parties to establish private rights affected by revenue records.
Civil Courts entertaining suits between superior holders/occupants and inferior holders/tenants regarding dues.
Civil Courts entertaining suits for possession of whole survey numbers or recognized shares of survey numbers (excluding against the Government).
administration: Implied to be administered by the Revenue and Civil authorities of the Bombay Presidency (now State of Maharashtra).
important_notes: The Act significantly limits the jurisdiction of Civil Courts in matters relating to land-revenue, aiming to streamline and centralize such disputes.
Specific exemptions and saving clauses are crucial for understanding when Civil Courts can still entertain suits.
The Act contains numerous references to other Bombay Acts and Regulations, indicating its place within a broader legal framework governing land revenue.
The Act was subject to amendments and repeals over time, as indicated by bracketed notes and repealing act references.
Section 2, 8, 9, 10, 15, and the Schedule have been repealed.

title: The Oudh Laws Act, 1876
purpose: To declare and amend the laws to be administered in Oudh.
scope: Applies to Oudh. Governs various aspects of law including land revenue, personal law, pre-emption, court procedures, and village/road police.

key_definitions.pre-emption: A right of certain persons to acquire immovable property in preference to all other persons in specified cases.

main_sections.description: Defines the short title as 'The Oudh Laws Act, 1876', states its local extent is Oudh, and that it commenced on the day of its passing.

main_sections.section_title: Statutory law to be administered in Oudh
main_sections.description: Outlines the hierarchy of laws to be administered by the Courts of Oudh, including land-revenue laws, personal laws (Muhammadan and Hindu law, subject to custom), rules within the Act, published rules, scheduled regulations and Acts, other applicable enactments, and finally, principles of justice, equity, and good conscience.

main_sections.section_title: Muhammadan dower contracts how to be enforced Rule applicable after husband's death
main_sections.description: Specifies that for Muhammadan dower contracts, if the stipulated amount is excessive relative to the husband's means, the court will award a reasonable amount based on the husband's means and wife's status. This rule applies whether the suit is brought during the husband's lifetime or after his death.
Defines the right of pre-emption as the right of specified persons to acquire immovable property in preference to others in certain circumstances.

States that the right of pre-emption is presumed to exist in all village communities and extends to the village site, houses, lands within the village boundary, and transferable rights affecting such lands, unless a custom or contract to the contrary is proven. It also applies to cases referred to in section 40 of the Oudh Land-revenue Act, 1876.

main_sections.section_title: Its existence in towns to be proved
main_sections.description: Declares that the right of pre-emption is not presumed in towns or cities, but its existence and exercise must be proven according to local custom.

main_sections.section_title: Devolution of right when property to be sold or foreclosed is a proprietary or under proprietary tenure
main_sections.description: Specifies the order of entitlement to the right of pre-emption for proprietary or under-proprietary tenures: first, co-sharers of the sub-division; second, co-sharers of the whole mahal; third, any member of the village community; and fourth, the proprietor (if it's an under-proprietary tenure). If multiple individuals are equally entitled, the right is determined by lot.

Requires a person proposing to sell property or foreclose a mortgage to give notice to pre-emptors of the price or amount due. The notice must be given through the Court and can be affixed to a public place in the village or city.
States that a person with a right of pre-emption loses that right if they do not pay or tender the specified price within three months of receiving the notice.

main_sections.section_title: Suit to enforce right of pre-emption
main_sections.description: Outlines the grounds on which a suit to enforce the right of pre-emption can be brought, including lack of due notice, refusal of tender, bad faith in price fixing for sales, or bad faith and overvaluation in claims for mortgages.

States that Judicial Commissioner's Circular No. 104 of July, 1860, is considered a notification under Section 24 of Act 14 of 1859, and that Act is deemed to have been in force in Oudh from July 4, 1862. Orders and decrees passed under the Circular or the Act are considered valid.

Refers to specific acts that are punishable and states that a penalty will be applied. (Details of specific acts and penalties are not fully described in the provided text snippet but are indicated as being covered).
Specifies that a penalty will be imposed for any breach of the rules made under the Act.

important_rules: Rule: In cases regarding succession, property of females, marriage, divorce, dower, adoption, guardianship, minority, etc., the rule of decision is: (1) any applicable custom not contrary to justice, equity, or good conscience; (2) Muhammadan law for Muhammadans and Hindu law for Hindus, as modified by custom or enactment; (3) rules in this Act; (4) published rules; (5) scheduled Regulations and Acts; (6) other applicable enactments; and (7) in cases not covered, act according to justice, equity, and good conscience.
Rule: Local customs and mercantile usages are valid unless contrary to justice, equity, or good conscience, or declared void by a competent authority.

Rule: For Muhammadan dower contracts, if the stipulated amount is excessive, the court will award a reasonable amount based on the husband's means and wife's status, applicable even after the husband's death.
Rule: The right of pre-emption is presumed to exist in village communities but must be proven in towns.
Rule: A suit for pre-emption cannot be filed for only a portion of the property sold or foreclosed, unless the plaintiff's right of pre-emption is only for that portion.

Rule: Notice to pre-emptors must be given through the Court and can be affixed publicly. Failure to pay or tender the price within three months of notice results in the loss of the right of pre-emption.
Rule: In foreclosure cases, the pre-emptor can acquire the property by paying the amount specified in the notice within three months of notice, along with interest and costs.

Rule: If the Court finds in favor of the plaintiff in a pre-emption suit, the decree will fix a date for payment. Non-payment by this date voids the decree and the plaintiff loses the right of pre-emption.
Rule: Judicial Commissioner's Circular No. 104 of July, 1860, is considered a notification under Section 24 of Act 14 of 1859, which is deemed in force in Oudh from July 4, 1862.

penalties: Penalty for certain acts specified in Section 37.
Penalty for breach of rules made under the Act (Section 42).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Courts of Oudh, Government (for appointments and rules).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through legal proceedings (suits), court decrees, and adherence to prescribed procedures. The Government has powers for appointment and rule-making.

rights: Right of pre-emption.
Right to nominate village-policemen (Section 29).
duties: Obligation to nominate village-policemen (Section 30).
Duties of village and road-policemen (Section 34).
obligations: Pay or tender the price to exercise the right of pre-emption.
Pay interest and costs when acquiring property through pre-emption on foreclosure.

key_procedures: Procedure for enforcing Muhammadan dower contracts, ensuring reasonableness with respect to husband's means and wife's status.
Procedure for exercising the right of pre-emption: receiving notice, paying/tendering the price within three months, or bringing a suit within specified grounds.
Procedure for foreclosure cases involving pre-emption: notice, payment/tender within three months, and subsequent payment of interest and costs.
Procedure for suits to enforce the right of pre-emption, including grounds for the suit and court's role in fixing fair market value if necessary.
Procedure for appointing village-policemen: nomination, discretion to appoint or reject, and power of Government to appoint if nominees are rejected.
Procedure on arrest by village or road-policeman (details not fully provided in snippet).
administration: The Act is administered by the Courts of Oudh. The Government has powers related to rules and appointments (e.g., village police, rule publication).
important_notes: Certain sections (2, 17, 18, 21, 23, 24, 25, 28, 43, 45) have been repealed.
The provisions of Section 3 have been repealed in so far as they are inconsistent with the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937.
The local extent was originally 'the territories for the time being administered by the Chief Commissioner of' Oudh, which has been updated.
References to the Oudh Land-revenue Act, 1876, should now be read as referring to the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901.

title: The Broach and Kaira Incumbered Estates Act, 1877
purpose: To relieve from incumbrances the estates of Thakurs in Broach and Kaira by providing for their relief through management and liquidation of their debts and liabilities.
scope: Applies to Thakurs, taluqdars, Jagirdars, and kasbatis, and other classes of estate holders declared as Thakurs by the Local Government, in the districts of Broach and Kaira. The act governs their immoveable property and related debts and liabilities.

key_definitions.Thakur: Means also taluqdar, Jagirdar and kasbati, and such other classes of holders of estates as the Local Government may, with the previous sanction of the Governor General in Council, declare to be Thakurs for the purposes of this Act.
key_definitions.Heir: Means the person for the time being entitled as heir to a Thakur.
key_definitions.Commissioner: Means the Revenue Commissioner of the Northern Division of the Presidency of Bombay.

main_sections.description: Establishes the short title of the Act as 'The Broach and Kaira Incumbered Estates Act, 1877' and states that it comes into force on the date of its passing.
Repeals Act No. XV of 1871, but specifies that all applications, appointments, rules, notices, and other actions duly done under the repealed Act shall be deemed to have been done under this Act.
Provides definitions for 'Thakur', 'Heir', and 'Commissioner' as used within the Act.

Allows a Thakur, or their sole heir, to apply to the Commissioner for the Act's provisions to be applied to their case if they are subject to debts or liabilities, or if their immoveable property is charged with debts or liabilities (excluding those due to Government). It also outlines provisions for minors or individuals of unsound mind.

Mandates the Commissioner to direct an inquiry into the nature and amount of debts/liabilities and the sufficiency of the debtor's property when an application is made by or on behalf of a Thakur or their sole heir. For other cases, it is at the Commissioner's discretion.

Requires the applicant to submit a verified statement detailing debts, liabilities, and property sufficiency to the appointed inquiry officer. It also includes a provision regarding false averments, deeming them as intentionally giving false evidence.

main_sections.section_title: Report of enquiry and proceedings thereon
main_sections.description: The inquiry officer submits a report to the Commissioner, who can then direct further inquiry, dismiss the application, or publish an order for management and liquidation of debts by a manager. The Taluqdari Settlement-officer is designated as the manager unless otherwise directed.

main_sections.section_title: Order of management to what it extends
main_sections.description: Defines the scope of the 'order of management', including all immoveable property of the debtor, debts and liabilities they are subject to, and property acquired or devolving during management. It also states that management commences from the date of publication.

Details the consequences of the order of management, including the stay of pending proceedings, bar of fresh proceedings, and the debtor's incompetence to contract debts, encumber/alienate property, or grant receipts for rent. It also bars any person other than the manager from dealing with the property.

main_sections.section_title: Manager to have powers of owner and to receive rents and profits
main_sections.description: Grants the manager all the powers of the owner to recover rents and profits, and additional powers of a Collector for recovery. However, the manager cannot demise the property for a term exceeding two years before the liquidation scheme is sanctioned.

Outlines how the manager should disburse collected funds: costs of management and repairs, government revenue and debts, rent to superior holders, maintenance allowance for the debtor and family, cost of improvements, and the residue for debt liquidation.

Requires the manager to publish a notice in the Bombay Government Gazette calling upon claimants to notify their claims within six months. Copies of the notice are also to be exhibited at local offices.
Specifies that claims must include full particulars and all supporting documents. It also gives the manager the power to refuse documents not produced with the claim.

main_sections.section_title: Claim not duly notified to be barred
main_sections.description: States that claims not notified within the specified time and manner are barred, except as provided in section 19(d). It allows for admission of claims within a further six months if the claimant proves inability to comply with the original notice.
The manager is to inquire into and determine the amount of debts and liabilities justly due to claimants, in accordance with rules made under the Act.

important_rules: All claims against the debtor or property (except Government claims) not notified within the specified time and manner are barred, with a provision for late claims under specific circumstances (Section 14).
The manager is empowered to recover rents and profits with the powers of a Collector and has the powers of the owner of the property under management (Section 10).

The manager must pay costs of management, repairs, government revenue, rent to superior holders, maintenance for the debtor and family, and costs of improvements from the collected funds (Section 11).
The residue of collected funds is to be retained by the manager for the liquidation of debts and liabilities (Section 11).

penalties: Intentionally giving false evidence in a verified statement is punishable under the Indian Penal Code (Section 6).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Commissioner, Manager (Taluqdari Settlement-officer unless otherwise directed).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through orders published in the Bombay Government Gazette, inquiries, management of property, liquidation of debts, and by exercising powers of a Collector for rent recovery.

rights: Thakurs (or their heirs) have the right to apply for the benefit of the Act if encumbered (Section 4).
Claimants have the right to present their claims with full particulars and supporting documents (Section 13).
The debtor and family have a right to a periodical maintenance allowance fixed by the Commissioner (Section 11).
duties: Applicants must submit verified statements detailing debts, liabilities, and property sufficiency (Section 6).
Claimants must notify their claims within the prescribed time and manner, and provide all supporting documents (Sections 12, 13).
obligations: The debtor is obligated to be incompetent to contract debts, encumber or alienate property, or grant receipts for rent during the management period (Section 9).
The manager is obligated to manage the property, recover rents and profits, pay specified expenses, and liquidate debts (Sections 10, 11).

key_procedures: Application for benefit of the Act by a Thakur or heir to the Commissioner (Section 4).
Commissioner orders an inquiry into debts and property sufficiency (Section 5).
Submission of a verified statement by the applicant (Section 6).
Inquiry officer submits a report to the Commissioner (Section 7).
Commissioner may order management and liquidation of debts by a manager (Section 7).
Manager publishes notice to claimants and collects claims with particulars and documents (Sections 12, 13).
Manager determines debts and liabilities (Section 15).
Development and submission of a scheme for liquidation (Sections 17, 18).
administration: Commissioner (Revenue Commissioner of the Northern Division, Presidency of Bombay) and the Manager (Taluqdari Settlement-officer by default).
important_notes: Debts due or liabilities incurred to Government are excluded from the application process and liquidation scheme under this Act (Section 4, Section 11).

The provisions of the Act can be applied to Thakurs, taluqdars, Jagirdars, and kasbatis, and other classes of holders if declared as such by the Local Government with the sanction of the Governor General in Council (Section 3).

title: The Indian Treasure-Trove Act, 1878
purpose: To amend the law relating to treasure-trove.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. (Subject to State Amendments and extensions to certain Union Territories and specific districts).

key_definitions.treasure: Anything of any value hidden in the soil, or in anything affixed thereto.
key_definitions.Collector: Any Revenue officer in independent charge of a district, and any officer appointed by the State Government to perform the functions of a Collector under this Act.
key_definitions.Owner: When any person is entitled, under any reservation in an instrument of transfer of any land or thing affixed thereto, to treasure in such land or thing, he shall, for the purposes of this Act, be deemed to be the owner of such land or thing.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act and its territorial extent.
Defines 'treasure', 'Collector', and 'owner'.

Mandates that the finder of treasure exceeding ten rupees in value must give written notice to the Collector about its nature, value, location, and date of finding, and either deposit it or provide security.
Requires the Collector to publish a notification for potential claimants to appear and also serve a special notice on the person in possession of the place where the treasure was found.

main_sections.section_title: Matters to be enquired into and determined by the Collector.
main_sections.description: Outlines that the Collector shall enquire into and determine who found the treasure, where, under what circumstances, and who hid it and under what circumstances.

main_sections.section_title: When treasure may be declared ownerless. Appeal against such declaration.
main_sections.description: Allows the Collector to declare treasure ownerless if no belief of recent hiding exists, no suit is filed, or a claim is rejected. Provides for an appeal against such a declaration.

main_sections.section_title: When no other person claims as owner of place, treasure to be given to finder.
main_sections.description: States that if no one else claims as owner of the place, the treasure is delivered to the finder after a declaration.

main_sections.section_title: When only one such person claims and his claim is not disputed, treasure to be divided, and shares to be delivered to parties.
main_sections.description: Details the division of treasure between the finder and the sole claimant owner of the place, outlining a three-fourths share for the finder unless an agreement exists or the Collector opts for alternative distribution methods.

main_sections.section_title: Power to acquire the treasure on behalf of Government.
main_sections.description: Grants the Government the power to acquire the treasure by paying the entitled persons a sum equal to its value plus one-fifth of that value.

main_sections.section_title: Decision of Collector final, and no suit to lie against him for acts done bona fide.
main_sections.description: States that the Collector's decisions and bona fide acts are final and not subject to challenge in Civil Courts.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty on finder failing to give notice, etc.
main_sections.description: Specifies the penalty for a finder failing to give notice or failing to produce the treasure.

important_rules: Rule 1: If treasure exceeding ten rupees is found, the finder must give written notice to the Collector within a reasonable time, specifying the nature, value, location, and date of the find. The finder must also either deposit the treasure or provide security to produce it when required.
Rule 2: The Collector shall publish a notification and may serve a special notice on the owner of the land, requiring any claimants to appear within four to six months.
Rule 3: Any person failing to appear as required forfeits their right to the treasure.
Rule 4: If the treasure was likely hidden within 100 years by a claimant or their predecessor, the Collector shall adjourn the hearing to allow a Civil Court suit to be filed.
Rule 5: If no claim is established or no suit is filed, the Collector may declare the treasure ownerless, with a right of appeal.
Rule 6: Upon declaration of ownerless treasure, it is either given to the finder or divided between the finder and the owner of the place.
Rule 7: If no one else claims as owner of the place, the treasure goes to the finder.

Rule 8: If only one person claims as owner of the place and the claim is undisputed, the treasure is divided: three-fourths to the finder and the rest to the owner, unless an agreement exists or the Collector makes alternative arrangements.
Rule 9: If there are disputes regarding the ownership of the place, the Collector shall stay proceedings and the matter must be settled by a Civil Court.

penalties: Penalty on finder failing to give notice or produce treasure.
Penalty on owner abetting an offense under section 20.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector (and Civil Courts for disputes)
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through enquiry, notification, declaration of ownership, division of treasure, potential acquisition by the government, and imposition of penalties. Collectors are empowered to exercise powers of a Civil Court for enquiries.

rights: Right of the finder to a share of the treasure (potentially up to three-fourths).
Right of the owner of the place to a share of the treasure (potentially up to one-fourth).
Right to appeal against the Collector's declaration of ownerless treasure.
Right to institute a Civil Court suit to establish ownership of the place where treasure was found.
Right to claim compensation if the Government acquires the treasure.
duties: Duty of the finder to give notice to the Collector.
Duty of the finder to produce the treasure or give security.
Duty of claimants to appear as required by the Collector's notification.
Duty of the finder and owner of the place to settle disputes if they arise.
Duty of the Collector to conduct enquiries and make determinations.
Duty to make payments or deposits as ordered by the Collector.
obligations: Obligation to report found treasure exceeding ten rupees.
Obligation to abide by the Collector's decisions and orders (subject to appeal).
Obligation to institute suits in Civil Court when disputes arise over ownership of the place.
Obligation to comply with rules made by the State Government.

key_procedures: Procedure 1: Finder discovers treasure > 10 rupees, provides written notice to Collector (nature, value, location, date), deposits treasure or provides security. Collector issues notification requiring claimants to appear within 4-6 months and may serve notice on the landowner. If no claim or suit is filed, Collector may declare treasure ownerless (appealable). If no owner of place claims, treasure goes to finder. If one owner claims and claim is undisputed, treasure divided (finder 3/4, owner 1/4, or as per agreement). If multiple owners claim or claim is disputed, Collector stays proceedings for Civil Court determination. Government has power to acquire treasure.

Procedure 2: Collector conducts enquiries to determine the circumstances of finding and hiding. If treasure is believed to be hidden within 100 years by a claimant, Collector adjourns to allow for a Civil Court suit. If suit filed and claim established, treasure is divided. If no suit or claim rejected, treasure goes to the finder. Government can acquire treasure by paying its value plus one-fifth.

Procedure 3: Making rules: State Government may make rules to regulate proceedings, which have the force of law upon publication in the Official Gazette. Rules are to be laid before the State Legislature.
administration: Collector (revenue officers appointed by the State Government). State Government also has the power to make rules.
important_notes: The Act has been extended to and brought into force in various Union Territories and specific areas through regulations and notifications.
The Act has been subject to amendments and repeal in specific districts or applications (e.g., Bellary District).
The Collector's decisions and bona fide acts are final and cannot be questioned in Civil Courts.
Collectors are empowered to exercise the powers of a Civil Court for the trial of suits during their enquiries.

title: THE DEKKHAN AGRICULTURISTS’ RELIEF ACT, 1879
purpose: To relieve indebted agriculturists in certain parts of the Dekkhan from indebtedness.

scope.geographical: Sections 11, 56, 60 and 62 extend to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. The rest of the Act extends only to the districts of Poona, Satara, Sholapur and Ahmednagar, but may be extended by the State Government to other districts in the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in the State of Bombay, or parts thereof.

main_sections.description: This section provides the short title of the Act as 'The Dekkhan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879', specifies its commencement date as November 1, 1879, and outlines the territorial extent of various sections.

main_sections.section_title: Agriculturists to be sued where they reside.
main_sections.description: This section stipulates that suits related to recovery of money lent, advanced, paid for, or price of goods sold, or on written/unwritten engagements for payment of money, where the defendant is an agriculturist, must be instituted and tried in the court within whose jurisdiction the defendant resides. If there are multiple agriculturist defendants, the suit can be filed where any one of them resides. This provision does not affect sections 22 to 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

main_sections.section_title: Instruments executed by agriculturist not to be deemed valid unless executed before a Village-registrar.
main_sections.description: Instruments executed by an agriculturist are not considered valid unless they are executed before a Village-registrar.

main_sections.section_title: Registration under this Act to be deemed equivalent to registration under Indian Registration Act, 1877.
main_sections.description: Registration of documents under this Act is considered equivalent to registration under the Indian Registration Act, 1877.

main_sections.section_title: Exemption of instruments to which the Government or any officer of the Government is a party.
main_sections.description: Instruments to which the Government or any of its officers are a party are exempt from the provisions of this Act.

important_rules: Rule: Instruments executed by an agriculturist must be registered before a Village-registrar to be deemed valid.
Rule: Registration of instruments under this Act is equivalent to registration under the Indian Registration Act, 1877.
Rule: Suits against agriculturists for recovery of debts must be filed in the court of their residence.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Not explicitly stated in the provided text, but implied to be the relevant courts and registration authorities.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through court proceedings for debt recovery and registration processes for instruments.

rights: Right of agriculturists to have suits filed in their local jurisdiction.
Right to have instruments executed by them deemed valid if registered before a Village-registrar.
duties: Duty of agriculturists to get their executed instruments registered before a Village-registrar for validity.
Duty of creditors to file suits against agriculturists in their place of residence.
obligations: Obligation to comply with registration requirements for instruments executed by agriculturists.
Obligation to adhere to jurisdictional rules for suits involving agriculturists.

key_procedures: Procedure: Filing a suit against an agriculturist: The suit must be instituted and tried in a Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the agriculturist defendant resides.
Procedure: Validity of instruments executed by agriculturists: Such instruments are only deemed valid if executed before a Village-registrar.
administration: The Act's administration would typically involve judicial courts and registration offices, with the State Government having powers to extend its application.
important_notes: Numerous sections of the Act have been repealed, particularly by the Bombay Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1947. The provided text focuses on the remaining operative sections.
The local extent of the Act is varied, with some sections having wider application than others.

title: THE CENTRAL PROVINCES LAND-REVENUE ACT, 1881
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to Land-revenue and the powers of Revenue-officers in the Central Provinces.
scope: Applies to all territories for the time being under the administration of the Chief Commissioner of the Central Provinces, except those specified in Part VI of the first schedule of the Scheduled Districts Act 1874. Covers matters related to land revenue, survey, settlement, and the powers and procedures of revenue officers.

key_definitions.Legal practitioner: Means an advocate, vakil or attorney of any High Court, a pleader, mukhtar or revenue-agent.
key_definitions.Village-cess: Means any cess which a person resident or holding lands in a village pays or renders to the proprietors as such of the village, and includes service rendered or things furnished as well as money paid.
key_definitions.Recognized agent: Means a person authorized in writing by any party to a proceeding under this Act to make appearances and applications and to do other acts on his behalf in such proceeding and also belonging to any class which the Chief Commissioner may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, declare in this behalf.
key_definitions.Agricultural year: Not fully defined in the provided text, but relates to the annual cycle of agricultural activities.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its geographical extent of application (Central Provinces excluding certain scheduled districts), and the provision for its commencement by notification.
States that existing enactments relating to settlement and collection of land-revenue in the territories covered by this Act will be repealed upon its commencement.
Defines various terms used in the Act, such as Assistant Commissioner, Legal practitioner, Village-cess, Recognized agent, and Agricultural year.
Identifies the Chief Controlling Revenue-authority.
Enumerates the categories of Revenue-officers.
Details the process and effect of notifying a revenue-survey.

main_sections.section_title: Settlement-officer to invite claims to lands appearing to have no owner
main_sections.description: Describes the procedure for inviting claims to lands that appear unowned during settlement operations.

main_sections.section_title: Separate sum to be assessed on every mahal
main_sections.description: Mandates that a separate sum shall be assessed on every mahal, with provisions for progressive assessments.
Defines the Record-of-rights and its purpose.
Defines 'Arrear' and 'Defaulters' in the context of land revenue collection.
Establishes the exclusive jurisdiction of Revenue-authorities and lists matters excepted from the jurisdiction of Civil Courts.

important_rules: Progressive assessments are permitted (Section 46).
When settlement is made with a superior proprietor, a sub-settlement is to be made with inferior proprietors (Section 50).
Revenue payable under a sub-settlement is a first charge on the land (Section 65).
Entries in the record-of-rights have a specific legal effect (Section 82).
The Chief Commissioner can regulate the payment of land-revenue (Section 90).
Interest is chargeable on arrears of revenue (Section 119).

penalties: Penalty for injuring boundary-marks (Section 134).
Punishment for violation of a rule or custom enforced by Government (Section 123).
Fine for neglect to give notice of possession (Section 127).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Revenue-officers, including Commissioners, Deputy Commissioners, Tahsildars, and Settlement-officers, under the overall direction of the Chief Commissioner.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through various procedures including assessment of revenue, collection processes, attachment and sale of property, imprisonment of defaulters, revision and review of orders, and enforcement of village rules and customs.

rights: Right to invite claims to unowned lands (Section 40).
Option to accept or refuse assessment (Section 54).
Occupancy-rights in sir-land for excluded proprietors (Section 62).
Right of pre-emption at sales of immoveable property (Section 110).
Right to mines and quarries (Section 151).
Right to inspect revenue-records (Section 131).
duties: Duty to attend in person or through a recognized agent before Revenue-officers (Section 20).
Duty to aid in the preparation of village-papers (Section 128).
Duty to notify possession of proprietary rights (Section 126).
obligations: Obligation to pay land revenue.
Obligation to provide for remuneration of mukaddams (in Sambalpur) (Section 150).

key_procedures: Procedure for survey and settlement operations, including notification, appointment of officers, demarcation, assessment, and preparation of the record-of-rights.
Procedures for the collection of land revenue, including notice of demand, processes for recovery, arrest, imprisonment, and sale of property (movable and immovable).
Procedures for appeals, revision, and review of orders passed by Revenue-officers.
Procedure for dealing with unowned lands and excluded lands during settlement.
Procedure for the partition of a mahal.
Procedure for the enforcement of village rules and customs.
administration: The Chief Commissioner of the Central Provinces, with the Governor General in Council having ultimate authority.
important_notes: The Act repeals previous enactments related to land revenue settlement and collection.
Pending proceedings are deemed to have commenced under this Act.
Legal practitioner's fees are generally not allowed unless for special reasons.
Certain matters are specifically excluded from the jurisdiction of Civil Courts.

title: THE INDIAN TRUSTS ACT, 1882
purpose: To define and amend the law relating to private trusts and trustees.
scope: Extends to the whole of India and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The Central Government may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend it to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands or to any part thereof.  It does not affect rules of Muhammadan law as to waqf, mutual relations of members of an undivided family, public or private religious or charitable endowments, or trusts to distribute prizes taken in war. Chapter II does not apply to trusts created before March 1, 1882.

key_definitions.trust: An obligation annexed to the ownership of property, arising out of a confidence reposed in and accepted by the owner, or declared and accepted by him, for the benefit of another, or of another and the owner.
key_definitions.author of the trust: The person who reposes or declares the confidence.
key_definitions.trustee: The person who accepts the confidence.
key_definitions.beneficiary: The person for whose benefit the confidence is accepted.
key_definitions.beneficial interest: The beneficiary's right against the trustee as owner of the trust-property.
key_definitions.instrument of trust: The instrument, if any, by which the trust is declared.
key_definitions.breach of trust: A breach of any duty imposed on a trustee, as such, by any law for the time being in force.
key_definitions.registered: Registered under the law for the registration of documents for the time being in force.
key_definitions.notice: A person has notice of a fact when he actually knows it, or when, but for wilful abstention from inquiry or gross negligence, he would have known it, or when information of the fact is given to or obtained by his agent under specific circumstances.

main_sections.section_title: Short title, Commencement, Local extent, Savings
main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its commencement date (March 1, 1882), its local extent, and important savings and exclusions from its provisions.
Repeals the Statute and Acts mentioned in the Schedule to the extent specified.

Defines key terms such as 'trust', 'author of the trust', 'trustee', 'beneficiary', 'trust-property', 'beneficial interest', 'instrument of trust', 'breach of trust', 'registered', and 'notice'. It also refers to definitions in the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
States that a trust may be created for any lawful purpose. It defines what constitutes an unlawful purpose and the consequences of creating a trust for an unlawful purpose.

main_sections.section_title: Trust of immoveable property. Trust of moveable property.
main_sections.description: Specifies the conditions for the validity of trusts related to immoveable property (must be declared by a non-testamentary instrument in writing, signed, and registered, or by will) and moveable property (declared as above, or ownership transferred to the trustee). Exceptions apply to prevent fraud.

Outlines the requirements for creating a trust, including indication of intention, purpose, beneficiary, trust-property, and transfer of property to the trustee (unless the author is the trustee or it's a will).

States that trusts can be created by persons competent to contract, and by or on behalf of a minor with the permission of a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction, subject to laws regarding disposal of trust property.
Defines the subject-matter of a trust as transferable property, excluding a merely beneficial interest under a subsisting trust.

main_sections.section_title: Who may be beneficiary. Disclaimer by beneficiary.
main_sections.description: States that any person capable of holding property can be a beneficiary. It also details how a beneficiary can renounce their interest.

main_sections.section_title: Who may be trustee. No one bound to accept trust. Acceptance of trust. Disclaimer of trust.
main_sections.description: Specifies who can be a trustee, who is not bound to accept a trust, and how acceptance and disclaimer of a trust occur.
Mandates that a trustee must execute the trust as nearly as possible in accordance with the author's intention.
Requires a trustee to exercise the same care in managing trust property as a prudent man would exercise in managing his own affairs.
Provides guidelines and restrictions on how trustees can invest trust money.
Outlines the liability of a trustee for losses caused by a breach of trust.
Provides for the indemnity of trustees against certain liabilities.
Grants trustees the right to hold the title deeds of trust property.
Confers general authority on trustees to perform acts necessary for the execution of the trust, subject to the instrument of trust and the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Power to sell in lots, and either by public auction or private contract
main_sections.description: Grants trustees the power to sell trust property in lots or as a whole, by public auction or private contract.
Prohibits trustees from delegating their powers except in specific circumstances.

main_sections.section_title: Trustee may not charge for services
main_sections.description: Generally prohibits trustees from charging for their services, unless specifically provided for.

main_sections.section_title: Trustee may not use trust-property for his own profit
main_sections.description: Prohibits trustees from using trust property for their personal gain.
Grants beneficiaries the right to receive rents and profits from the trust property.

main_sections.section_title: Right to inspect and take copies of instrument of trust, accounts, etc.
main_sections.description: Entitles beneficiaries to inspect and take copies of trust documents and accounts.

main_sections.section_title: Right to sue for execution of trust
main_sections.description: Allows beneficiaries to sue for the execution of the trust.
Grants beneficiaries the right to have proper persons appointed as trustees.
Enables beneficiaries to follow trust property into the hands of third persons and into that into which it has been converted.
Details the various ways in which the office of a trustee can be vacated.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment of new trustees on death, etc.
main_sections.description: Provides for the appointment of new trustees in case of death, discharge, or removal of existing trustees.
Describes the various ways in which a trust can be extinguished.

main_sections.section_title: Where obligation in nature of trust is created
main_sections.description: Deals with situations where an obligation in the nature of a trust is created, which are not express trusts but arise from certain circumstances.

important_rules: A trustee must execute the trust as nearly as possible in accordance with the author's intention (Section 11).
A trustee must inform himself of the state of the trust-property (Section 12).
A trustee must protect the title to the trust-property (Section 13).
A trustee must not set up a title adverse to the beneficiary (Section 14).
A trustee must exercise the same care in managing trust property as a prudent person would exercise in managing their own affairs (Section 15).
A trustee must be impartial in administering the trust (Section 17).
A trustee must prevent waste of trust property (Section 18).
A trustee must keep clear and accurate accounts and provide information to beneficiaries (Section 19).
Trustees are generally prohibited from delegating their powers (Section 47).
Trustees are generally prohibited from charging for their services (Section 50).
Trustees are prohibited from using trust property for their own profit (Section 51).

penalties: Liability for breach of trust leading to loss (Section 23).
Potential forfeiture of beneficiary's interest to the Government in certain cases (Section 29).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Courts of law. Specific provisions may involve the Civil Court for certain approvals (e.g., minor creating trusts).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through legal proceedings initiated by beneficiaries or other interested parties to compel the trustee to act, account for property, or remedy breaches of trust. Courts can also appoint new trustees and make orders for the administration of the trust.

rights: Beneficiary's right to rents and profits (Section 55).
Beneficiary's right to specific execution of the trust (Section 56).
Beneficiary's right to transfer of possession (Section 56).
Beneficiary's right to inspect and take copies of trust documents and accounts (Section 57).
Beneficiary's right to transfer their beneficial interest (Section 58).
Beneficiary's right to sue for execution of the trust (Section 59).
Beneficiary's right to proper trustees (Section 60).
Trustee's right to title-deeds (Section 31).
Trustee's right to reimbursement of expenses (Section 32).
Trustee's right to apply to Court for opinion in management of trust-property (Section 34).
Trustee's right to settlement of accounts (Section 35).
duties: Trustee's duty to execute the trust (Section 11).
Trustee's duty to inform himself of the state of trust-property (Section 12).
Trustee's duty to protect the title to trust-property (Section 13).
Trustee's duty to be impartial (Section 17).
Trustee's duty to prevent waste (Section 18).
Trustee's duty to keep accounts and provide information (Section 19).
Beneficiary's duty not to join in a breach of trust (Section 68).
obligations: Obligation of a trustee to act in accordance with the trust deed and law.
Obligations in the nature of trusts that arise from certain relationships or transactions (Chapter IX).

key_procedures: Creation of a trust: Requires indication of intention, purpose, beneficiary, trust-property, and transfer of property (Section 6).
Declaration of trusts of immoveable property: Must be by a written instrument signed and registered, or by will (Section 5).
Disclaimers by beneficiary or trustee: Specific procedures for renouncing interests or trusts (Sections 9, 10).
Application to Court for opinion: Trustees can seek court guidance on trust management (Section 34).
Appointment of new trustees: Procedures for filling vacancies in the office of trustee, including by Court appointment (Sections 73, 74).
Extinguishment of trusts: Various methods by which a trust can cease to exist (Section 77).
administration: The Act does not explicitly name a single administering department or agency. Rather, its administration is through the civil courts and the legal framework governing trusts and trustees in India.
important_notes: The Act is a law relating to PRIVATE trusts and trustees.
It clarifies that certain religious, charitable, and customary endowments are outside its scope.
The Act incorporates definitions and principles from the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

title: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882
purpose: To define and amend certain parts of the law relating to the transfer of property by act of parties.
scope: Initially extended to the whole of India except Part B States, Bombay, Punjab, and Delhi. State governments have the power to extend it to other territories and exempt certain areas from specific provisions. It covers both moveable and immoveable property transfers by act of parties.

key_definitions.immoveable property: Does not include standing timber, growing crops or grass.
key_definitions.attested: In relation to an instrument, means and shall be deemed always to have meant attested by two or more witnesses each of whom has seen the executant sign or affix his mark to the instrument, or has seen some other person sign the instrument in the presence and by the direction of the executant, or has received from the executant personal acknowledgement of the execution of the instrument.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, the date it comes into force, and its territorial extent. It also outlines provisions for extending the Act to other territories and for exemptions.

main_sections.section_title: Repeal of Acts. Saving of certain enactments, incidents, rights, liabilities, etc.
main_sections.description: Specifies the enactments repealed by this Act and provides savings for existing laws, contracts, rights, and liabilities that are not inconsistent with the Act, as well as transfers by operation of law or court decrees.
Defines key terms used in the Act, such as 'immoveable property' and 'instrument', and provides rules for their interpretation.

Defines what constitutes a 'transfer of property', which is an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more living persons, or to himself, or to himself and one or more other living persons.

main_sections.section_title: “Sale” defined. Sale how made. Contract for sale.
main_sections.description: Defines 'sale' as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price. It details how sale is made for immoveable property (by registered deed for value over Rs. 100, or by delivery of possession for value under Rs. 100) and for moveable property.

Defines various terms related to mortgages, including simple mortgage, mortgage by conditional sale, usufructuary mortgage, English mortgage, mortgage by deposit of title-deeds, and anomalous mortgage.

main_sections.section_title: Lease defined. Lessor, lessee, premium and rent defined.
main_sections.description: Defines 'lease' as a transfer of the right to enjoy an immoveable property for a certain time, expressed or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specific occasions to the transferor.

important_rules: Rule 1: Property can be transferred by any person competent to transfer. (Section 7)
Rule 2: Transfer for the benefit of unborn persons is permissible under certain conditions, primarily related to the rule against perpetuity. (Section 13 & 14)

Rule 3: An ostensible owner (one who is not the real owner but appears to be so) can transfer property if the real owner has by conduct led others to believe the ostensible owner is the real owner, and the transferee has acted in good faith and paid valuable consideration. (Section 41)
Rule 4: A transfer of property pending a suit relating thereto is not void but is subject to the rights of the other parties to the suit. (Section 52)

Rule 5: A sale of immoveable property for a value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or a reversion or other interest in immoveable property, can only be made through a registered instrument. (Section 54)

rights: Right of mortgagor to redeem the property. (Section 60)
Right to enforce a mortgage (foreclosure or sale) for the mortgagee. (Section 67)
Rights and liabilities of buyer and seller in a sale of immoveable property. (Section 55)
Rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee. (Section 108)
duties: Duty of seller to disclose material defects of the property. (Section 55)
Duty of buyer to pay the price. (Section 55)
obligations: Obligation of a person transferring property to the extent of their own interest therein. (Section 8)
Obligation of a mortgagor to transfer to a third party instead of re-transferring to the mortgagor, under certain conditions. (Section 60A)
Obligation of a transferor to pay or deliver to the transferee the instrument of title, or to enable the transferee to obtain possession. (Section 55)

key_procedures: Procedure for sale of immoveable property: For property valued at Rs. 100 or upwards, it must be made by a registered instrument. For property valued under Rs. 100, it can be made by delivery of possession. (Section 54)

Procedure for mortgage: Mortgages of immoveable property other than the mortgage by deposit of title-deeds can only be effected by a registered instrument signed by the mortgagor and attested by at least two witnesses. (Section 59)
administration: The Act itself does not specify a single administering department. Enforcement and interpretation are handled by the judiciary and relevant government bodies responsible for property registration and land records.
important_notes: The Act is subject to repeal and amendment by other legislation. (Section 2)
Certain provisions of the Act, particularly those relating to sale, registration, and leases, may be exempted for specific territories by State Governments. (Section 1)
The Act does not affect the provisions of any enactment not expressly repealed. (Section 2)
The Act does not affect any right or liability arising out of a legal relation constituted before the Act came into force. (Section 2)
The Act does not affect transfers by operation of law or by, or in execution of, a decree or order of a competent court, except as provided by Section 57 and Chapter IV. (Section 2)
Certain provisions of Chapter II are not deemed to affect any rule of Muhammadan law. (Section 2)

title: THE INDIAN EASEMENTS ACT, 1882
purpose: To define and amend the law relating to Easements and Licenses.
scope: The Act extends to the territories administered by the Governor of Madras in Council and the Chief Commissioners of the Central Provinces and Coorg. It has been extended to various other regions and states through amendments and notifications. It applies to immovable property and rights associated with it, including easements and licenses.

key_definitions.easement: A right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own.
key_definitions.dominant_heritage: The land for the beneficial enjoyment of which the right exists.
key_definitions.dominant_owner: The owner or occupier of the dominant heritage.
key_definitions.servient_heritage: The land on which the liability (easement) is imposed.
key_definitions.servient_owner: The owner or occupier of the servient heritage.
key_definitions.license: A right to do or continue to do something in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land which would, but for the existence of such right, be unlawful, but is not in effect an easement or a right in rem.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its geographical extent (originally Central Provinces and Coorg, with state amendments extending it further), and the date it came into force (July 1, 1882).

Specifies that the Act does not affect existing laws not expressly repealed, nor does it derogate from the Government's rights to regulate water resources, customary or other rights in immovable property not tied to other properties, or rights acquired before the Act's commencement.

Defines what constitutes an easement, including the concepts of dominant and servient heritages and their owners. It also clarifies that 'land' includes things permanently attached to the earth and 'beneficial enjoyment' includes convenience and advantage.

main_sections.section_title: Continuous and discontinuous, apparent and non-apparent, easements
main_sections.description: Classifies easements into continuous or discontinuous (based on whether enjoyment requires human intervention) and apparent or non-apparent (based on visible signs of existence).
States that an easement can be imposed by any person who has the power to transfer their interest in the servient heritage.

main_sections.section_title: Easements of necessity and quasi easements
main_sections.description: Deals with the creation of easements that are necessary for the enjoyment of property or arise from the circumstances of a previous quasi-easement.
Outlines the conditions under which easements can be acquired by long and uninterrupted use (prescription).
Establishes the right of a dominant owner to enjoy their easement without disturbance.
Defines what a license is in the context of the Act.

important_rules: An easement is a right attached to one land (dominant heritage) for the beneficial enjoyment of which the owner can do or prevent something on another's land (servient heritage).
Easements can be permanent or for a limited time, or subject to conditions.
Easements are restrictions of the exclusive right to enjoy property or the right to natural advantages arising from its situation.
An easement can be imposed by the owner of the servient heritage, with certain limitations for lessors, mortgagors, and lessees.
Easements can be acquired through grant, prescription, or necessity.
The transfer of the dominant heritage usually transfers the easement with it.
The exercise of an easement can be confined to specific times, places, or purposes.
The servient owner is generally not bound to do anything to preserve or maintain the easement, but may be liable for damage from lack of repair.
Easements can be extinguished by various means, including dissolution of rights, release, revocation, expiration of time, termination of necessity, unity of ownership, or non-enjoyment.
A license is a right to do something that would otherwise be unlawful, but is not an easement.

rights: Right to beneficial enjoyment of land through an easement.
Right to enjoy natural advantages arising from land's situation without disturbance.
Right to acquire easements through grant, prescription, or necessity.
Right to enjoy an easement without disturbance.
Right to seek injunction or abatement for disturbance of an easement.
Licensee's rights on revocation or eviction (as defined in Chapter VI).
duties: Duty of the servient owner to allow the exercise of the easement.
Grantor's duty to disclose defects in property when granting a license.
Grantor's duty not to render property unsafe when granting a license.
obligations: Obligation of the dominant owner to bear expenses necessary for the preservation of the easement.
Obligation of the dominant owner to compensate for damage from want of repair of the easement.

key_procedures: Acquisition of easements by prescription: Continuous and uninterrupted use for a specified period (typically 20 years) without interruption and under conditions prescribed by the Act.
Suit for disturbance of an easement: Legal action to seek remedy for the obstruction or interference with an easement.
Injunction to restrain disturbance: Obtaining a court order to prevent further disturbance of an easement.
Abatement of obstruction of an easement: Taking steps to remove an obstruction to an easement, subject to legal limitations.
administration: While not explicitly stated, the administration and enforcement of easements and licenses would generally fall under civil courts and relevant land revenue authorities or departments responsible for property law.
important_notes: The Act does not affect existing laws not expressly repealed.
The Act does not affect the Government's rights regarding regulation of water resources.
Customary rights and rights acquired before the Act's commencement are generally saved.
State amendments may alter the local extent of the Act.
References to certain sections of the Indian Limitation Act, 1877, are to be read as references to corresponding sections of this Act in the territories where it applies.

title: The Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to loans of money by the Government for agricultural improvements.
scope: Applies to the whole of India except the territories which, immediately before the 1st November, 1956, were comprised in Part B States. It comes into force upon appointment by the State Government via notification. Specific state amendments indicate extension to various regions and modifications in application.

key_definitions.Collector: The Collector of land-revenue of a district, or the Deputy Commissioner, or any officer empowered by the State Government by name or by virtue of his office to discharge the functions of a Collector under this Act.
key_definitions.Improvement: Any work which adds to the letting value of land. This includes construction of wells, tanks, works for water storage/supply/distribution for agriculture, preparation of land for irrigation, drainage, reclamation, protection from water damage, permanent improvement of land for agricultural purposes, renewal/reconstruction/alterations/additions to these works, and other works declared as improvements by the State Government.

main_sections.description: Establishes the short title of the Act as the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883. Defines its local extent and the procedure for its commencement, which is subject to State Government notification. Also includes state amendments regarding its extension to specific areas.

Repeals the Land Improvement Act, 1871, and Act XXI of 1876, except for the recovery of advances made before this Act comes into force. It also stipulates that references to the repealed Acts in other legislation shall be read as referring to this Act.
Provides the definition of 'Collector' for the purposes of this Act.

main_sections.section_title: Purposes for which loans may be granted under this Act.
main_sections.description: Outlines that loans may be granted for making any 'improvement' to any person having a right to make that improvement, or with their consent, to another person. Defines what constitutes an 'improvement'.

main_sections.section_title: Mode of dealing with applications for loans.
main_sections.description: Describes the process for handling loan applications, including the option for public notice of applications and consideration of objections. If an objection raises a question requiring Civil Court decision, proceedings are postponed.

Specifies that loans are repayable by instalments within a period fixed by rules, ordinarily not exceeding thirty-five years. The period should consider the durability of the work and the beneficiaries.

Details the modes of recovery for loans, interest, and costs. These include recovery as arrears of land-revenue from the borrower, their surety, or from the land for which the loan was granted. Recovery from collateral security is also provided. It also outlines procedures for sureties and owners of collateral security to recover amounts paid on behalf of the borrower.

main_sections.section_title: Order granting loan conclusive on certain points.
main_sections.description: States that a written order granting a loan is conclusive evidence that the described work is an improvement, the person had the right to make it, and it benefits the specified land.

main_sections.section_title: Liability of joint borrowers as among themselves.
main_sections.description: Addresses the liability of joint borrowers, stipulating that a statement entered on the loan order, showing the portion each borrower is bound to contribute among themselves, is conclusive evidence of their respective liabilities.

Empowers the State Government to make rules for various matters, including application procedures, loan-granting officers, inquiries, security, interest rates, loan disbursement, inspection of works, repayment schedules, accounts, and other working aspects of the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Exemption of improvements from assessment to land revenue.
main_sections.description: Provides that the increase in value derived from improvements made with loan aid will not be considered in revising land revenue assessment, with exceptions for wasteland reclamation and irrigation of unirrigated land after a specified period. It also clarifies that this does not allow questioning existing land revenue assessments.

main_sections.section_title: Certain powers of State Government to be exercisable by Board of Revenue or Financial Commissioner.
main_sections.description: Allows for certain powers of the State Government (related to sections 4(1), 5(1), and 10) to be exercised by the Board of Revenue or Financial Commissioner in states where they exist, subject to State Government control on rules made by these bodies.

important_rules: Loans may be granted for 'improvements' as defined by the Act.
Repayment of loans must occur within a period not ordinarily exceeding thirty-five years.
Loans, interest, and costs are recoverable as arrears of land-revenue from the borrower, surety, or the land itself.
The increase in land value due to improvements is generally exempt from land revenue assessment.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector (or empowered officer), and State Government (for making rules).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Recovery as arrears of land-revenue, and through adherence to rules made under the Act.

rights: Right to apply for loans for agricultural improvements.
Right to have loan orders considered conclusive on specified points.
Right to not have increased value from improvements assessed for land revenue (with exceptions).
duties: Duty to repay loans with interest and costs as per the Act.
Duty to comply with rules made under the Act.
Duty to ensure that improvements are for the benefit of agricultural purposes.
obligations: Obligation to provide security for the loan.
Obligation for joint borrowers to contribute their share as specified.
Obligation to adhere to the repayment schedule.

key_procedures: Application for a loan is made to an empowered officer.
The officer may publish a public notice to invite objections.
Objections are considered, and a decision is made in writing.
If an objection requires Civil Court intervention, proceedings are postponed.
Loan repayment is scheduled by instalments over a period, typically not exceeding 35 years.
Loan recovery is managed by the Collector through land revenue recovery mechanisms.
The State Government makes rules governing applications, loan granting, recovery, and other aspects.
administration: State Government (and delegated authorities like Collectors, Board of Revenue, Financial Commissioner).
important_notes: The Act has undergone several state amendments and extensions to various territories.
Instruments related to loans (executed by borrowers or sureties) are exempted from stamp duty under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
