main_sections.description: Clarifies how orders of a Court or Judge are to be interpreted in the context of investigations under certain sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure, specifying a minimum rank for the ordering officer.

important_rules: Rule 1: Certified copies of entries in a banker's book are prima facie evidence in legal proceedings.
Rule 2: Bank officers cannot be compelled to produce books or testify in legal proceedings where the bank is not a party, unless a court order for special cause is issued.
Rule 3: Courts or Judges can order the inspection of bankers' books or require certified copies to be produced for use in legal proceedings.
Rule 4: Specific conditions and certifications are required for printouts of electronic data from bank records to be admissible as evidence.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Courts and Judges in legal proceedings.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through court orders for production of evidence, inspection, and the admissibility of certified copies. Orders regarding costs can be enforced as if the bank were a party to the proceeding.

rights: Right of parties in a legal proceeding to apply for inspection and copies of entries in bankers' books.
Right of banks to show cause against orders for inspection or production of books.
duties: Duty of banks to maintain ordinary account books.
Duty of banks to provide certified copies of entries when ordered by a Court or Judge.
obligations: Obligation of banks to comply with court orders regarding inspection and production of books, subject to the provisions of the Act.
Obligation to ensure accuracy and integrity of data when using electronic storage and printouts.

key_procedures: Procedure 1: To use an entry from a banker's book as evidence, a certified copy must be obtained.
Procedure 2: In a legal proceeding, a party can apply to the Court or Judge for an order to inspect and take copies of entries from a banker's book, or for the bank to produce certified copies.
Procedure 3: When using printouts of electronic data, specific certificates regarding system integrity, safeguards, and data accuracy must accompany the printout.
administration: Not explicitly stated, but generally falls under the judicial system and relevant government departments responsible for evidence and banking regulations.
important_notes: The Act has been extended to the Union territory of Lakshadweep and Pondicherry.
The Act applies to Development Banks as if they were banks.
Provisions regarding electronic data storage and printouts have been updated with amendments.
In investigations by police officers, orders are to be construed as coming from an officer of a specified rank not lower than Superintendent of Police.

title: THE BENGAL MILITARY POLICE ACT, 1892
purpose: To make provision for the better regulation of the Bengal Reserve Police.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of the territories subject to the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal. It applies to persons appointed to the Bengal Police Force under section 7 of Act V of 1861 who sign the statement in the schedule to this Act, thus becoming 'Military Police-officers'. It also covers disciplinary and other powers of Commandants and Seconds-in-Command with respect to other Police-officers not designated as Military Police-officers.

key_definitions.Military Police-officer: A person appointed to the Bengal Police Force under section 7 of Act V of 1861, who has signed the statement in the schedule to this act, in accordance with the provisions of this Act.
key_definitions.active service: Service against hostile tribes or other persons in the field.
key_definitions.District Magistrate: Includes a Deputy Commissioner, an Assistant Commissioner in charge of a sub-division, and the Superintendent of the South Lushai Hill.
key_definitions.Commandant: A person appointed by the Local Government to be a Commandant of Military Police and includes a District Superintendent of Police and an Assistant District Superintendent of Police in charge of the civil police of a district or of a sub-division.
key_definitions.Second-in-Command: A person appointed by the Local Government to be a Second-in-Command of Military Police, and includes an Assistant District Superintendent of Police not in charge of the civil police of a district or of a sub-division.
key_definitions.reason to believe: Has the meaning assigned in the Indian Penal Code (XV of 1860).
key_definitions.criminal force: Has the meaning assigned in the Indian Penal Code (XV of 1860).
key_definitions.assault: Has the meaning assigned in the Indian Penal Code (XV of 1860).
key_definitions.fraudulently: Has the meaning assigned in the Indian Penal Code (XV of 1860).
key_definitions.voluntarily causing hurt: Has the meaning assigned in the Indian Penal Code (XV of 1860).

main_sections.description: Specifies the name of the Act (The Bengal Military Police Act, 1892), its geographical extent (whole of the territories subject to the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal), and the date it comes into force (as appointed by the Local Government via notification in the Calcutta Gazette).

Provides definitions for key terms used in the Act, including 'Military Police-officer', 'active service', 'District Magistrate', 'Commandant', 'Second-in-Command', and references definitions from the Indian Penal Code for 'reason to believe', 'criminal force', 'assault', 'fraudulently', and 'voluntarily causing hurt'.

main_sections.section_title: Enrolment and discharge of Military Police-officers.
main_sections.description: Outlines the process for appointing officers to the Bengal Police Force as Military Police-officers, requiring them to sign a statement in the schedule after it's read and explained in the presence of a Magistrate, Commandant, or Second-in-Command. It also states that discharge is subject to the terms of this signed statement, overriding general discharge provisions in Act V of 1861.

main_sections.section_title: Classes and grades of Military Police-officers.
main_sections.description: Lists the classes and grades of Military Police-officers (subadars-major, subadars, jamadars, havildars-major, havildars, naiks, buglers, and sepoys) and defines 'superior officer' in relation to any Police-officer.

Details serious offences committed by Military Police-officers, such as mutiny, sedition, assaulting a superior officer, desertion, sleeping on post while on active service, plundering, and spreading false alarms. It specifies punishments including transportation for life or for a term of not less than seven years, imprisonment up to fourteen years, and/or fines.

Describes less severe offences, including intoxication on duty, striking a sentry, negligent release of prisoners, insubordination, ill-treating subordinate officers, injuring equipment, malingering, and desertion when not on active service. Punishments include imprisonment up to one year, fines, or both.

Empowers certain officers (District Magistrate, Commandant, Second-in-Command, or officers of subadar rank commanding detachments) to award minor punishments without a formal trial for petty offences against discipline. These include imprisonment up to seven days with pay forfeiture, and punishment drill, extra guard, or fatigue duty up to thirty days, with or without confinement to quarters. Punishments can be awarded separately or in combination.

Specifies where persons sentenced to imprisonment under the Act are to be imprisoned. If dismissed from the force, they are imprisoned in the nearest jail or as directed by the Local Government. If not dismissed, they may be confined in the quarter-guard or another suitable place as directed by the convicting officer or District Magistrate.

main_sections.section_title: Saving of prosecutions under other laws.
main_sections.description: Clarifies that the Act does not prevent prosecution under Act V of 1861 or other enactments for acts or omissions punishable under this Act. It also states that no person shall be punished twice for the same offence.

main_sections.section_title: Conferment of magisterial powers on Police-officers.
main_sections.description: Grants the Local Government the power to invest Police-officers of or above the rank of Commandant with magisterial powers for inquiring into or trying offences committed by Military Police-officers under Act V of 1861 or this Act.

main_sections.section_title: Disciplinary and other powers of Commandants and Seconds-in-Command of Military Police otherwise than in respect of Military Police.
main_sections.description: Confers disciplinary powers on Commandants and Seconds-in-Command of Military Police with respect to Police-officers under section 7 of Act V of 1861 who are not Military Police-officers. These powers are similar to those of a District Superintendent of Police under that section, subject to rules made by the Local Government.

main_sections.section_title: Privileges of Commandants and Seconds-in-Command of Military Police as Police-officers.
main_sections.description: Grants Commandants and Seconds-in-Command of Military Police all the privileges afforded to Police-officers under specific sections of Act V of 1861, the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and any other relevant enactment.
Empowers the Local Government to make orders and rules consistent with the Act regarding the Military Police as it deems expedient.

important_rules: Military Police-officers must sign a statement after it's read and explained to them before being appointed, which governs their discharge.
Discharge from the Bengal Police Force for a Military Police-officer is strictly in accordance with the terms of the signed statement.
While on active service, Military Police-officers have no claim to discharge and must remain until the necessity ceases.
Re-enlistment after discharge does not allow previous service to be reckoned for pension or other purposes.
Superior officers are defined by rank and grade, or as a Second-in-Command, Commandant, or District Magistrate.
Specific acts constituting 'more heinous offences' and 'less heinous offences' are detailed, with corresponding penalties.
Minor offences against discipline can be punished summarily without formal trial by designated officers.
Imprisonment sentences for offences under this Act have specific provisions regarding the place of confinement.
Prosecution under other laws for the same acts or omissions is permitted, but double punishment for the same offence is prohibited.
The Local Government can grant magisterial powers to certain Police-officers for trying offences by Military Police-officers.
Commandants and Seconds-in-Command have disciplinary powers over other Police-officers not designated as Military Police-officers.
Commandants and Seconds-in-Command are entitled to privileges of Police-officers.
The Local Government has the power to make rules for the Military Police.

penalties: More heinous offences: Transportation for life or for a term of not less than seven years, or imprisonment for a term extending to fourteen years, or fine which may extend to three months’ pay, or fine in addition to such transportation or imprisonment.
Less heinous offences: Imprisonment for a term extending to one year, or fine which may extend to three months' pay, or both.

Minor punishments (without formal trial): Imprisonment to the extent of seven days in the quarter-guard or other suitable place, with forfeiture of all pay and allowances; punishment drill, extra guard, fatigue, or other duty, not exceeding thirty days in duration, with or without confinement to quarters.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Commandants, Seconds-in-Command, District Magistrates, and the Local Government. For magisterial powers, officers invested by the Local Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through disciplinary proceedings, prosecution in Criminal Courts, and the award of punishments as specified in the Act. The Local Government may also make rules for enforcement.

rights: Right to apply for discharge after three years of service, subject to conditions (two months' notice, not on active service, and not causing vacancies to exceed one-tenth of sanctioned strength).
Right to be discharged in accordance with the terms of the signed statement.
Commandants and Seconds-in-Command have the right to exercise disciplinary powers and possess privileges of Police-officers.
Right to not be punished twice for the same offence.
Military Police-officers have a duty to suppress mutiny or sedition and report intentions of mutiny.
Military Police-officers have a duty to obey lawful commands of their superior officers.
Military Police-officers have a duty to defend any garrison, fortress, post, or guard committed to their charge.
Military Police-officers have a duty to report correspondence with persons in arms against the State.
duties: Military Police-officers have a duty to sign a statement acknowledging its understanding upon enrolment.
Military Police-officers have a duty to perform their service diligently and without desertion.
Military Police-officers on duty, parade, or march must not be intoxicated.
Military Police-officers in command of guards, picquets, or patrols must receive prisoners duly committed and not negligently suffer any prisoner to escape.
Military Police-officers must report to their commanding or superior officer without delay any information of mutiny or intention to mutiny.
Military Police-officers must use their utmost endeavors to suppress any mutiny or sedition.
Military Police-officers must not use criminal force or assault their superior officer.
Military Police-officers must not shamefully abandon or deliver up any garrison, fortress, post or guard committed to their charge.
Military Police-officers must not hold correspondence with, or assist or relieve, any person in arms against the State, and must discover such correspondence to their superior officer.

Military Police-officers on active service must not disobey lawful commands, desert, sleep on post, quit post without relief or leave, go in search of plunder without authority, quit guard/picquet/party/patrol without relief or leave, use criminal force to persons bringing provisions, force safeguard, break into houses for plunder, plunder/destroy/damage property, or intentionally cause false alarms.
Military Police-officers not on active service must not disobey lawful commands, plunder/destroy/damage property, sleep on post, quit post without relief or leave, or desert.
Military Police-officers must not strike or attempt to force any sentry.
Military Police-officers must not leave their arrest or confinement before being set at liberty by proper authority.
Military Police-officers must not be grossly insubordinate or insolent to their superior officer.
Military Police-officers must not refuse to superintend or assist in field-work or other work.
Military Police-officers must not strike or ill-use any subordinate officer.
Officers in command must ensure reparation is made for maltreatment or oppression by subordinates and report such cases.

Military Police-officers must not designedly or through neglect injure, lose, or fraudulently dispose of their arms, clothes, tools, equipment, ammunition, accoutrements, or necessaries, or those entrusted to them.
Military Police-officers must not malinger, feign disease or infirmity, delay their cure, or aggravate their disease or infirmity.
Military Police-officers must not voluntarily cause hurt to themselves or others to render themselves or others unfit for service.
District Magistrates, Commandants, Seconds-in-Command, and certain other officers have the duty to maintain discipline and award punishments for petty offences.
obligations: To serve for the duration specified or until discharged according to the signed statement.
To uphold the discipline and security of the Bengal Military Police and the State.
To comply with all lawful orders and directions from superior officers.
To protect property and citizens as per their role in the Military Police.

key_procedures: Enrolment: An officer appointed to the Bengal Police Force under section 7 of Act V of 1861 is read and explained the statement in the schedule in the presence of a Magistrate, Commandant, or Second-in-Command, and signs it in acknowledgment.

Discharge: A Military Police-officer can apply for discharge after three years of service when not on active service, through their superior officer, to a Commandant or District Magistrate. Discharge is granted after two months, unless it causes vacancies to exceed one-tenth of the sanctioned strength, in which case the officer must remain until the objection is waived or removed. No claim to reckon previous service for pension or other purposes upon re-enlistment after discharge.

Awarding Minor Punishments: A District Magistrate, Commandant, Second-in-Command, or an officer of subadar rank commanding a separate detachment or outpost, or temporarily in command at headquarters, can award minor punishments without formal trial for petty offences against discipline. These punishments include imprisonment up to seven days with pay forfeiture, and punishment drill, extra guard, or fatigue duty up to thirty days with or without confinement to quarters. These can be awarded separately or in combination.

Conferment of Magisterial Powers: The Local Government may invest any Police-officer not below the rank of Commandant with the powers of a Magistrate of any class for the purpose of enquiring into or trying any offence committed by a Military Police-officer and punishable under Act V of 1861 or this Act.
administration: The Local Government is responsible for making orders and rules for the Military Police and appointing Commandants and Seconds-in-Command. District Magistrates, Commandants, and Seconds-in-Command are involved in disciplinary actions and enforcement.
important_notes: The Act is an extension and regulation of the Bengal Reserve Police, integrating them into a 'Military Police' structure.
Discharge procedures are more stringent than general police discharge provisions, being tied to the specific statement signed by the officer.
The Act draws definitions and references from the Indian Penal Code (XV of 1860) and Act V of 1861.
The definition of 'superior officer' is broad and includes officers of higher rank/grade and specific command positions.
Penalties for 'more heinous offences' are severe, reflecting the military-like nature of the unit.
The Act allows for the conferment of magisterial powers on specific Police-officers, enabling them to try cases involving Military Police-officers.
The schedule contains a statement that must be read to and signed by every Military Police-officer, detailing terms of service and discharge.

title: The Madras City Civil Court Act, 1892
purpose: To establish an additional Civil Court for the City of Madras.
scope: The Act applies to suits and other proceedings of a civil nature arising within the City of Madras, with a pecuniary limit of two thousand five hundred rupees. It excludes matters cognizable by the High Court (Admiralty, testamentary, matrimonial, etc.), the Court for insolvent debtors, and the Small Cause Court.

key_definitions.City Court: The Court established under the next following section (Section 3).
key_definitions.City of Madras: The area within the local limits for the time being of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of the High Court.
key_definitions.High Court: The High Court of Judicature at Madras.
key_definitions.Small Cause Court: The Court of Small Causes of Madras.

main_sections.description: States the short title of the Act and its commencement.
Defines key terms used in the Act, including 'City Court', 'City of Madras', 'High Court', and 'Small Cause Court'.

Empowers the Local Government to establish the Madras City Civil Court with jurisdiction over civil suits and proceedings not exceeding two thousand five hundred rupees in value, excluding specific categories of cases.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment, suspension and removal of Judges
main_sections.description: Grants the Local Government the power to appoint, suspend, and remove Judges of the City Court.

main_sections.section_title: Judge of City Court to be Judge of Small Cause Court
main_sections.description: Stipulates that every Judge of the City Court shall also be a Judge of the Small Cause Court and liable to perform duties assigned by the Chief Justice of the High Court.

main_sections.section_title: Powers of Judges when City Court consists of more than one Judge
main_sections.description: Outlines the powers of Judges when the City Court has multiple Judges, including distribution of business and appointment of a principal Judge.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment, powers, duties and punishment of ministerial officers
main_sections.description: Details the appointment, powers, duties, and disciplinary actions (suspension, removal, fines) for ministerial officers of the City Court.

main_sections.section_title: Questions arising in suits, etc., under Act to be dealt with according to law administered by High Court
main_sections.description: Mandates that all questions arising in suits or proceedings under this Act in the City Court shall be determined according to the law administered by the High Court in its ordinary original civil jurisdiction.

main_sections.section_title: Valuation of immoveable property for jurisdictional purposes
main_sections.description: Specifies how the value of immoveable property is determined for jurisdictional purposes, following the Court-fees Act, 1870.
Authorizes the High Court to prescribe process fees with the approval of the Governor of Fort St. George in Council.
Confers upon the City Court the power to appoint Receivers, similar to High Courts and District Courts under the Code of Civil Procedure.

main_sections.section_title: Repayment of half fees on settlement before hearing
main_sections.description: Provides for the repayment of half the institution fees to a plaintiff if a suit is settled by agreement before issues are settled or evidence is recorded.

main_sections.section_title: Allowance for fees paid in City Court in cases removed to High Court
main_sections.description: Addresses the allowance for fees paid in the City Court when a case is removed to the High Court for trial.
Establishes the High Court as the appellate authority for the City Court and sets the period of limitation for appeals.

main_sections.section_title: Saving of original civil jurisdiction of High Court
main_sections.description: Ensures that the original civil jurisdiction of the High Court is not affected, while also providing mechanisms for transferring cases between the High Court and the City Court and implications for costs.
Requires the City Court to use a seal of a form and dimensions prescribed by the Local Government.
Details the process for drawing up and approving lists of holidays and vacations for the City Court.

important_rules: All questions arising in suits or proceedings in the City Court must be dealt with according to the law administered by the High Court in its ordinary original civil jurisdiction (Section 8).
When the City Court consists of more than one Judge, each Judge can exercise all powers conferred by the Act or other laws (Section 6(a)).
Ministerial officers can be fined for misconduct or neglect, with the fine deductible from their salary (Section 7(3) & (4)).
Half the institution fees are repaid to a plaintiff if a suit is settled before issues are settled or evidence is recorded (Section 13).
If a suit instituted in the High Court ought to have been in the City Court, no costs are allowed to a successful plaintiff, and a successful defendant gets their costs (Section 16(1)).

penalties: Fines can be imposed on ministerial officers for misconduct or neglect in the performance of their duties (Section 7(3)).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The High Court (for appeals and prescribing process fees), the Local Government (for establishing the court, appointing judges, and appointing ministerial officers), and the Judge/Principal Judge of the City Court (for directing ministerial officers' duties and imposing fines).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the judicial process by the City Court and High Court, and administrative actions by the Local Government and the court's presiding officers.

rights: Right to have civil suits within the specified pecuniary limit and geographical area tried by the City Court.
Right to appeal to the High Court from decrees or orders of the City Court.
Right to have half institution fees repaid if a suit is settled before evidence is recorded.
Right to receive costs as between attorney and client if a defendant is successful in a suit wrongly instituted in the High Court but belonging to the City Court's jurisdiction.
duties: Duty of the City Court to try suits within its jurisdiction.
Duty of Judges to perform duties of Small Cause Court judges when required.
Duty of ministerial officers to exercise powers and discharge duties as directed by the Judge.
Duty of the City Court to allow fees paid in the City Court as credit when a case is removed to the High Court.
obligations: Obligation for all questions in City Court proceedings to be dealt with according to High Court law.
Obligation for the City Court to use a prescribed seal.
Obligation for the City Court to observe approved holidays and vacations.

key_procedures: Establishment of the City Court: The Local Government notifies the establishment of the Court (Section 3).
Appointment of Judges: The Local Government appoints Judges via notification (Section 4).
Appointment of Ministerial Officers: The Judge/Principal Judge appoints clerks, bailiffs, etc., with Local Government sanction (Section 7(1)).
Distribution of Business: The principal Judge arranges for the distribution of court business (Section 6(c)).
Appeals: Appeals from the City Court are heard by the High Court (Section 15(1)).
Transfer of Cases: A High Court Judge may transfer a case to the City Court (Section 16(2)).
Setting Holidays and Vacations: The Judge/Principal Judge draws up a list for approval and publication (Section 18).
administration: The Local Government and the High Court of Judicature at Madras have administrative oversight. The City Court itself, through its Judges, administers justice within its purview.
important_notes: The pecuniary jurisdiction of the City Court is limited to ₹2,500 (Section 3).
Cases falling under specific jurisdictions of the High Court, insolvency court, or Small Cause Court are excluded (Section 3).
The Act does not affect the High Court's original civil jurisdiction, but it provides for cost implications and transfer of cases (Section 16).
The Act has been amended, with certain sections repealed (e.g., Section 12 by the Repealing Act, 1938).

title: The General Clauses Act, 1897
purpose: To consolidate and extend the General Clauses Acts of 1868 and 1887, providing a standard set of definitions and rules for interpretation of Central Acts and Regulations.
scope: Applies to all Central Acts and Regulations made after its commencement, and certain definitions also apply to Indian Laws. It defines terms and provides rules of construction for legislative instruments.

key_definitions.abet: Includes grammatical variations and cognate expressions, with the same meaning as in the Indian Penal Code.
key_definitions.act: When referring to an offence or civil wrong, includes a series of acts, and words referring to acts done extend to illegal omissions.
key_definitions.affidavit: Includes affirmation and declaration for persons allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing.
key_definitions.barrister: Means a barrister of England or Ireland, or a member of the Faculty of Advocates in Scotland.
key_definitions.British India: Refers to territories governed by the Governor General or subordinate officers, and later to Governors' Provinces and Chief Commissioners' Provinces, with specific exclusions.
key_definitions.Central Act: Means an Act of Parliament, including Acts of the Dominion or Indian Legislature passed before the Constitution, and Acts made by the Governor General in Council or Governor General before such commencement.
key_definitions.Central Government: Refers to the Governor General or Governor General in Council before the Constitution, and the President after commencement, with provisions for provincial governments, chief commissioners, and union territory administrators.
key_definitions.enactment: Includes a Regulation and any provision contained in an Act or Regulation.
key_definitions.good faith: Means done honestly, regardless of negligence.
key_definitions.Government: Includes both the Central Government and any State Government.
key_definitions.immovable property: Includes land, benefits arising from land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth.
key_definitions.India: Refers to British India and related territories before the Dominion, territories within the Dominion after its establishment, and all territories comprised in the territory of India after the commencement of the Constitution.
key_definitions.Indian law: Includes Acts, Ordinances, Regulations, rules, orders, bye-laws, or other instruments having the force of law in India before the Constitution, or in Part A/C States thereafter, excluding UK Acts and Orders in Council.
key_definitions.local authority: Means a municipal committee, district board, body of port Commissioners, or other authority legally entitled to or entrusted with the control or management of a municipal or local fund.
key_definitions.Magistrate: Includes every person exercising powers of a Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act as 'The General Clauses Act, 1897'.

Defines various terms and expressions that are to be used in Central Acts and Regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context. This is a comprehensive section with numerous definitions.

Deals with the commencement and coming into operation of enactments. For instance, it specifies that an Act or Regulation shall be deemed to come into operation at the beginning of the day on which it is assented to or promulgated.

Outlines the legal consequences of repealing an enactment, including the effect on rights and liabilities accrued or incurred, and investigations or legal proceedings commenced under the repealed enactment.

main_sections.section_title: Power to issue, to include power to add to, amend, vary or rescind notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws
main_sections.description: States that where a power to issue, make or grant an order, rule, bye-law or notification is conferred, that power includes the power to impose conditions, and to add to, amend, vary or rescind any such order, rule, bye-law or notification.

important_rules: Definitions provided in Section 3 apply to all Central Acts and Regulations made after the commencement of this Act, unless the context suggests otherwise.

When an Act or Regulation is repealed, the repeal shall not, unless a different intention appears, affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment.
If a power is conferred to issue an order, rule, bye-law or notification, that power includes the power to add to, amend, vary or rescind any such instrument.

When any Central Act or Regulation is after the commencement of this Act, amended, any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act which refers to such enactment shall be construed to refer to the amended enactment.

penalties: Section 25 deals with the recovery of fines, stating that 'all fines directed to be paid by any sentence or order, and all penalties directed to be paid by any sentence or order, may be recovered as if they were fines to be returned to the village accountant under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1882.'
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Not explicitly detailed for the Act itself, but its provisions are applied by various authorities responsible for enforcing the Central Acts and Regulations it interprets.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: The provisions of the General Clauses Act are enforced through their application in the interpretation and execution of other Central Acts and Regulations.

rights: Rights, privileges, obligations, or liabilities acquired, accrued, or incurred under a repealed enactment are generally preserved.
The right to take any proceeding against any person for any offence committed under a repealed enactment is preserved.
duties: Any investigation, legal proceeding, or remedy may be instituted, continued, or enforced under a repealed enactment as if the repealing Act or Regulation had not been passed.
obligations: Obligations incurred under a repealed enactment are generally preserved.

key_procedures: Coming into operation: Enactments come into operation on the day they receive assent or are promulgated.
Effect of Repeal: When an Act is repealed, it does not affect rights accrued or proceedings commenced under it. Investigations and remedies can continue as if the repeal had not occurred.
Construction of References: References to repealed enactments are to be construed as references to the enactments substituted for them.
Computation of Time: When a period of time is to be reckoned from a particular day, or by reference to a particular day, the same shall be exclusive of the day from which it is reckoned.
administration: As a general clauses act, it is not administered by a single department but its provisions are applied by various government departments and judicial bodies responsible for implementing Central Acts and Regulations.
important_notes: The Act has been amended by several subsequent Acts, as listed in the beginning of the document.
Certain sections have been repealed or substituted over time.

The Act's application has been extended to various territories, including Goa, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry, Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindivi Islands, and the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Union territory of Ladakh.

title: THE EPIDEMIC DISEASES ACT, 1897
purpose: To provide for the better prevention of the spread of dangerous epidemic diseases.
scope: Applies to the whole of India. It empowers the State and Central Governments to take special measures and prescribe regulations when faced with an outbreak or threat of a dangerous epidemic disease. It also defines and penalizes acts of violence against healthcare service personnel and damage to property during an epidemic.

key_definitions.act_of_violence: Includes harassment, harm, injury, hurt, intimidation, danger to life, obstruction, or hindrance to healthcare service personnel, or loss/damage to property in their custody during an epidemic.
key_definitions.healthcare_service_personnel: Includes public and clinical healthcare providers (doctors, nurses, etc.), other persons empowered by the Act, and anyone declared as such by the State Government, who may come in direct contact with affected patients and are at risk of contracting the disease.
key_definitions.property: Includes clinical establishments, quarantine/isolation facilities, mobile medical units, and any other property in which healthcare service personnel have a direct interest relating to the epidemic.
key_definitions.culpable_mental_state: Includes intention, motive, knowledge of a fact, and the belief in, or reason to believe, a fact.

main_sections.description: States the short title of the Act as the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, and its territorial extent (whole of India).
Provides definitions for 'act of violence', 'healthcare service personnel', 'property', and clarifies terms defined in other related Acts.

main_sections.section_title: Power to take special measures and prescribe regulations as to dangerous epidemic disease
main_sections.description: Empowers the State Government to take special measures and prescribe regulations to prevent the outbreak or spread of dangerous epidemic diseases if ordinary laws are insufficient. This includes measures for inspection and segregation of suspected individuals.

Empowers the Central Government to take measures and prescribe regulations for the inspection and detention of transport (buses, trains, ships, aircraft) and persons traveling therein, when ordinary laws are insufficient to prevent the spread of a dangerous epidemic disease.

main_sections.section_title: Prohibition of violence against healthcare service personnel and damage to property
main_sections.description: Prohibits any person from indulging in acts of violence against healthcare service personnel or causing damage or loss to any property during an epidemic.

Specifies penalties for disobeying regulations or orders under the Act, and for acts of violence against healthcare personnel or damage to property. It outlines imprisonment terms and fines for various offenses, including those causing grievous hurt.

main_sections.section_title: Cognizance, investigation and trial of offences
main_sections.description: Details procedures for cognizance, investigation, and trial of offenses under Section 3, making them cognizable and non-bailable, specifying investigation by an Inspector-rank officer, time limits for investigation and trial.
Allows for the compounding of certain offenses punishable under sub-section (2) of Section 3 with the permission of the Court.
States that the Court shall presume that a person committed an offense under sub-section (3) of Section 3 unless proven otherwise.
Provides that in prosecutions requiring a culpable mental state, the Court shall presume its existence, but the accused can defend by proving the absence of such mental state.

Mandates that convicted persons pay compensation for hurt or grievous hurt to healthcare personnel, and for damage to property (twice the market value). Unpaid compensation is recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

main_sections.section_title: Protection to persons acting under Act
main_sections.description: Provides protection from suits or legal proceedings for any act done or intended in good faith under the Act.

important_rules: Any person disobeying any regulation or order made under this Act is punishable under section 188 of the Indian Penal Code.
Acts of violence against healthcare service personnel or damage to property during an epidemic are prohibited.
Offenses of violence against healthcare personnel or damage to property carry imprisonment from three months to five years and fines.
Offenses involving grievous hurt to healthcare personnel during an act of violence carry imprisonment from six months to seven years and higher fines.
Cases registered under Section 3 (offenses against healthcare personnel and property) must be investigated within thirty days of FIR registration.
Inquiry or trial of cases under Section 3 should be concluded expeditiously, ideally within one year.
The Court shall presume a culpable mental state for offenses under Section 3(3), but the accused can prove otherwise.
Convicted persons are liable to pay compensation for hurt/grievous hurt to healthcare personnel and for property damage.
No suit or legal proceeding shall lie against any person for anything done or intended in good faith under this Act.

penalties: Disobeying regulations/orders: Punishable under Section 188 of the Indian Penal Code.
Acts of violence against healthcare personnel or damage to property: Imprisonment of 3 months to 5 years and fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2,00,000.
Acts of violence causing grievous hurt to healthcare personnel: Imprisonment of 6 months to 7 years and fine of ₹1,00,000 to ₹5,00,000.
Compensation for hurt/grievous hurt to healthcare personnel.
Compensation for damage to property (twice the fair market value).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The State Government and the Central Government have powers to take measures and prescribe regulations. Police officers (not below the rank of Inspector) are responsible for investigation. Courts handle trials and sentencing.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the implementation of regulations and orders by government authorities, investigation by police, and prosecution and sentencing by courts. Compensation is recovered as arrears of land revenue upon failure to pay.

rights: Right to protection for healthcare service personnel from violence and damage to property.
Right to have offenses investigated and tried expeditiously.
Right to compensation for hurt, grievous hurt, or property damage.
duties: Duty to obey regulations and orders made under the Act.
Duty not to commit acts of violence against healthcare service personnel.
Duty not to cause damage or loss to any property during an epidemic.
Duty of the accused to prove lack of culpable mental state when required.
obligations: Obligation of the convicted person to pay compensation for injuries and damages.
Obligation of the Court to presume certain mental states or offenses unless proven otherwise.
Obligation of the investigating officer to complete investigation within a specified period.

key_procedures: When a State Government is satisfied of an epidemic outbreak, it may take special measures and prescribe regulations (Section 2).
The Central Government may take measures and prescribe regulations for inspection and detention of transport and persons during an epidemic outbreak (Section 2A).
Prohibition of violence against healthcare personnel and damage to property (Section 2B).
Offenses under Section 3 are cognizable and non-bailable.
Investigation of offenses under Section 3 is to be conducted by a police officer not below the rank of Inspector and completed within 30 days.
Inquiry or trial of cases under Section 3 shall be held expeditiously, aiming for conclusion within one year, with provisions for extension.
Certain offenses under Section 3(2) may be compounded with the permission of the Court (Section 3B).
Court shall presume commission of offense under Section 3(3) unless contrary is proved (Section 3C).
Court shall presume culpable mental state under Section 3(3), but accused may prove absence of it (Section 3D).
Convicted persons are liable to pay compensation, recoverable as arrears of land revenue if not paid (Section 3E).
administration: The primary administration and enforcement powers are vested with the State Governments and the Central Government, who are empowered to take measures and prescribe regulations. The police and judiciary handle investigation and trial of offenses.
important_notes: The Act has been subject to amendments and extensions in its application to various regions of India.
The 2020 amendment significantly expanded the definitions and penalties related to violence against healthcare service personnel and damage to property.

The Act provides broad powers to governments during epidemic situations, with a focus on public health and safety, but also introduces specific protections and penalties for acts of violence and property damage.

title: THE CENTRAL PROVINCES TENANCY ACT, 1898
purpose: To consolidate and amend the law relating to agricultural tenancies in the Central Provinces.
scope: Applies to all territories administered by the Chief Commissioner of the Central Provinces.

key_definitions.agricultural year: As defined in the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881.
key_definitions.malik makbuza: As defined in the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881.
key_definitions.sir-land: As defined in the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881.
key_definitions.survey-number: As defined in the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881.
key_definitions.record-of-rights: As defined in the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881.
key_definitions.village: As defined in the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881.
key_definitions.arrear: An installment or part of an installment of rent not paid on or before its due date.
key_definitions.holding: A parcel of land held by a tenant from a landlord under a single lease or set of conditions.
key_definitions.improvement: A work that increases the letting-value of a holding, is suitable and consistent with its purpose, and is either directly executed for its benefit or made directly beneficial to it.
key_definitions.land: Land let or occupied for agricultural purposes or subservient to agriculture, including sites of appurtenant buildings.
key_definitions.landlord: The person from whom a tenant holds land and to whom rent is or would be payable.
key_definitions.rent: Whatever is paid, delivered, or rendered in money, kind, or service by a tenant for the use or occupation of let land.
key_definitions.Revenue-officer and Settlement-officer: Officers appointed under the Central Provinces Land-Revenue Act, 1881, as directed by the Local Government.
key_definitions.tenant: A person who holds land from another and is or would be liable to pay rent for it. Excludes farmers, mortgagees, or thikadars of proprietary rights.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its territorial extent (Central Provinces), and states it comes into force immediately.

Defines key terms used throughout the Act, referencing the Central Provinces Land-revenue Act, 1881 for some definitions, and providing specific definitions for others such as 'arrear', 'holding', 'improvement', 'land', 'landlord', 'rent', and 'tenant'.
Classifies tenants into five categories: absolute occupancy-tenants, occupancy-tenants, village-service-tenants, sub-tenants, and ordinary tenants.

main_sections.section_title: Presumption as to amount of rent payable
main_sections.description: Establishes a presumption in legal proceedings that the rent payable for an agricultural year is the same as the rent payable in the preceding year, unless proven otherwise.

main_sections.section_title: Date from which order fixing rent operates
main_sections.description: Specifies when orders to fix, alter, or commute rent take effect, allowing for it to be from the next agricultural year, a subsequent day, or from the date of an increase, diminution, or deterioration of the holding.
Defines how and when rents are to be paid, based on Local Government notifications, contract, or local usage.

main_sections.section_title: Rents payable to a number of landlords
main_sections.description: Addresses situations where a tenant has multiple landlords for the same holding, allowing the tenant to appoint one person to receive rent, subject to Local Government rules and contracts.

main_sections.section_title: Power to deposit rent in certain cases with Revenue officer
main_sections.description: Grants tenants the power to deposit rent with a Revenue Officer if the landlord refuses to accept it, or if there is uncertainty about the rightful recipient.
Clarifies that a rent deposit is considered payment to the landlord and outlines the Revenue Officer's role in notifying claimants and potentially paying out the deposit.

important_rules: Presumption of rent continuity: In disputes, rent is presumed to be the same as the previous year unless proven otherwise (Section 4).
Rent payment flexibility: Rent payment can be prescribed by the Local Government, or follow contract or local usage (Section 6).
Consolidated rent payment: Tenants with multiple landlords can pay rent to a single designated recipient (Section 7).
Rent deposit for tenant protection: Tenants can deposit rent with a Revenue Officer if landlords refuse to accept it or if there's doubt about the recipient (Section 8).
Deposited rent is considered paid: Rent deposited with a Revenue Officer is legally treated as payment to the landlord (Section 9).

penalties: Penalty for levying anything in excess of rent by landlord (Section 10).
Penalty for refusing receipt or giving defective receipt (Section 12).
Penalty for illegal distraint by landlord and for illegal removal of produce (Section 30).
Recovery of fines and penalties (Section 98).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Revenue officers, Settlement officers, and Civil Courts are involved in enforcing the Act.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through legal proceedings, suits for rent, ejectment suits, attachment of produce, and recovery of fines/penalties.

rights: Tenant's right to make improvements (Section 31).
Tenant's right to compensation for improvements upon ejectment (Section 32).
Tenant's right to reap produce (Section 26).
Tenant's right to apply to set aside certain transfers (Sections 47, 71).
Tenant's right to reinstatement if illegally ejected (Section 92).
Landlord's lien on the produce of a holding (Sections 23-29).
duties: Tenant's duty to pay rent (Section 8).
Tenant's duty to provide a substitute (for village-service-tenants) (Section 57).
Landlord's duty to provide a receipt for rent (Section 12).
Landlord's duty to confer occupancy-rights on ordinary tenants (Section 73).
obligations: Obligation of village-service-tenant to provide substitute (Section 57).
Obligation of landlord to confer occupancy-rights on ordinary tenant (Section 73).

key_procedures: Procedure for depositing rent with a Revenue Officer (Section 8).
Procedure when produce is under attachment (Section 28).
Procedure for assessing compensation for improvements (Section 33).
Procedure on applications to set aside transfers (Sections 48, 72).
Procedure in ejectment suits (Section 66).
Procedure in execution by sale of holding (Section 84).
Procedure in execution by ejectment (Section 85).
Procedure when, on sale or ejectment, money is due by the landlord to the tenant (Section 91).
Procedure on applications to Revenue and Settlement Officers and appeals (Section 96).
administration: The Chief Commissioner of the Central Provinces, with the Local Government empowered to make rules. Revenue-officers and Settlement-officers administer specific functions.
important_notes: Tenant rights under Chapter II do not apply to tenants of land in reserved forests (Section 38).
Certain sections regarding rent fixation are subject to provisions in Sections 66 and 78 (Section 5).
Certain actions by Revenue Officers are protected from suits against the Secretary of State for India in Council (Section 9).
Jurisdiction of Civil Courts is barred in certain cases (Section 95) but also specified in others (Section 97).

title: The Government Buildings Act, 1899
purpose: To provide for the exemption from the operation of municipal building laws of certain buildings and lands which are the property, or in the occupation, of the Government and situate within the limits of a municipality.
scope: Applies to the whole of India except territories which were comprised in Part B States before November 1, 1956. It concerns government-owned or occupied buildings and lands within municipal limits.

key_definitions.municipal_authority: Includes a municipal corporation or a body of municipal commissioners constituted by, or under the provisions of, any law or enactment for the time being in force.

main_sections.description: Names the Act as the Government Buildings Act, 1899, and specifies its territorial application.
Defines what constitutes a 'municipal authority' for the purposes of this Act.

main_sections.section_title: Exemption of certain Government buildings from municipal laws to regulate the erection, etc., of buildings within municipalities
main_sections.description: States that municipal laws regulating building erection, re-erection, construction, alteration, or maintenance do not apply to government-owned or occupied buildings used for public service or public purposes, or on government land. However, reasonable notice must be given to the municipal authority for material structural alterations, unless the building is related to defense or is confidential/secret.

main_sections.section_title: Objections or suggestions as to erection, etc., of certain Government buildings within municipalities, how to be made and dealt with
main_sections.description: Outlines the process for municipal authorities or their authorized representatives to inspect plans and buildings (excluding defense or confidential ones) and submit objections or suggestions to the State Government. The State Government will consider these and pass orders, providing written reasons if objections are overruled. The building will then be constructed or altered according to these orders.

important_rules: Government buildings used for public service or public purposes, or built on government land within municipal limits, are exempt from municipal building regulations.
For material structural alterations to non-defense and non-confidential government buildings, reasonable notice must be given to the municipal authority before commencement.
Municipal authorities can inspect plans and buildings of non-defense and non-confidential government projects with prior State Government permission.
Any objections or suggestions from municipal authorities regarding government building projects must be submitted in writing to the State Government.
The State Government will consider objections/suggestions and issue orders for the construction or alteration of the building.
If the State Government overrules an objection or suggestion, it must provide written reasons.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: State Government and Municipal Authorities (in a consultative capacity for Section 4)
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the State Government's consideration of objections/suggestions and issuance of orders for building construction/alteration. Enforcement of compliance with State Government orders regarding building projects.

rights: Government's right to exempt its public service buildings and lands from municipal building laws.
Right of municipal authorities (with permission) to inspect government building plans and sites.
Right of municipal authorities to submit objections or suggestions regarding government building projects.
duties: Duty of the Government to provide reasonable notice for material structural alterations of certain buildings to the municipal authority.
Duty of the State Government to consider objections or suggestions submitted by municipal authorities.
Duty of the State Government to provide written reasons if it overrules an objection or suggestion.

key_procedures: Submission of reasonable notice to the municipal authority for material structural alterations to non-defense/non-confidential government buildings.
Obtaining prior permission from the State Government for municipal authorities to inspect government building plans and sites.
Submission of written objections or suggestions by municipal authorities to the State Government regarding proposed government building projects.
Consideration of submitted objections/suggestions by the State Government and issuance of orders.
Construction or alteration of government buildings in accordance with the State Government's orders.
administration: State Government (for overall decision-making and orders)
important_notes: Buildings connected with defense are entirely exempt from the objection/suggestion process in Section 4.
Buildings whose plans or construction are considered confidential or secret by the State Government are also exempt from the objection/suggestion process in Section 4.
The extent of the Act was amended to exclude territories previously comprised in Part B States.

title: The Indian Tolls (Army and Air Force) Act, 1901
purpose: To amend the law relating to the exemption from tolls of persons and property belonging to the Army or Air Force.
scope: Extends to the whole of India. Applies to tolls levied on persons and property associated with the Army and Air Force.

key_definitions.authorised_followers: Persons other than officers, soldiers or airmen, who are employed by, or are in the service of, the Forces or Corps concerned, or are in the service of any officer, soldier or airman of such Forces or Corps.
key_definitions.carriage: A vehicle for carriage or haulage other than one specially constructed for use on rails.
key_definitions.ferry: Includes every bridge and other thing which is a ferry within the meaning of any enactment authorising the levy of tolls on ferries, but does not include any ferry or other thing which is included in the definition of “railway” in section 3 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890.
key_definitions.regular_forces: The "regular Army" as defined in clause (xxi) of section 3 of the Army Act, 1950, and includes the "Air Force" as defined in clause (iv) of section 4 of the Air Force Act, 1950.
key_definitions.horse: Includes a mule and any beast of whatever description which is used for burden or draught or for carrying persons.
key_definitions.irregular_corps: Any force (other than the Regular Forces or the Territorial Army or the National Cadet Corps) raised and maintained in India under the authority of the Central Government, or any other force which may be notified in this behalf by order published in the Official Gazette.
key_definitions.indian_reserve_forces: The forces constituted by the Indian Reserve Forces Act, 1888 and includes officers belonging to the Army in India Reserve of Officers or to the Regular Reserve of Officers and members of the Indian Air Force Volunteer Reserve when subject to military or air force law.
key_definitions.landing_place: Includes a pier, wharf, quay jetty and a stage whether fixed or floating.
key_definitions.public_authority: The Central Government or a State Government or a local authority; and, so far as regards tolls levied by a railway company under section 4 of the Indian Guaranteed Railways Act, 1879, or section 51 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890, includes such a railway company.
key_definitions.tolls: Includes duties, dues, rates, rents, fees and charges, but does not include customs duties levied under the Indian Tariff Act, 1934, octroi duties or town duties on the import of goods, or fares paid for the conveyance of passengers on a tramway.

main_sections.description: This section provides the short title of the Act as 'The Indian Tolls (Army and Air Force) Act, 1901', specifies its extent to the whole of India, and states its commencement date as April 1, 1901.

This section defines various terms used in the Act, including 'authorised followers', 'carriage', 'ferry', 'regular forces', 'horse', 'irregular Corps', 'Indian Reserve Forces', 'landing-place', 'public authority', and 'tolls'.

This section lists various categories of persons and property that are exempted from paying tolls. This includes officers, soldiers, airmen, members of Territorial Army/NCC, Indian Reserve Forces, authorised followers, families of these individuals, prisoners under escort, and their associated carriages, horses, and baggage.

main_sections.section_title: Tolls on vessels transporting troops and baggage, etc., of troops embarked or disembarked
main_sections.description: This section specifies that no tolls shall be leviable by any local authority in respect of vessels solely for the transport of troops, or the horses, baggage, or other effects of troops embarking or disembarking at any port, or Government carriages used in military or air-force service embarking or disembarking. It also mandates local authorities to provide reasonable services and accommodation in such cases.
Any person who demands and receives any toll in contravention of sections 3 or 4 shall be punishable with a fine which may extend to fifty rupees.

If any owner, lessee, company, railway administration, or local authority claims compensation for loss incurred due to the Act, the claim shall be submitted to the Central Government, which will pass orders and direct necessary actions for assessment.

The Central Government may make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act, particularly for the form of passes for exemptions. Such rules require previous publication and must be laid before Parliament.
This section dealt with repeals and has been repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1914.

important_rules: Officers, soldiers, airmen, and associated personnel and property of the Regular Forces, Irregular Corps, Territorial Army, National Cadet Corps, and Indian Reserve Forces are generally exempted from tolls.
Carriages, horses, and baggage accompanying exempted persons are also exempted.
Government carriages and horses employed in military or air-force service, and persons in charge, are exempted when conveying exempted persons or stores.
No tolls are leviable on vessels used by the Central Government solely for troop transport, or on the effects of troops embarking or disembarking at ports.
Local authorities must provide services and accommodation for troops and their effects at ports, with payment determined by the Central Government.

penalties: Fine which may extend to fifty rupees for demanding or receiving tolls in contravention of section 3 or 4.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Central Government (for compensation claims and rule-making), and potentially local authorities or other designated bodies for toll collection and enforcement of penalties.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through penal provisions for contravention of toll exemptions and through rules made by the Central Government. Compensation claims are handled by the Central Government.

rights: Right to exemption from tolls for specified persons and property.
Right to claim compensation for losses incurred due to the Act.
duties: Duty of local authorities to provide services and accommodation for troops at ports.
Duty of individuals to comply with the provisions of the Act.
obligations: Obligation of the Central Government to frame rules for the Act's implementation.
Obligation of the Central Government to process compensation claims.

key_procedures: Procedure for claiming exemption from tolls: Ensuring the person or property falls under the categories specified in Section 3 and accompanying documentation if required.
Procedure for claiming compensation: Submitting a claim for losses incurred due to the Act to the Central Government, which will then investigate and decide on the claim.
Procedure for rule-making: The Central Government may make rules, subject to previous publication and laying before Parliament, to carry out the Act's purposes.
administration: Central Government
important_notes: The Act has been extended to Berar, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry, and Lakshadweep.
The definition of 'tolls' specifically excludes customs duties, octroi, and town duties on imports, as well as tramway fares.

The explanation to section 3 clarifies that exempted persons or property are considered to be accompanying the Forces even if there's an interval of space and time, provided the move is a direct result of or connected to the move of the Forces.
Section 8 and the Schedule were repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1914.

title: The Victoria Memorial Act, 1903
purpose: To provide for the erection and management of the Victoria Memorial at Calcutta, a building intended as a memorial to Her late Majesty Victoria of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Queen, Empress of India.
scope: This act applies to the erection, maintenance, and management of the Victoria Memorial at Calcutta. It establishes a body of Trustees and defines their powers and responsibilities.

main_sections.description: States that the Act may be called the Victoria Memorial Act, 1903.

Establishes the Trustees of the Victoria Memorial as a body corporate with perpetual succession. It lists the members of the Trustees, including ex officio members such as the Government of West Bengal, the Chief Justice of the High Court of West Bengal, representatives from Central Government ministries, the Mayor of Calcutta, an officer nominated by the Comptroller and Auditor General, the Secretary to the Government of West Bengal in the Department of Education, and nominated persons with expertise in relevant fields. It also outlines provisions for proxy attendance, the validity of acts despite vacancies, the functioning of ex officio trustees, the appointment of a Secretary, and the authentication of payment orders.
Declares that all sums of money and other property, whether movable or immovable, given, bequeathed, transferred, or acquired for the purposes of the Memorial shall vest in the Trustees.

main_sections.section_title: Officers and servants to be public servants
main_sections.description: States that all officers and servants employed by the Trustees are deemed to be public servants under the Indian Penal Code, with an exception for persons in the service of contractors employed by the Trustees.

Empowers the Central Government to make rules, by notification in the Official Gazette, to carry out the purposes of the Act. These rules can cover the appointment and tenure of Trustees, the convening and procedure of Trustees' meetings, the formation and powers of committees, the erection, maintenance, management, and public access to the Memorial, fees for admission, and the form, audit, and publication of accounts. Rules made by the Central Government must be laid before Parliament for approval.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Trustees to make regulations
main_sections.description: Grants the Trustees the power, with the approval of the Central Government, to make regulations for discharging their functions. These regulations can include conditions for loaning articles, and recruitment and service conditions for employees. Regulations made by the Trustees must also be laid before Parliament for approval.

important_rules: The Central Government may make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act, which will be laid before Parliament for approval.
The Trustees may make regulations, with the approval of the Central Government, for the management of the Victoria Memorial, which will also be laid before Parliament for approval.
All officers and servants employed by the Trustees, except those of contractors, are considered public servants.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Central Government and the Trustees of the Victoria Memorial
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through rules made by the Central Government and regulations made by the Trustees, subject to parliamentary oversight. Enforcement of duties and liabilities falls under the general legal framework for public servants and corporate bodies.

rights: The Trustees have the right to sue and be sued, acquire and hold property, enter into contracts, and perform acts consistent with the Act's purposes.
The public may have rights of access to the Victoria Memorial under conditions specified by rules.
duties: The Trustees have a duty to manage the Victoria Memorial and its property.
The Trustees have a duty to ensure that officers and servants are deemed public servants.
The Trustees have a duty to keep accounts and have them audited and published.
The Central Government has a duty to make rules and lay them before Parliament.
The Trustees have a duty to make regulations and lay them before Parliament.
obligations: The Trustees are obligated to act as a body corporate with perpetual succession.
The Trustees are obligated to adhere to rules and regulations made under the Act.
The Trustees are obligated to ensure that payments are properly authenticated.

key_procedures: Appointment of Trustees: The Act specifies ex officio Trustees and provides for nominated Trustees by the Central Government and by the Trustees themselves.
Decision Making by Trustees: Decisions are made by a majority present and voting at meetings, or by a majority decision obtained through circulation.
Rule and Regulation Making: The Central Government makes rules, and the Trustees make regulations, both requiring parliamentary scrutiny and approval.
Authentication of Payments: Orders for payment must be signed by two Trustees and countersigned by the Secretary.
administration: The Central Government (for making rules) and the Trustees of the Victoria Memorial (for management and regulations).
important_notes: Amendments to the Act have been made over time, for example, by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1914, and Act 32 of 1981.
The list of Trustees has been updated, notably by Act 32 of 1981.
Provisions for parliamentary scrutiny of rules and regulations are included.

title: THE ANCIENT MONUMENTS PRESERVATION ACT, 1904
purpose: To provide for the preservation of ancient monuments, for the exercise of control over traffic in antiquities and over excavation in certain places, and for the protection and acquisition in certain cases of ancient monuments and of objects of archaeological, historical or artistic interest.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India, with an exception for the State of Jammu and Kashmir (prior to its current constitutional status). It applies to ancient monuments, antiquities, and archaeological excavations, as well as places of worship from misuse, pollution, or desecration.

key_definitions.ancient_monument: Any structure, erection or monument or any tumulus or place of interment, or any cave, rock-sculpture, inscription or monolith, which is of historical, archeological or artistic interest, or any remains thereof. It includes the site, adjoining land for preservation, and means of access.
key_definitions.antiquities: Include any moveable objects which the Central Government may think it necessary to protect against injury, removal or dispersion due to their historical or archeological associations.
key_definitions.maintain_maintenance: Includes the fencing, covering in, repairing, restoring and cleansing of a protected monument, and doing any act necessary for maintaining it or securing convenient access thereto.
key_definitions.owner: Includes a joint owner invested with powers of management, any manager or trustee exercising powers of management, and their successors in title or office. It does not extend powers beyond what is lawfully exercisable.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act and its geographical applicability.
Defines key terms used in the Act, such as 'ancient monument', 'antiquities', 'Commissioner', 'maintain', 'land', and 'owner'.
Empowers the Central Government to declare an ancient monument as a protected monument through notification in the Official Gazette and outlines the procedure for objections and confirmation.

main_sections.section_title: Acquisition of rights in or guardianship of an ancient monument
main_sections.description: Details how the Collector, with the Central Government's sanction, can purchase, lease, or accept gifts/bequests of protected monuments. It also covers the Commissioner assuming guardianship and the binding nature of such arrangements.

main_sections.section_title: Preservation of ancient monument by agreement
main_sections.description: Allows the Collector to propose agreements with owners for the preservation of protected monuments, specifying matters such as maintenance, custody, restrictions on alteration, public access, sale notice, expenses, vesting of rights, dispute resolution, and other connected matters. It also details procedures for altering or terminating such agreements.

main_sections.section_title: Owners under disability or not in possession
main_sections.description: Specifies who can exercise an owner's powers under Section 5 when the owner is under disability or when dealing with village property. It also includes a restriction on making agreements related to religious worship if the acting person is not of the same religion.

Outlines the Collector's powers to prohibit contraventions of preservation agreements and to authorize actions for maintenance if the owner refuses or neglects. It also provides for an appeal against the Collector's orders.

main_sections.section_title: Purchasers at certain sales and persons claiming through owner bound by instrument executed by owner
main_sections.description: Ensures that purchasers at certain sales (land revenue arrears, public demands, Bengal Patni Taluks Regulation sales) and those claiming title through an owner are bound by instruments executed for the preservation of a monument.

main_sections.section_title: Application of endowment to repair of an ancient monument
main_sections.description: Allows the Collector to institute a suit or make an application to the District Judge for the proper application of an endowment created for the repair of a monument, especially if the owner fails to enter into a preservation agreement.

Grants the Central Government power to direct the acquisition of a protected monument under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, if it apprehends danger of destruction, injury, or decay. This power is subject to limitations, especially for monuments forming part of a dwelling-house.

main_sections.section_title: Power Central Government to control mining, etc., near ancient monument
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to control mining operations, quarrying, construction, or any other activity likely to damage an ancient monument within a specified distance.
Specifies that the Central Government may undertake the maintenance of certain protected monuments and recover expenses from the owner or occupier under certain conditions.

main_sections.section_title: Protection of place of worship from misuse, pollution or desecration
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to make rules for protecting places of worship, which are ancient monuments, from misuse, pollution, or desecration.
Outlines the penalties for contravening the provisions of the Act, including destruction, removal, or defacement of protected monuments.

main_sections.section_title: Power to Central Government to control traffic in antiquities
main_sections.description: Grants the Central Government the power to control traffic in antiquities, including their export.

main_sections.section_title: Power to Central Government to control moving of sculptures, carvings or like objects
main_sections.description: Allows the Central Government to control the moving of sculptures, carvings, images, bas-reliefs, inscriptions or like objects of archaeological or artistic interest.

main_sections.section_title: Purchase of sculptures, carvings or like objects by the Government
main_sections.description: Enables the Government to purchase sculptures, carvings, images, bas-reliefs, inscriptions or like objects if they are in danger of being lost or dispersed.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government to notify areas as protected
main_sections.description: Authorizes the Central Government to notify areas containing ancient archaeological sites and remains as protected areas.

main_sections.section_title: Power to enter upon and make excavations in a protected area
main_sections.description: Grants the Central Government the power to enter upon and make excavations in a protected area.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government to make rules regulating Archaeological excavation in protected areas
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to frame rules regulating archaeological excavations in protected areas.

main_sections.section_title: Power to acquire a protected area
main_sections.description: Allows the Central Government to acquire a protected area under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for the purpose of its preservation.
Confers power on the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Protection to public servants acting under Act
main_sections.description: Provides protection to public servants acting in good faith under the provisions of the Act.

important_rules: A monument declared as protected must have a copy of its notification fixed conspicuously on or near it, with an intimation for objections within one month.

Owners of protected monuments can enter into agreements with the Central Government for preservation, which may cover maintenance, custody, restrictions on alteration, public access, sale of land, and expenses.
Purchasers at certain sales and persons claiming title through an owner are bound by any preservation instruments executed by the owner.
The Central Government can control mining, quarrying, and construction near ancient monuments.
The Central Government can control traffic in antiquities and their export.
The Central Government can control the movement of sculptures, carvings, and similar objects of historical or artistic interest.
The Central Government can notify areas as protected for archaeological excavation and can acquire such areas.

penalties: Destruction, removal, alteration, or defacement of a protected monument: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both (Section 16).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Central Government, Collector, Commissioner, and other officers authorized by the Central Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through notifications, agreements with owners, purchase or lease of monuments, assuming guardianship, direct action for maintenance, and through legal proceedings for contraventions. Rules can be made for archaeological excavations and control of traffic in antiquities.

rights: Right of the Central Government to declare ancient monuments as protected.
Right of the Collector to purchase, lease, or accept gifts/bequests of protected monuments.
Right of the Central Government to control mining, traffic in antiquities, and movement of objects of interest.
Right of access to certain protected monuments for the public (as specified by agreement or rules).
Right of the Central Government to acquire protected areas for preservation.
duties: Duty of the owner to preserve the monument as per agreement or legal requirements.
Duty of persons to comply with orders and rules made under the Act.
Duty of public servants to act in good faith.
obligations: Obligation of owners to allow access for inspection and maintenance.
Obligation to provide notice to the Central Government if land with a monument is offered for sale.
Obligation to pay expenses incurred by the Central Government in preservation, as per agreement.
Obligation for individuals to comply with the Central Government's control over mining, traffic in antiquities, and movement of objects.

key_procedures: Declaration of a monument as protected: Central Government issues a notification, fixes it on the monument, considers objections within one month, and then confirms or withdraws the notification.

Agreement for preservation: Collector proposes an agreement to the owner, detailing terms for maintenance, custody, restrictions, access, etc. The agreement can be altered or terminated with sanction and notice.
Enforcement of agreement: If contravention is apprehended, the Collector can issue an order prohibiting it. If an owner refuses to act, the Collector can authorize someone else and recover expenses.
Compulsory purchase of a monument: If a monument is in danger, the Central Government can direct its acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act.
Archaeological Excavation: Central Government can notify areas, enter and excavate, and make rules for regulating such excavations. Areas can also be acquired.
