Specifies the monthly emoluments to be paid to the President.
Details the pension entitlement for individuals who cease to hold the office of President, including provisions for furnished residence, secretarial staff, medical attendance, and travel.

main_sections.section_title: Family pension to spouse of President.
main_sections.description: Establishes the provision for a family pension to the spouse of a President who dies while holding office or after ceasing to hold office.

main_sections.section_title: Free medical attendance and treatment to spouse of President dying in office.
main_sections.description: Grants entitlement to free medical attendance and treatment to the spouse of a President who dies while in office.

main_sections.section_title: Free Accommodation to spouse of President.
main_sections.description: Outlines the entitlement to furnished accommodation, secretarial staff, telephone, motor-car, and travel benefits for the spouse of a deceased President.

main_sections.section_title: Sums to be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
main_sections.description: Declares that any sum payable under this Act is a charge on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act, with provisions for laying such rules before Parliament.
Grants the Central Government the power to issue orders to remove difficulties in giving effect to the provisions of the Act, within a specified time frame.

important_rules: Rule 1: A retiring President is entitled to a pension of fifty percent of the President's emoluments per month for life.
Rule 2: Retiring Presidents are entitled to the use of a furnished residence, secretarial staff, medical attendance and treatment, and travel anywhere in India by the highest class.
Rule 3: The spouse of a President who dies in office or after retirement is entitled to a family pension at the rate of fifty percent of the pension admissible to a retiring President for life.
Rule 4: The spouse of a President who dies in office is entitled to free medical attendance and treatment for life.
Rule 5: The spouse of a deceased President is entitled to furnished accommodation, secretarial staff, a telephone, a motor-car, and limited travel benefits for life.
Rule 6: Any sums payable under this Act are to be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Central Government
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through rules made by the Central Government and laid before Parliament. The Act itself mandates payments from the Consolidated Fund of India.

rights: The President's right to emoluments.
Retiring Presidents' right to a pension.
Retiring Presidents' right to furnished residence, secretarial staff, medical attendance, and travel.
Spouses' right to family pension.
Spouses' right to medical attendance and treatment.
Spouses' right to furnished accommodation, secretarial staff, telephone, motor-car, and travel benefits.
duties: The duty to pay emoluments to the President.
The duty to pay pensions and benefits to retiring Presidents and their spouses.
The duty to charge these payments on the Consolidated Fund of India.

key_procedures: Payment of emoluments to the President as specified.
Calculation and payment of pension to retiring Presidents at fifty percent of emoluments per month.
Provision of specified benefits (residence, staff, medical, travel) to retiring Presidents.
Calculation and payment of family pension to the spouse of a deceased President.
Provision of specified benefits (accommodation, staff, telephone, car, travel) to the spouse of a deceased President.
Rules to be made by the Central Government for carrying out the Act's purposes, subject to parliamentary approval.
administration: Central Government
important_notes: A person who has held the office of Vice-President before assuming the office of President is not entitled to any pension and other benefits under the Vice-President’s Pension Act, 1997.
If a person is re-elected as President, they or their spouse are not entitled to any benefits under this section for the period they hold office again.
The Act has been amended multiple times since its enactment in 1951, with significant amendments in 1962, 1976, 1985, 1990, 1993, 1998, 2000, 2008, and 2013 (Finance Act).
The 'residence' for the purpose of this sub-section has the meaning assigned in the Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952.

Any difficulty in implementing the Act as amended by the President’s Emoluments and Pension (Amendment) Act, 2008, can be resolved by the Central Government through orders, provided they are consistent with the Act and made within two years of the Act's commencement.

title: The Marking of Heavy Packages Act, 1951
purpose: To give effect to the International Convention for the marking of weight on heavy packages transported by sea or inland waterways, by ensuring that packages of one metric ton or more gross weight have their weight plainly and durably marked on the outside to prevent accidents caused by lifting unmarked heavy packages with mechanical means intended for smaller loads.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India and applies to heavy packages transported by sea or inland waterways from any place in India. A 'heavy package' is defined as a package or object weighing not less than one metric ton (equal to 1000 kilogrammes, 2204.6 standard pounds, or 26.8 standard maunds). An 'inland water-way' is defined as any canal, river, lake, or other navigable water in India.

key_definitions.heavy_package: A package or other object weighing not less than one metric ton, which is equal to one thousand kilogrammes or 2204.6 standard pounds or 26.8 standard maunds.
key_definitions.inland_water-way: Any canal, river, lake or other navigable water in India.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its territorial extent (whole of India), and the procedure for its commencement via notification by the Central Government.
Defines key terms used in the Act, specifically 'heavy package' and 'inland water-way'.

main_sections.section_title: Obligation to mark weight on heavy packages
main_sections.description: Mandates that every person consigning a heavy package for transport by sea or inland waterway must clearly, durably, and conspicuously mark its gross weight. It also allows for marking approximate weight in circumstances specified by rules where determining the exact weight is difficult.
Empowers the Central Government to appoint inspectors to enforce the Act, assign them specific areas, and deems them as public servants.

Outlines the powers of inspectors, including entering and inspecting places or vessels, examining packages, and directing that non-compliant packages cannot be transported until marked. Inspectors can also mark the package themselves and recover expenses.
Specifies penalties for contravening Section 3 or inspector's directions (fine up to five hundred rupees) and for wilfully obstructing an inspector (fine up to two hundred rupees).
Addresses liability for offences committed by companies, holding the company and its responsible officers guilty, with provisions for individuals to prove lack of knowledge or due diligence.

Stipulates that only Presidency Magistrates or First Class Magistrates can try offences under this Act, and cognizance can only be taken upon a written complaint by an inspector within six months of the alleged offence.

main_sections.section_title: Protection of action taken in good faith
main_sections.description: Protects individuals from legal proceedings for any action taken in good faith or intended to be taken under the Act.

Grants the Central Government the power to make rules regarding the manner of marking, packing, and covering of heavy packages, circumstances for marking approximate weight, and other related matters. Rules are subject to parliamentary approval.

important_rules: Every person consigning a heavy package for transport by sea or inland waterway must clearly, durably, and conspicuously mark its gross weight on the package.
In specific cases or circumstances where determining the correct weight is difficult, as defined by rules, only the approximate weight may be marked.
Inspectors can direct that a heavy package not marked in accordance with Section 3 shall not be transported until it is correctly marked.
Expenses incurred by an inspector for marking a package themselves are recoverable as arrears of land revenue from the consignor.

penalties: Contravention of Section 3 or an inspector's direction under Section 5(b): fine up to five hundred rupees.
Wilful obstruction of an inspector: fine up to two hundred rupees.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Inspectors appointed by the Central Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through inspection of packages, direction of non-transportation of non-compliant packages, and legal proceedings for contravention or obstruction. Enforcement is also facilitated by the power of inspectors to mark packages and recover costs.

rights: Right to have packages transported if they comply with the Act's marking requirements.
Protection from legal proceedings for actions taken in good faith under the Act.
duties: Duty to mark the gross weight of heavy packages clearly, durably, and conspicuously before transport by sea or inland waterway.
Duty to comply with directions issued by inspectors.
Duty to not wilfully obstruct inspectors.
obligations: Every person consigning a heavy package has the obligation to ensure it is correctly marked.
Companies have an obligation to ensure their employees and operations comply with the Act, with specific liabilities for directors and officers.

key_procedures: Appointment of Inspectors: Central Government appoints inspectors via notification, assigning them specific areas.

Inspection and Enforcement: An inspector may enter, inspect, and examine packages. If a package is non-compliant, the inspector can direct it not to be transported or mark it themselves and recover costs.
Rule Making: Central Government can make rules for marking, packing, and other related aspects, subject to parliamentary review and approval.
Cognizance of Offences: A complaint in writing by an inspector within six months of the offence is required for a court to take cognizance. Only specific magistrates can try these offences.
administration: Central Government (through notifications and rule-making powers). Inspectors are appointed by the Central Government.
important_notes: The Act gives effect to an International Convention of 1929.
An amendment act, The Marking of Heavy Packages (Amendment) Act, 1961 (29 of 1961), is mentioned.
The definition of 'heavy package' includes specific weight conversions in pounds and maunds.
Inspectors are considered public servants under Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.

title: The Rajghat Samadhi Act, 1951
purpose: To provide for the administration and control of the Rajghat Samadhi in Delhi, ensuring its proper maintenance, preservation, and regulation, and establishing a statutory committee for these purposes.
scope: Applies to the Rajghat Samadhi in Delhi, including its premises and all buildings contained therein, as described in the Schedule. It covers the administration, control, and regulation of the Samadhi and its affairs.

key_definitions.Committee: The Rajghat Samadhi Committee constituted under this Act.
key_definitions.Samadhi: The structure built in token of reverence for Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat on the Western bank of the Jamuna in Delhi, and includes the premises described in the Schedule with all buildings contained therein, together with all additions thereto or alterations thereof which may be made after the commencement of this Act.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act and specifies that it comes into force on a date appointed by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette.
Defines 'Committee' and 'Samadhi' for the purposes of the Act.
Vests the administration and control of the Samadhi in a Committee and declares the Committee as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal, to sue and be sued through its Chairman.

Details the composition of the Rajghat Samadhi Committee, including ex-officio members (Mayor of Delhi), nominated officials and non-officials by the Central Government, and members of Parliament. It also outlines the appointment of the Chairman and the terms of office.

main_sections.section_title: Powers and duties of the Committee
main_sections.description: Outlines the powers and duties of the Committee, including administering the affairs of the Samadhi, keeping it in proper order and repair, organizing periodical functions, and doing other things conducive to efficient administration.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government to make rules
main_sections.description: Grants the Central Government the power to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out the objects of the Act and regulate access to the Samadhi.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Committee to make bye-laws
main_sections.description: Empowers the Committee to make bye-laws for matters such as convening meetings, quorum, appointment of employees, duties of employees, and submission of accounts. These bye-laws are subject to previous publication and approval by the Central Government.

main_sections.section_title: Rules and bye-laws to be laid before Parliament
main_sections.description: Mandates that all rules and bye-laws made under the Act must be laid before each House of Parliament for a specified period, allowing for modifications or annulment.

main_sections.section_title: Validity of acts of Committee not to be questioned by reason of vacancy, etc.
main_sections.description: States that no act or proceeding of the Committee shall be deemed invalid due to any vacancy or defect in its constitution.

important_rules: The Central Government may make rules to regulate access to the Samadhi or any portion thereof.
The Committee may make bye-laws for the conduct of its meetings, appointment and service conditions of employees, and submission of accounts.
All rules and bye-laws made under the Act must be laid before Parliament for a specified period.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Rajghat Samadhi Committee, under the general supervision and rule-making power of the Central Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the administration and control exercised by the Rajghat Samadhi Committee, by enforcing rules and bye-laws made under the Act, and potentially through actions by the magistracy and police as mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Reasons if legislative enactment is necessary for enforcement.

rights: The right of the public to access the Samadhi, subject to regulations made by the Central Government and the Committee.
duties: Duty of the Committee to administer the affairs of the Samadhi, keep it in proper order and repair, and organize periodical functions.
Duty of employees of the Committee to perform their assigned duties.
obligations: Obligation for rules and bye-laws to be laid before Parliament.
Obligation for bye-laws to be approved by the Central Government and to have undergone previous publication.

key_procedures: Establishment of the Rajghat Samadhi Committee with a specified composition.
Process for the Central Government to make rules and for the Committee to make bye-laws, including approval and parliamentary laying.
Conduct of meetings by the Committee, including convening, quorum, and procedure, as may be defined by bye-laws.
administration: The Rajghat Samadhi Committee, with oversight and rule-making powers vested in the Central Government.
important_notes: The Act was amended by the Rajghat Samadhi (Amendment) Act, 1958 and the Rajghat Samadhi (Amendment) Act, 1988.
Members nominated by the Central Government hold office during the pleasure of the Central Government.
The office of a member of the Committee does not disqualify them from being a member of Parliament.

title: The Assam (Alteration of Boundaries) Act, 1951
purpose: To alter the boundaries of the State of Assam consequent on the cession of a strip of territory comprised in that State to the Government of Bhutan, in accordance with the Indo-Bhutan Treaty of Friendship.
scope: This act applies to the State of Assam in India and cedes a specific strip of territory to the Government of Bhutan. The subject matter is the alteration of state boundaries due to territorial cession.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act as 'The Assam (Alteration of Boundaries) Act, 1951'.

main_sections.section_title: Alteration of the boundaries of Assam
main_sections.description: States that on and from the commencement of the Act, the territory of the State of Assam shall cease to comprise the strip of territory specified in the Schedule, which shall be ceded to the Government of Bhutan, and that the boundaries of Assam shall be deemed to have been altered accordingly.

main_sections.section_title: Amendment of the First Schedule to the Constitution
main_sections.description: Details the amendment to the First Schedule of the Constitution, specifically to Part A under the heading 'TERRITORIES OF STATES'. It inserts a clause stating that the territories of Assam shall not include the territories specified in the Schedule to this Act.

important_rules: Rule: The State of Assam shall cede the specified strip of territory to the Government of Bhutan.
Rule: The boundaries of the State of Assam are legally altered to reflect this cession.
Rule: The Constitution of India is amended to exclude the ceded territory from the territories of Assam.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Parliament of India (as this is an Act of Parliament).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the legislative process and the formal enactment of the law. The Act itself is the enforcement mechanism for the cession and boundary alteration.

duties: Duty of the Government of India to cede the specified territory to the Government of Bhutan as per the Indo-Bhutan Treaty of Friendship.
Duty to amend the First Schedule of the Constitution to reflect the altered boundaries of Assam.
obligations: Obligation to implement the undertaking given in Article 4 of the Indo-Bhutan Treaty of Friendship.
Obligation to act in accordance with Article 3 of the Constitution for altering state boundaries.

key_procedures: Procedure: Cession of a specified strip of territory from Assam to Bhutan.
Procedure: Amendment of the First Schedule of the Indian Constitution to reflect the altered boundaries of Assam.
administration: The Act is an enactment by the Parliament of India, implementing an international treaty. The administration of the ceded territory would fall under Bhutan's governance, and the remaining territory of Assam would continue to be administered by the State of Assam and the Union of India.
important_notes: The specific territory ceded is a strip measuring 32.81 square miles, located south of Bhutan, within defined geographical coordinates and demarcated by boundary pillars.
The Act was enacted to implement the provisions of Article 4 of the Indo-Bhutan Treaty of Friendship concluded on August 8, 1949, and ratified subsequently.
The views of the Legislature of Assam were ascertained and its Legislative Assembly adopted a resolution recommending the transfer of territory.

title: The All-India Services Act, 1951
purpose: To regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the All-India Services common to the Union and the States.
scope: Applies to the Indian Administrative Service, the Indian Police Service, and other All-India Services as specified in Section 2A (Indian Service of Engineers, Indian Forest Service, Indian Medical and Health Service). It regulates recruitment and conditions of service for individuals appointed to these services.

key_definitions.an All-India Service: Means the service known as the Indian Administrative Service or the service known as the Indian Police Service, or any other service specified in section 2A.

main_sections.description: States that the Act may be called the All-India Services Act, 1951.
Defines what constitutes an 'All-India Service' under this Act.

Specifies the constitution of additional All-India Services, including the Indian Service of Engineers, the Indian Forest Service, and the Indian Medical and Health Service, with effect from dates appointed by the Central Government.

main_sections.section_title: Regulation of recruitment and conditions of service
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to make rules for the regulation of recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to an All-India Service, after consultation with the concerned State Governments. It also outlines the procedure for laying these rules before Parliament and the process for modification or annulment.
States that all rules in force immediately before the commencement of this Act and applicable to an All-India Service shall continue to be in force and are deemed to be rules made under this Act.

important_rules: Central Government may make rules for recruitment and conditions of service of All-India Services after consultation with State Governments (Section 3(1)).
Rules can have retrospective effect, but not to prejudicially affect any person's interests (Section 3(1A)).
Rules and regulations made under this section must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and are subject to modification or annulment by Parliament (Section 3(2)).
Existing rules applicable to All-India Services before the Act's commencement continue in force and are deemed made under this Act (Section 4).

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Central Government
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through rules made under Section 3, which are subject to parliamentary oversight.

duties: State Governments have a duty to consult with the Central Government regarding rules for All-India Services.
obligations: Central Government has an obligation to make rules for the regulation of recruitment and conditions of service for All-India Services.
Rules made by the Central Government are subject to parliamentary scrutiny and modification.

key_procedures: Making of rules for recruitment and conditions of service: Central Government consults State Governments, notifies rules, and lays them before Parliament for approval/modification within a specified period (Section 3).
Establishment of new All-India Services: Central Government may appoint dates by notification in the Official Gazette for the constitution of new All-India Services (Section 2A).
administration: Central Government
important_notes: The Act was enacted to provide statutory authority for the management of All-India Services, filling a constitutional lacuna (Statement of Objects and Reasons).
The Act allows for the retrospective effect of rules but not in a manner that prejudicially affects individual interests (Section 3(1A)).
Parliament has significant oversight over rules and regulations made under this Act (Section 3(2)).

title: The Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951
purpose: To provide for the development and regulation of certain industries in India.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India and applies to industries specified in the First Schedule. It aims to bring these industries under the control of the Union Government in the public interest.

key_definitions.Advisory Council: The Central Advisory Council established under section 5 for advising on matters concerning the development and regulation of scheduled industries.
key_definitions.ancillary industrial undertaking: An industrial undertaking entitled to be regarded as ancillary under specific conditions outlined in section 11B.
key_definitions.current assets: Includes bank balances, cash, and other assets expected to be realized in cash or sold/consumed within twelve months in the ordinary course of business, excluding employee welfare fund contributions.
key_definitions.current liabilities: Liabilities that must be met on demand or within twelve months of being incurred, including any suspended under section 18FB.
key_definitions.Development Council: A Development Council established under section 6 for a scheduled industry or group of industries.
key_definitions.existing industrial undertaking: An undertaking in existence or for which effective steps were taken before the Act's commencement (or amendment date for added industries).
key_definitions.factory: Premises where manufacturing is carried out with or without power, involving a specified number of workers.
key_definitions.High Court: The High Court having jurisdiction over the registered office of a company.
key_definitions.industrial undertaking: Any undertaking pertaining to a scheduled industry, carried on in one or more factories by any person or authority, including the Government.
key_definitions.new article: An article falling under a different item in the First Schedule, or an article with a specific trademark or patent not previously manufactured/produced by the undertaking.
key_definitions.notified order: An order published in the Official Gazette.
key_definitions.owner: The person or authority with ultimate control over an industrial undertaking, including its manager, managing director, or managing agent.
key_definitions.prescribed: As defined by rules made under this Act.
key_definitions.scheduled industry: Any industry specified in the First Schedule.
key_definitions.small scale industrial undertaking: An industrial undertaking entitled to be regarded as small scale under requirements specified in section 11B.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its territorial extent (whole of India), and the date of commencement through notification.

main_sections.section_title: Declaration as to expediency of control by the Union
main_sections.description: Declares it expedient in the public interest for the Union Government to control the industries specified in the First Schedule.
Defines various terms used in the Act, such as 'Advisory Council', 'Development Council', 'industrial undertaking', 'scheduled industry', etc.

main_sections.section_title: Establishment and constitution of Central Advisory Council and its functions
main_sections.description: Describes the establishment of the Central Advisory Council to advise the government on matters concerning scheduled industries and outlines its composition and functions.

main_sections.section_title: Establishment and constitution of Development Councils and their functions
main_sections.description: Details the establishment of Development Councils for specific scheduled industries or groups of industries, their constitution, and functions.
Mandates the registration of existing industrial undertakings.
Provides for the licensing of new industrial undertakings.

main_sections.section_title: Power to cause investigation to be made into scheduled industries or industrial undertakings
main_sections.description: Grants the Central Government power to investigate scheduled industries or industrial undertakings.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government to assume management or control of an industrial undertaking in certain cases
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to take over the management or control of an industrial undertaking under specific circumstances.
Outlines the penalties for contravention of the provisions of the Act.
Confers the power on the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

important_rules: Existing industrial undertakings must be registered (Section 10).
New industrial undertakings require a licence (Section 11).
Licences can be revoked or amended under certain conditions (Section 12).
The Central Government can investigate scheduled industries or undertakings (Section 15).
The Central Government has the power to assume management or control of industrial undertakings in certain cases (Section 18A).
Specific rules for the management or control of industrial undertakings owned by companies in liquidation exist (Chapter IIIAA).
The Central Government can control the supply, distribution, and price of certain articles (Section 18G).
Penalties are prescribed for violations of the Act (Section 24).

penalties: Fines for contravention of the Act's provisions (Section 24).
Specific penalties may be detailed within other sections for particular offenses.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Central Government and authorities appointed by it.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through investigations, licensing, taking over management, imposing penalties, and making rules and orders.

rights: Undertakings have the right to operate if licensed or registered according to the Act.
Persons have the right to appeal against certain decisions (Section 24B).
duties: Industrial undertakings must comply with registration and licensing requirements.
Owners of industrial undertakings have a duty to allow investigations and adhere to government directions.
Companies in liquidation must cooperate with takeover or management by the Central Government.
obligations: Obligation to obtain licenses for new industrial undertakings.
Obligation to register existing industrial undertakings.
Obligation to comply with orders issued by the Central Government under the Act.
Obligation for companies in liquidation to facilitate the management or control of their industrial undertakings by authorized persons.
Obligation to adhere to controls on supply, distribution, and price of specified articles.

key_procedures: Procedure for Registration of Existing Industrial Undertakings: Undertakings must apply for and obtain registration as per Section 10.
Procedure for Licensing of New Industrial Undertakings: Undertakings must apply for and obtain a licence before establishment or expansion as per Section 11.
Investigation Procedure: If the Central Government suspects contravention or maladministration, it can order an investigation under Section 15, appointing persons to conduct it.
Procedure for Taking Over Management/Control: Under Section 18A, the Central Government can take over management/control of an undertaking by issuing a notified order.
Procedure for Rule Making: The Central Government can make rules for the Act's implementation, often after consulting the Advisory Council (Section 30).
administration: The Central Government, with the assistance of the Central Advisory Council and Development Councils.
important_notes: The Act can be amended by subsequent legislation, as indicated by the list of amending Acts.
The Act provides for the delegation of powers by the Central Government (Section 25).
Actions taken in good faith under the Act are protected (Section 29C).
Debts incurred by an authorized person taking over an undertaking have priority (Section 29D).
The Act's application does not bar other laws from applying (Section 31).

title: The Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
purpose: To provide for the requisitioning and acquisition of immovable property for the purposes of the Union.
scope: Extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir (now applicable to Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh). It applies to immovable property.

key_definitions.award: Any award of an arbitrator made under section 8.
key_definitions.competent authority: Any person or authority authorized by the Central Government to perform functions of the competent authority under this Act for a specified area.
key_definitions.landlord: Any person who is receiving or is entitled to receive rent for any premises, whether on their own account or on behalf of another, or as a trustee, guardian, or receiver.
key_definitions.person interested: Includes all persons claiming or entitled to claim an interest in the compensation payable on account of requisitioning or acquisition of property.
key_definitions.premises: Any building or part of a building, including its garden, grounds, outhouses, and fittings.
key_definitions.prescribed: Prescribed by rules made under this Act.
key_definitions.property: Immovable property of every kind, including rights in or over such property.
key_definitions.tenant: Any person by whom or on whose account rent is payable for any premises, including sub-tenants and others who have derived title under the tenant.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its territorial extent, and its duration.
Defines various terms used in the Act, such as 'award', 'competent authority', 'landlord', 'person interested', 'premises', 'prescribed', 'property', and 'tenant'.

Empowers the competent authority to requisition immovable property if it is needed for a public purpose of the Union. It outlines the procedure involving showing cause and potential orders to prevent disposal or alteration of the property.

main_sections.section_title: Power to take possession of requisitioned property.
main_sections.description: Grants the competent authority the power to order the surrender of possession of requisitioned property and to use necessary force if there is non-compliance.
Details the circumstances and procedures for releasing requisitioned property. It mandates release if the purpose ceases to exist and sets time limits for requisitioned properties.
Allows the Central Government to acquire requisitioned property for a public purpose by publishing a notice, after providing an opportunity for the owner and interested parties to show cause.

main_sections.section_title: Principles and method of determining compensation.
main_sections.description: Outlines how compensation for requisitioned or acquired property is to be determined.
Specifies penalties for contravening the provisions of the Act.

important_rules: Rule 1: The competent authority must call upon the owner or possessor of property to show cause within fifteen days why it should not be requisitioned for a public purpose of the Union. (Section 3(1)(a))

Rule 2: The competent authority may order that the property shall not be disposed of, structurally altered, or let out to a tenant without permission for a period not exceeding two months. (Section 3(1)(b))

Rule 3: Property bona fide used by the owner as residence for themselves or their family, or exclusively used for religious worship, or as a school, hospital, public library, or orphanage, shall not be requisitioned. (Section 3(2) proviso)
Rule 4: Tenants residing in premises for at least two months before notice shall be provided with alternative suitable accommodation. (Section 3(2) further proviso)
Rule 5: Requisitioned property must be used for the purposes specified in the notice of requisition. (Section 5(1))

Rule 6: Landlords may be ordered to execute necessary repairs on requisitioned premises, and failure to do so will result in the competent authority carrying out repairs at the landlord's expense, deductible from compensation. (Section 5(2))
Rule 7: The Central Government shall release requisitioned property within seventeen years from commencement or from the date possession was taken, unless acquired under section 7. (Section 6(1A))

penalties: Penalty for offences as specified in Section 20 of the Act.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Competent authority, authorized by the Central Government.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through notices, orders, taking possession of property, and potentially using necessary force. Enforcement also includes the power to make rules and conduct inquiries.

rights: Right to show cause against requisitioning of property.
Right to be provided with alternative accommodation if a tenant is displaced.
Right to receive compensation for requisitioned or acquired property.
Right to appeal orders of requisitioning and awards of compensation.
duties: Duty to surrender or deliver possession of requisitioned property when ordered.
Duty to comply with orders regarding disposal, alteration, or letting of property.
Duty of landlord to carry out necessary repairs.
obligations: Obligation to provide information as required by the competent authority.
Obligation to allow entry and inspection of property.

key_procedures: Procedure for Requisitioning: 1. Competent authority forms an opinion that property is needed for a Union purpose. 2. Notice is issued to the owner/possessor to show cause within 15 days. 3. Orders may be issued to prevent disposal/alteration. 4. After considering cause, competent authority may issue a written requisition order. 5. Alternative accommodation provided to existing tenants. (Section 3)

Procedure for Taking Possession: 1. Competent authority issues a written notice to surrender possession within 30 days. 2. If no compliance, competent authority can take possession using necessary force. (Section 4)

Procedure for Release from Requisition: 1. Central Government may release property. 2. Property must be restored as far as possible in the same condition. 3. Specific time limits for release are mandated. 4. Competent authority specifies to whom possession should be given. (Section 6)

Procedure for Acquisition: 1. Central Government may decide to acquire requisitioned property for a public purpose. 2. Owner/interested parties are given an opportunity to show cause and be heard. 3. Notice of acquisition is published in the Official Gazette. (Section 7)
administration: Central Government (via the 'competent authority' designated by it).
important_notes: The Act has been extended to various Union Territories over time.
Sub-section (3) of Section 1 was omitted.
The Act is now applicable to the Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
The duration for releasing requisitioned property has been specified as seventeen years.
Provisions exist for re-issuing notices for acquisition if opportunities were not adequately given, with provisions for interest on compensation.

title: The Cinematograph Act, 1952
purpose: To make provision for the certification of cinematograph films for exhibition and for regulating exhibitions by means of cinematographs.
scope: Parts I, II, and IV extend to the whole of India. Part III extends to the Union territories only. The Act is administered by the Central Government.

key_definitions.adult: A person who has completed their eighteenth year.
key_definitions.board: The Board of Film Certification constituted by the Central Government.
key_definitions.certificate: The certificate granted by the Board under section 5A.
key_definitions.cinematograph: Includes any apparatus for the representation of moving pictures or series of pictures.
key_definitions.infringing_copy: Has the same meaning as assigned in sub-clause (ii) of clause (m) of section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957.
key_definitions.prescribed: Prescribed by rules made under this Act.
key_definitions.ua_marker: An age-based indicator for a film which has received or is intended to receive a “UA” Certificate under section 4, such as “UA 7+”, “UA 13+”, or “UA 16+”.

main_sections.description: Specifies the short title of the Act, its territorial extent (Parts I, II, IV to whole of India; Part III to Union territories), and the commencement date.
Provides definitions for various terms used in the Act, including 'adult', 'Board', 'certificate', 'cinematograph', 'film', 'infringing copy', 'prescribed', and 'UA marker'.
Establishes the Board of Film Certification, its composition (Chairman and other members), appointment by the Central Government, and terms and conditions of service for its members.

Outlines the process for examining films. Applicants must apply to the Board. The Board can sanction films for unrestricted public exhibition (with or without a UA marker), restricted to adults, or restricted to specific professions/classes. It can also direct modifications or refuse sanction. Applicants have a right to be heard. Provisions for exhibition on television are also included.

Empowers the Central Government to establish regional advisory panels to assist the Board in its functions. It also details the appointment of regional officers and the consultation process with advisory panels.

Details the types of certificates that can be granted: 'U' for unrestricted public exhibition, 'UA' with a UA marker, 'A' for restricted to adults, and 'S' for restricted to members of any profession or class of persons. It also states that certified films are not liable for obscenity charges. Orders of refusal or grant of certificates are published in the Gazette of India.

main_sections.section_title: Principles of guidance in certifying films
main_sections.description: Sets out principles guiding the certification of films. Films against the sovereignty, integrity, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency, morality, defamation, contempt of court, or incitement to offences, shall not be certified. The Central Government can issue directions on guiding principles.

Provides for appeals against orders of the Board (refusal, 'A' or 'S' certificate, 'UA' certificate with any UA marker, or direction for excisions/modifications) to the High Court within thirty days, extendable by another thirty days for sufficient cause.

main_sections.section_title: Revisional powers of the Central Government
main_sections.description: Grants the Central Government revisional powers over the Board's orders.

main_sections.section_title: Penalties for contraventions of this Part
main_sections.description: Specifies penalties for contraventions of Part II of the Act.
States that cinematograph exhibitions must be licensed.
Defines the licensing authority.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government or local authority to suspend exhibition of films in certain cases
main_sections.description: Grants power to the Central Government or local authority to suspend exhibition of films in specific circumstances.

main_sections.section_title: Penalties for contravention of this Part
main_sections.description: Specifies penalties for contravention of Part III of the Act.
Deals with the repeal of previous enactments.

important_rules: Films must be certified by the Board of Film Certification before public exhibition.
Films certified 'U' are for unrestricted public exhibition.
Films certified 'UA' are for unrestricted public exhibition with parental guidance.
Films certified 'A' are restricted to adults.
Films certified 'S' are restricted to members of any profession or specific class of persons.
Exhibitions by means of cinematographs require a license.
The Central Government or local authority can suspend film exhibitions in certain cases.
Unauthorized recording or exhibition of films is prohibited (Section 6AA and 6AB).

penalties: Penalties for contraventions of Part II (Certification of Films for Public Exhibition) are specified in Section 7.
Penalties for contraventions of Part III (Regulation of Exhibitions by Means of Cinematographs) are specified in Section 14.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Central Government, Board of Film Certification, and licensing authorities are involved in enforcement.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Enforcement involves examination and certification of films, licensing of exhibitions, power to suspend exhibitions, and imposition of penalties for contraventions. The Central Government has revisional powers. Power of seizure is also provided.

rights: Applicants for film certification have the right to be heard.
Appeals can be filed against the Board's orders.
Certified films are generally protected from prosecution for obscenity.
Parents and lawful guardians have the right to decide if a child should view a film with a UA marker.
duties: Applicants have a duty to apply for certification.
Distributors and exhibitors have a duty to comply with the Act and the terms of the certification.
The Board has a duty to examine films and issue certificates based on prescribed principles.
Advisory panels have a duty to examine films and make recommendations to the Board.
obligations: Obligation to obtain a license for cinematograph exhibitions.
Obligation to adhere to the classification of films (U, UA, A, S).
Obligation to provide information and documents to distributors and exhibitors regarding certified films.
Prohibition of unauthorized recording and exhibition of films.

key_procedures: Application for film certification to the Board of Film Certification.
Examination of the film by the Board, potentially with consultation of advisory panels.
Sanctioning of the film with a specific certificate (U, UA, A, S) or refusal, possibly with directions for modifications.
Publication of certification orders in the Gazette of India.
Appealing against Board orders to the High Court.
Obtaining a license for conducting cinematograph exhibitions.
Suspension or revocation of film certificates or exhibition licenses under certain conditions.
administration: Central Government
important_notes: The Act has been amended multiple times since its enactment in 1952.
Part III of the Act only extends to the Union territories.
Specific provisions have been omitted over time, for example, Section 2A concerning references to laws not in force in Jammu and Kashmir.
The definition of 'UA marker' and its application have been updated by recent amendments (2023).

title: The Notaries Act, 1952
purpose: To regulate the profession of notaries, empowering the Central and State Governments to appoint them and define their functions, thereby replacing the old system where notaries derived authority from an English institution.
scope: Extends to the whole of India. Applies to legal practitioners and other persons appointed as notaries under the Act.

key_definitions.instrument: Includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, modified, limited, extended, suspended, extinguished or recorded.
key_definitions.legal_practitioner: Means an advocate entered in any roll under the provisions of the Advocates Act, 1961 (25 of 1961).
key_definitions.notary: A person appointed as such under this Act. Includes, for a period of two years from the commencement of the Act, persons appointed as notary public under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and in practice immediately before such commencement.
key_definitions.prescribed: Means prescribed by rules made under this Act.
key_definitions.register: A Register of Notaries maintained by the Government under section 4.
key_definitions.state_government: In relation to a Union territory, means the administrator thereof.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, its territorial extent (whole of India), and the date of commencement (as appointed by the Central Government by notification).
Defines key terms used in the Act, including 'instrument', 'legal practitioner', 'notary', 'prescribed', 'Register', and 'State Government'.
Empowers the Central Government and State Governments to appoint any legal practitioners or other persons with prescribed qualifications as notaries.

Mandates the Central and State Governments to maintain Registers of appointed notaries, including particulars like name, date of birth, address, date of entry, qualifications, and other prescribed details.

main_sections.section_title: Entry of names in the Register and issue or renewal of certificates of practice
main_sections.description: Outlines the process for a notary to get their name entered in the Register and obtain a certificate of practice, which is valid for five years and can be renewed.

main_sections.section_title: Annual publication of lists of notaries
main_sections.description: Requires the Central and State Governments to publish an annual list of practicing notaries in the Official Gazette.
Stipulates that every notary shall have and use a prescribed seal.

Details the acts a notary may perform by virtue of their office, including verifying instruments, presenting negotiable instruments, noting dishonour, administering oaths, preparing mercantile documents, translating documents, and acting as a Commissioner, arbitrator, mediator, or conciliator.
Prohibits practice as a notary or doing any notarial act without a valid certificate of practice, with an exception for the clerk of a notary presenting negotiable instruments.

Specifies the grounds for removing a notary's name from the Register, including request, non-payment of fees, insolvency, professional misconduct, conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude, or failure to renew the certificate of practice.

main_sections.section_title: Construction of references to notaries public in other laws
main_sections.description: Clarifies that any reference to a 'notary public' in other laws shall be construed as a reference to a notary entitled to practice under this Act.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for falsely representing to be a notary, etc.
main_sections.description: Prescribes a penalty (imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both) for falsely representing oneself as a notary or practicing without a valid certificate.
Regulates the cognizance of offences under the Act, requiring a complaint from an authorized officer and limiting trial to Presidency Magistrates or First Class Magistrates.

main_sections.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements for recognition of notarial acts done by foreign notaries
main_sections.description: Allows the Central Government to declare reciprocal recognition of notarial acts done by foreign notaries based on the laws and practices of other countries.

Grants the Central Government the power to make rules for carrying out the Act's purposes, including qualifications, application procedures, fees, register forms, seal design, and procedures for misconduct inquiries.
This section, dealing with the amendment of Act 26 of 1881, has been repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1957.

important_rules: A notary must have a prescribed seal of a specific form and design.
A notary's act is only considered a notarial act when done under their signature and official seal.
No person shall practice as a notary or perform notarial acts without a valid certificate of practice, except for a notary's clerk presenting negotiable instruments on behalf of the notary.
Notaries must ensure their certificate of practice is renewed to continue practicing.
The Central Government can make rules regarding notary qualifications, appointment procedures, fees, and the conduct of notaries.

penalties: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both, for falsely representing to be a notary or practicing in contravention of section 9.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Central Government or State Government (through authorized officers for cognizance of offences).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Complaints for offences must be in writing by an officer authorized by the Central or State Government. Trials are limited to specific magistrates. Removal of names from the Register by the appointing Government for specified reasons.

rights: Right to have one's name entered in the Register and to receive a certificate of practice.
Right to practice as a notary upon holding a valid certificate.
Right to perform specified notarial acts.
Right to have foreign notarial acts recognized in India under reciprocal arrangements.
duties: Duty to possess prescribed qualifications.
Duty to pay prescribed fees.
Duty to maintain a prescribed seal.
Duty to act within the scope of authorized notarial functions.
Duty to get the certificate of practice renewed.
Duty to adhere to rules regarding professional conduct and avoid misconduct.
Duty to comply with rules made by the Central Government.
obligations: Obligation to obtain and maintain a certificate of practice to perform notarial acts.
Obligation to be registered with the relevant Government.
Obligation to undergo inquiry if accused of professional misconduct.
Obligation to cooperate with the enforcement of the Act and rules.

key_procedures: Appointment of a notary: Legal practitioners or other qualified persons may be appointed by the Central or State Government upon meeting prescribed qualifications.

Obtaining a certificate of practice: A notary intending to practice pays a prescribed fee to the appointing government to have their name entered in the Register and receive a certificate valid for five years.
Renewal of certificate of practice: The appointing government may renew a notary's certificate for a period of five years upon application and payment of prescribed fee.
Removal from Register: A notary's name can be removed by the appointing government upon request, non-payment of fees, insolvency, misconduct, conviction, or failure to renew the certificate.
Cognizance of offences: No court shall take cognizance of an offence without a written complaint from an authorized officer.
Reciprocal recognition of foreign notarial acts: Central Government may issue notification for recognizing foreign notarial acts in India.
Rule making process: Central Government makes rules by notification, which are laid before Parliament for modification or annulment.
administration: Central Government and State Governments administer the Act. The Central Government is responsible for making rules and ensuring reciprocal arrangements.
important_notes: The Act was extended to the State of Jammu and Kashmir (now Union Territories) and other specified regions over time.
There was a transitional provision for persons already appointed as notary public under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, to continue for two years from the commencement of this Act.
The period of imprisonment for falsely representing to be a notary or practicing without a certificate has been enhanced from three months to one year.
The period of validity of a certificate of practice has been changed from three years to five years.

title: The Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952
purpose: To provide for the salaries and allowances of Ministers, formalizing privileges previously regulated by executive instructions, and removing statutory reductions in salaries previously subjected to voluntary cuts.
scope: Applies to Ministers (including Deputy Ministers) of the Council of Ministers. The scope is national within India. Certain provisions also relate to the allowances and privileges of Members of Parliament for comparative purposes.

key_definitions.Minister: A member of the Council of Ministers, by whatever name called, and includes a Deputy Minister.

main_sections.description: States the short title of the Act as 'The Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952'.
Defines 'Minister' to include any member of the Council of Ministers, regardless of their title, and also Deputy Ministers.

Entitles each Minister to a monthly salary and a daily constituency allowance at the same rates specified for Members of Parliament in the Salaries, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954.

Grants Ministers the entitlement to a furnished residence free of rent during their term of office and for one month thereafter, with no personal charges for maintenance. Also provides for the continued use of the residence by the Minister's family for a period after their death.

Specifies the monthly sumptuary allowance rates for the Prime Minister, Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers. It also includes a temporary reduction in this allowance due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

main_sections.section_title: Travelling and daily allowances to Ministers
main_sections.description: Entitles Ministers to travelling allowances for themselves and their families for journeys to assume or relinquish office, and for tours undertaken in the discharge of official duties. It also allows for an annual personal travel allowance within India for the Minister, spouse/children, or companions, with a limit on the number of fares.
Grants Ministers and their family members free medical treatment and accommodation in government-maintained hospitals.

main_sections.section_title: Advances to Ministers for purchase of motor-cars
main_sections.description: Allows for repayable advances to Ministers for the purchase of motor-cars to facilitate the convenient and efficient discharge of their duties.

main_sections.section_title: Ministers not to draw salary or allowances as Members of Parliament
main_sections.description: Prohibits individuals receiving salary or allowances under this Act from also drawing salary or allowances for their membership of either House of Parliament.

main_sections.section_title: Notification respecting appointment, etc., of Ministers to be conclusive evidence thereof
main_sections.description: States that the publication of a notification in the Official Gazette regarding a person becoming or ceasing to be a Minister is conclusive evidence for all purposes of the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Exemption from liability to pay income-tax on certain perquisites received by a Minister
main_sections.description: Exempts the value of rent-free furnished residences (including maintenance) provided to Ministers under Section 4 from being included in their taxable income under the head 'Salaries' as per the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Empowers the Central Government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act. Rules made after a specific amendment date must be laid before each House of Parliament and approved before coming into force.

Regularizes certain payments made or incurred before the commencement of the Act, including salaries to Ministers of Cabinet rank (not Members of the Cabinet), charges for hospital accommodation and medical treatment, and travelling/daily allowances to Deputy Ministers.
This section pertains to the repeal of Act 53 of 1947 and has been repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1957.

important_rules: Ministers are entitled to a monthly salary and a daily constituency allowance at rates equivalent to those for Members of Parliament.

Ministers are entitled to rent-free furnished residence during their term and for a period thereafter, with maintenance covered. The family of a deceased Minister is also entitled to use the residence for a specified period.
Specific monthly sumptuary allowances are prescribed for different categories of Ministers, with a temporary reduction for COVID-19 exigencies.
Ministers are eligible for travelling allowances for official journeys and a limited personal travel allowance for themselves and family/companions annually.
Ministers and their families are entitled to free medical treatment and accommodation in government hospitals.
Ministers may receive repayable advances for the purchase of motor-cars.
Ministers receiving salaries and allowances under this Act cannot also draw benefits as Members of Parliament.
Notifications regarding a Minister's appointment or cessation are conclusive proof.
Rent-free furnished residences provided to Ministers are exempt from income tax.
The Central Government is empowered to make rules to implement the Act, with rules subject to parliamentary approval.
Certain payments made before the Act's commencement are deemed to have been properly made.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Central Government and Parliament (through rule-making and approval processes). Specific enforcement mechanisms are not detailed in the provided sections.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the provisions of the Act, rules made by the Central Government, and potentially through parliamentary oversight.

rights: Right to receive a salary and daily constituency allowance.
Right to use a furnished residence free of rent and maintenance charges.
Right to receive a sumptuary allowance.
Right to travelling and daily allowances for official duties and personal travel.
Right to free medical treatment and hospital accommodation.
Right to receive repayable advances for motor-car purchase.
Right to have perquisites like rent-free residence exempted from income tax.
obligations: Ministers must not draw salary/allowances as Members of Parliament while receiving benefits under this Act.
Ministers (or their families) must comply with rules regarding the use and payment for residences after a Minister's death.
Ministers must adhere to rules regarding travel allowances.
Rules made by the Central Government are subject to parliamentary approval.

key_procedures: Assumption and relinquishment of office by Ministers, leading to entitlements for travel allowances.
Application for and receipt of repayable advances for motor-car purchase.
Publication of official gazette notifications to establish facts about ministerial appointments.
Procedure for making and approving rules under the Act, involving laying before Parliament and obtaining approval.
Regularization of past payments and expenditures.
administration: The Central Government (indicated through the power to make rules and specific entitlements).

title: The Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952
purpose: To provide for the appointment of Commissions of Inquiry and to vest such Commissions with certain powers for the purpose of making an inquiry into any definite matter of public importance.
scope: Extends to the whole of India. Applicable to inquiries into matters relatable to entries in List I, List II, or List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Certain sections may also apply to other inquiring authorities.

key_definitions.appropriate government: The Central Government (for inquiries into List I, II, or III entries appointed by it) or the State Government (for inquiries into List II or III entries appointed by it).
key_definitions.commission: A Commission of Inquiry appointed under section 3.
key_definitions.prescribed: Prescribed by rules made under this Act.

main_sections.description: States the short title of the Act, its extent (whole of India), and the commencement date (to be appointed by the Central Government).
Defines key terms used in the Act, including 'appropriate Government', 'Commission', and 'prescribed'.

Details the process for appointing a Commission of Inquiry by the appropriate Government, including circumstances where it is mandatory (if a resolution is passed by Parliament or State Legislature). It also outlines provisions for concurrent inquiries by Central and State Governments and the laying of reports before Parliament/Legislature.

Grants the Commission the powers of a civil court for specific matters, including summoning and examining persons, requiring discovery and production of documents, receiving evidence on affidavits, requisitioning public records, and issuing commissions for examinations.

Empowers the appropriate Government to extend certain provisions related to the Commission's powers, such as requiring information, seizing documents, and treating offenses before the Commission as offenses under the Indian Penal Code. It also specifies that proceedings before the Commission are judicial proceedings.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Commission to utilise the services of certain officers and investigation agencies for conducting investigation pertaining to inquiry
main_sections.description: Allows the Commission to utilize the services of officers and investigation agencies of the Central or State Governments for conducting investigations related to the inquiry, with the concurrence of the relevant government. These officers can summon persons, require documents, and requisition public records.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Commission to appoint assessors
main_sections.description: Grants the Commission the power to appoint assessors with special knowledge to assist and advise in the inquiry.

main_sections.section_title: Statements made by persons to the Commission
main_sections.description: Provides protection against the use of statements made by a person in the course of giving evidence before the Commission in civil or criminal proceedings, except for prosecutions for giving false evidence.

main_sections.section_title: Commission to cease to exist when so notified
main_sections.description: Allows the appropriate Government to declare, by notification, that a Commission shall cease to exist.

main_sections.section_title: Procedure to be followed by the Commission
main_sections.description: Mandates that the Commission shall be guided by the principles of natural justice and shall follow such procedure as the appropriate Government may by rule from time to time prescribe.

main_sections.section_title: Members, etc., to be public servants
main_sections.description: Declares that members of a Commission and any officer or other person appointed to assist the Commission shall be deemed to be public servants within the meaning of the Indian Penal Code.
Empowers the appropriate Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

important_rules: The appropriate Government may appoint a Commission of Inquiry for inquiring into any definite matter of public importance.
A Commission shall have the powers of a civil court in matters like summoning persons, discovery of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits.
Statements made by persons to the Commission are protected from being used against them in civil or criminal proceedings, except for false evidence.
Proceedings before the Commission are deemed to be judicial proceedings.
The Commission may utilize services of government officers and investigation agencies for its inquiries.

penalties: Penalty for acts calculated to bring the Commission or any member thereof into disrepute (Section 10A).
Offences like obstruction, giving false evidence, or disobedience of summons before the Commission can be treated as offenses under the Indian Penal Code (Sections 4 and 5).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The 'appropriate Government' (Central or State Government) appoints and can dissolve Commissions. The Commission itself exercises powers to enforce its inquiries.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the powers vested in the Commission (civil court powers, summoning, document production), by treating certain acts before it as offenses under the IPC, and by the appropriate Government's ability to issue notifications and make rules.

rights: Right to be heard if likely to be prejudicially affected (Section 8B).
Right of cross-examination and representation by a legal practitioner (Section 8C).
duties: Duty to furnish information when required by the Commission, subject to privilege (Section 5(2)).
Duty to appear and give evidence before the Commission when summoned.
Duty to assist the Commission in its inquiries.
obligations: Persons required to furnish information are legally bound to do so (Section 5(2)).
Proceedings before the Commission are judicial proceedings, implying obligations associated with such proceedings.

key_procedures: Appointment of a Commission by the appropriate Government through notification.
Inquiry conducted by the Commission, with powers similar to a civil court.
Utilization of investigation agencies for preliminary inquiries.
Persons likely to be affected are given a chance to be heard.
Submission of a report by the Commission to the appropriate Government.
Laying of the Commission's report and action taken memorandum before Parliament or the State Legislature.
administration: The Central Government or State Government, as the 'appropriate Government', administers this Act by appointing Commissions and making rules. Various government departments and investigation agencies can be utilized for inquiries.
important_notes: The Act was significantly amended in 1971 and subsequent years.
Certain provisions regarding Jammu and Kashmir have been adapted or omitted due to reorganization.

title: The Reserve and Auxiliary Air Forces Act, 1952
purpose: To provide for the constitution and regulation of certain Air Force Reserves and also an Auxiliary Air Force and for matters connected therewith.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India. It applies to persons eligible for service in the Regular Air Force Reserve, Air Defence Reserve, and Auxiliary Air Force, based on their qualifications, age, and previous service in the Air Force.

key_definitions.Air Force Reserve: Any of the Air Force Reserves raised and maintained under this Act.
key_definitions.competent authority: An air officer or a committee consisting of two or more air officers appointed under section 3.
key_definitions.prescribed: Prescribed by rules made under this Act.
key_definitions.Air Force Act, 1950: Words and expressions defined in the Air Force Act, 1950, and not defined in this Act shall have the meanings assigned to them by that Act.

main_sections.description: Provides the short title of the Act, specifies its territorial extent (whole of India), and outlines its commencement. Chapter I comes into force immediately, while other provisions come into force on dates appointed by the Central Government.
Defines key terms used in the Act, including 'Air Force Reserve', 'competent authority', and 'prescribed'. It also references the Air Force Act, 1950, for other definitions.
Empowers the Central Government to appoint an air officer or a committee of air officers as the 'competent authority' to perform functions under the Act for a specified area.

main_sections.section_title: Constitution of Regular Air Force Reserve
main_sections.description: Details the Central Government's power to raise and maintain the Regular Air Force Reserve, consisting of persons transferred or appointed to it.
Outlines the Central Government's authority to establish and maintain the Air Defence Reserve, comprising persons deemed enrolled under Section 16.
Grants the Central Government the power to raise and maintain an Auxiliary Air Force and to constitute squadrons and units.

main_sections.section_title: Liability to be called up for service
main_sections.description: Specifies the liability of members of the Reserve and Auxiliary Air Forces to be called up for service.
States that the Air Force Act, 1950, applies to members of the Reserve and Auxiliary Air Forces when called up for service.
Details the penalties for contraventions of the Act's provisions.

main_sections.section_title: Power of Central Government to grant exemptions
main_sections.description: Grants the Central Government the power to exempt certain persons or categories of persons from the provisions of the Act.
Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

important_rules: Members of the Regular Air Force Reserve are liable to serve for their prescribed Reserve liability period, or the remainder of their liability in the Air Defence Reserve/Auxiliary Air Force, with potential extensions by the competent authority up to five years.

Citizens of India meeting specific criteria related to pilot's licenses, flying experience, navigation experience, radio operator's licenses, ground engineer's licenses, or employment in aviation are obligated to register for the Air Defence Reserve within a prescribed period.

Persons liable for inquiry for the Air Defence Reserve are subject to this liability until they reach specific age limits (37 for certain pilot/navigation roles, 50 for ground engineer/aerodrome control roles).

Individuals registered and found fit for the Air Defence Reserve are liable for service until they complete specific ages (42 for pilot/navigation roles, 55 for ground engineer/aerodrome control roles).
Members of the Reserve and Auxiliary Air Forces are subject to the provisions of the Air Force Act, 1950, when called up for service.
Reinstatement in civil employment for persons performing service under this Act, and preservation of certain rights, are provided for.

penalties: The Act includes a section on 'Penalties' (Section 30), indicating that contraventions of its provisions will attract penalties, although the specific nature of these penalties is not detailed in the provided text excerpt.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The 'competent authority' appointed under Section 3, and potentially other designated authorities under the Air Force Act, 1950.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the appointment of a competent authority, calling up individuals for inquiry and service, registration processes, and the application of the Air Force Act, 1950, to members when on service. The Central Government also has powers to make rules and grant exemptions.

rights: Right to reinstatement in civil employ upon completion of service under the Act (Section 27).
Preservation of certain rights for persons called up for service (Section 28).
Officers transferred or appointed to the Regular Air Force Reserve are entitled to hold the same rank they last held (Section 6).
duties: Obligation to register for the Air Defence Reserve if meeting specific criteria (Section 11).
Obligation to present oneself for inquiry and medical examination when called up (Sections 13, 14).
Obligation to comply with directions from medical officers during examination (Section 14).
Obligation to serve in the Reserve or Auxiliary Air Force for the prescribed periods.
Obligation to adhere to the provisions of the Air Force Act, 1950, when on service.
obligations: Members of the Regular Air Force Reserve are liable to serve for their specified periods.
Persons eligible for the Air Defence Reserve are obligated to register and are liable to be called up for inquiry and service.
Members of the Auxiliary Air Force are constituted and are subject to service obligations as prescribed.

key_procedures: Constitution and maintenance of the Regular Air Force Reserve by the Central Government (Section 4).
Recruitment to the Regular Air Force Reserve by transfer or appointment by the competent authority (Section 5).
Obligation for eligible citizens to register for the Air Defence Reserve by filling and lodging a prescribed form (Section 11).
Calling-up for inquiry by the competent authority for individuals liable under Section 12, requiring them to present themselves for inquiry regarding fitness for service (Section 13).
Medical examination of persons called up for inquiry as directed by the competent authority (Section 14).
Registration of persons found fit for enrolment in the Air Defence Reserve by the competent authority (Section 15).
Calling-up for service in the Air Defence Reserve by the competent authority, leading to deemed enrolment upon appearance (Section 16).
administration: The Central Government, with the appointment of a 'competent authority' (an air officer or committee).
important_notes: The Act has been extended to Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry, and the State of Sikkim.

Chapters II and III and certain provisions of Chapters V and VI came into force on 15th August, 1955. Chapter IV and provisions relating to the Auxiliary Air Force came into force on 15th October, 1955.
The Deputy Chief of Air Staff has been appointed as the competent authority.
Sections 35 and 36 have been repealed.

title: The State Armed Police Forces (Extension of Laws) Act, 1952
purpose: To provide for the extension of disciplinary laws in force in any State relating to the armed police force of that State to members of the said force when serving outside that State.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India. It applies to members of armed police forces of a State when they are serving in any part of another State, whether independently or attached to the police force of that other State.

key_definitions.armed_police_force: Any police force constituted by any of the enactments specified in the Schedule for the time being in force.

main_sections.description: Names the Act as the State Armed Police Forces (Extension of Laws) Act, 1952, and states its territorial application to the whole of India.
Defines 'armed police force' as any police force constituted by enactments listed in the Schedule.

main_sections.section_title: Extension of disciplinary laws of any State to members of the armed police force of that State when serving outside that State
main_sections.description: Mandates that members of an armed police force detachment serving outside their home State remain subject to the disciplinary laws of their home State, irrespective of where they are serving, notwithstanding Section 3 of the Police Act, 1888.

main_sections.section_title: Power to add to, or omit from, the Schedule
main_sections.description: Empowers the Central Government to amend the Schedule by adding or removing enactments through a notification in the Official Gazette.

important_rules: Members of an armed police force detachment serving outside their home State shall continue to be subject to the disciplinary laws of their home State.
This disciplinary liability applies while they are discharging functions as police officers in the other State.
The provisions of this Act override anything contained in section 3 of the Police Act, 1888, concerning such detachments.

rights: Members continue to be subject to the disciplinary framework of their originating State.
duties: Members of armed police forces serving outside their home State have a duty to remain subject to their home State's disciplinary laws.
obligations: To uphold discipline as per the laws of the State to which the armed police force belongs, even when serving in another State.

key_procedures: The Central Government may notify additions or omissions to the Schedule, thereby amending the list of enactments defining 'armed police force'.
administration: Central Government (for adding/omitting from Schedule)
important_notes: The Act was originally not applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir but was later extended.

The purpose of the Act is to ensure that special units of armed police maintain their specific disciplinary liabilities regardless of their location, as their rights and liabilities under the Police Act, 1888, would otherwise default to those of the State in which they are serving.

title: The Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952
purpose: To provide for the regulation of certain matters relating to forward contracts, the prohibition of options in goods, and for matters connected therewith.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India. Its provisions apply to forward contracts and options in goods, with specific applications to notified goods and recognized/registered associations. Different dates can be appointed for different provisions, states, areas, and goods.

key_definitions.association: Any body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, constituted for the purpose of regulating and controlling the business of the sale or purchase of any goods.
key_definitions.commission: The Forward Markets Commission established under section 3.
key_definitions.forward_contract: A contract for the delivery of goods which is not a ready delivery contract.
key_definitions.goods: Every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money and securities.
