It covers debts due to banks, financial institutions, and consortia of banks/financial institutions.

key_definitions.Appellate Tribunal: An Appellate Tribunal established under sub-section (1) of section 8.
key_definitions.bank: Includes a banking company, a corresponding new bank, State Bank of India, a subsidiary bank, a Regional Rural Bank, and a multi-State co-operative bank.
key_definitions.debt: Any liability (inclusive of interest) claimed as due from any person or a pooled investment vehicle by a bank or financial institution or a consortium, whether secured or unsecured, assigned, or payable under a decree, order, or arbitration award. It also includes liabilities towards debt securities unpaid after 90 days' notice.
key_definitions.financial institution: Includes a public financial institution, a securitisation company or reconstruction company, a debenture trustee registered with the Board and appointed for secured debt securities, and other institutions specified by the Central Government.
key_definitions.Tribunal: The Tribunal established under sub-section (1) of section 3, also known as the Debts Recovery Tribunal.

main_sections.section_title: Short title, extent, commencement and application
main_sections.description: Specifies the short title of the Act, its geographical extent, date of commencement, and conditions for its application based on the debt amount.
Provides definitions for various terms used in the Act, including 'Appellate Tribunal', 'bank', 'debt', 'financial institution', and 'Tribunal'.
Empowers the Central Government to establish one or more Debts Recovery Tribunals and specify their jurisdiction.
Empowers the Central Government to establish one or more Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunals.

main_sections.section_title: Jurisdiction, powers and authority of Tribunals
main_sections.description: Defines the jurisdiction, powers, and authority vested in the Tribunals.
Outlines the procedure for filing applications before the Tribunal.
Specifies the methods by which debts determined by the Tribunal can be recovered.
States that the provisions of this Act shall have an effect overriding other laws in certain circumstances.

important_rules: Minimum debt amount of ten lakh rupees (or as specified by Central Government) for the Act's application.
Tribunals are to be established by the Central Government through notification.
Presiding Officer of a Tribunal must be qualified to be a District Judge.
Debts can be recovered through various modes as specified in Chapter V, including through Recovery Officers.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Recovery Officers appointed by the Central Government for each Tribunal, and the Tribunals/Appellate Tribunals themselves.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through various modes of recovery of debts determined by the Tribunal, including attachment and sale of property, and by exercising powers similar to civil courts.

rights: Right to file an application to the Tribunal for recovery of debt.
Right to appeal against orders of the Tribunal to the Appellate Tribunal.
Right to legal representation before the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal.
duties: Banks and financial institutions have a duty to recover debts expeditiously.
Individuals and partnership firms are subject to insolvency resolution and bankruptcy proceedings under the Act.
obligations: Borrowers have an obligation to repay debts to banks and financial institutions.
Parties involved in proceedings before the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal must comply with its orders and procedures.

key_procedures: Filing of an application to the Tribunal for recovery of debt (Section 19).
Appeal against the order of a Tribunal to the Appellate Tribunal (Section 20).
Recovery of debts through various modes, including orders for attachment and sale of property, by the Recovery Officer (Chapter V).
administration: The Central Government is responsible for establishing Tribunals and Appellate Tribunals and making rules. The Tribunals and Appellate Tribunals, with their Presiding Officers and staff, administer the Act.
important_notes: The Act was amended to include 'insolvency resolution and bankruptcy of individuals and partnership firms' and the application to Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has been extended via notification.
Amendments introduced provisions related to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, and updated qualifications and terms for Presiding Officers and Chairpersons.
The Act has an overriding effect, meaning its provisions supersede conflicting provisions in other laws.

title: THE FOOD SAFETY AND STANDARDS ACT, 2006
purpose: To consolidate the laws relating to food and to establish the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India for laying down science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import, to ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human consumption and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
scope: The Act extends to the whole of India. It applies to all stages of manufacture, processing, packaging, storage, transportation, distribution of food, import, and includes food services and catering services.

key_definitions.adulterant: Any material which is or could be employed for making the food unsafe or sub-standard or mis-branded or containing extraneous matter.
key_definitions.advertisement: Any audio or visual publicity, representation or pronouncement made by means of any light, sound, smoke, gas, print, electronic media, internet or website and includes through any notice, circular, label, wrapper, invoice or other documents.
key_definitions.food: Any substance, whether processed, partially processed or unprocessed, which is intended for human consumption and includes primary food, genetically modified or engineered food or food containing such ingredients, infant food, packaged drinking water, alcoholic drink, chewing gum, and any substance, including water used into the food during its manufacture, preparation or treatment but does not include any animal feed, live animals unless they are prepared or processed for placing on the market for human consumption, plants, prior to harvesting, drugs and medicinal products, cosmetics, narcotic or psychotropic substances.
key_definitions.food_business: Any undertaking, whether for profit or not and whether public or private, carrying out any of the activities related to any stage of manufacture, processing, packaging, storage, transportation, distribution of food, import and includes food services, catering services, sale of food or food ingredients.
key_definitions.food_safety: Assurance that food is acceptable for human consumption according to its intended use.
key_definitions.contaminant: Any substance, whether or not added to food, but which is present in such food as a result of the production (including operations carried out in crop husbandry, animal husbandry or veterinary medicine), manufacture, processing, preparation, treatment, packing, packaging, transport or holding of such food or as a result of environmental contamination and does not include insect fragments, rodent hairs and other extraneous matter;

main_sections.description: This section states the short title of the Act as the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, its extent to the whole of India, and the provisions for its commencement through notification by the Central Government.

main_sections.section_title: Declaration as to expediency of control by the Union.
main_sections.description: Declares that it is expedient in the public interest that the Union should take under its control the food industry.
Provides definitions for various terms used in the Act, such as adulterant, advertisement, food, food business, food safety, contaminant, etc.

main_sections.section_title: Establishment of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.
main_sections.description: Establishes the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSAAI).

main_sections.section_title: Duties and functions of Food Authority.
main_sections.description: Outlines the various duties and functions of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.

main_sections.section_title: General principles to be followed in administration of Act.
main_sections.description: Specifies the general principles that should be followed in the administration of the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Responsibilities of the food business operator.
main_sections.description: Details the responsibilities that food business operators must adhere to for ensuring food safety.

main_sections.section_title: Power of search, seizure, investigation, prosecution and procedure thereof.
main_sections.description: Grants powers to relevant authorities for search, seizure, investigation, and prosecution related to food safety offenses.
Provides general provisions concerning offenses under the Act.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for selling food not of the nature or substance or quality demanded.
main_sections.description: Specifies penalties for selling food that does not meet the demanded nature, substance, or quality.
Defines the punishment for dealing with unsafe food.

main_sections.section_title: Overriding effect of this Act over all other food related laws.
main_sections.description: States that this Act has an overriding effect over all other existing food-related laws.

important_rules: General principles of food safety are to be followed in the administration of the Act (Section 18).
Food business operators have specific responsibilities to ensure compliance with the Act, rules, and regulations (Section 26).
All imports of articles of food are subject to this Act (Section 25).
Packaging and labelling of foods must comply with the Act's provisions (Section 23).
Restrictions on advertisements and prohibition of unfair trade practices related to food are stipulated (Section 24).
Food recall procedures are to be followed (Section 28).

penalties: Penalty for selling food not of the nature or substance or quality demanded (Section 50).
Penalty for sub-standard food (Section 51).
Penalty for misbranded food (Section 52).
Penalty for misleading advertisement (Section 53).
Penalty for food containing extraneous matter (Section 54).
Penalty for failure to comply with the directions of Food Safety Officer (Section 55).
Penalty for unhygienic or unsanitary processing or manufacturing of food (Section 56).
Penalty for possessing adulterant (Section 57).
Penalty for contraventions for which no specific penalty is provided (Section 58).
Punishment for unsafe food (Section 59).
Punishment for interfering with seized items (Section 60).
Penalty for false information (Section 61).
Punishment for obstructing or impersonating a Food Safety Officer (Section 62).
Penalty for carrying out a business without licence (Section 63).
Punishment for subsequent offences (Section 64).
Compensation in case of injury or death of consumer (Section 65).
Offences by companies (Section 66).
Penalty for contravention of provisions of this Act in case of import of articles of food to be in addition to penalties provided under any other Act (Section 67).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Authorities responsible for enforcement of the Act include the Commissioner of Food Safety of the State, Designated Officers, and Food Safety Officers (Sections 29, 30, 36, 37). The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India also plays a key role.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Enforcement involves licensing and registration of food businesses, issuance of improvement notices, prohibition orders, emergency prohibition notices and orders, notification of food poisoning, powers of search, seizure, investigation, prosecution, and analysis of food. Adjudication and Food Safety Appellate Tribunals are established for resolving disputes and hearing appeals.

rights: Consumers have the right to purchase safe and wholesome food.
Purchasers may have food analysed (Section 40).
duties: Duties of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (Section 16).
Responsibilities of the food business operator (Section 26).
Food Safety Officers have duties related to inspection, seizure, and enforcement (Section 38).
obligations: Food business operators are obligated to ensure compliance with the Act, rules, and regulations.
Manufacturers, packers, wholesalers, distributors, and sellers have liabilities related to food safety (Section 27).

key_procedures: Procedure for selection of Chairperson and Members of the Food Authority (Section 6).
Procedure for Scientific Committee and Scientific Panel (Section 15).
Procedure for launching prosecution (Section 42).
Procedure for analysis of food (Section 47).
Procedure and powers of the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal (Section 71).
administration: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSAAI) is established for the administration of the Act. The Central Government and State Governments also have roles in administration and rule-making.
important_notes: The Act may come into force on different dates for different provisions (Section 1(3)).
The Act has an overriding effect over all other food-related laws (Section 89).
Milk and Milk Products Order, 1992 is deemed to be regulations made under this Act (Section 99).
Amendments are made to the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992 (Section 100).
The Central Government has the power to make rules and issue directions, while the Food Authority has the power to make regulations (Sections 91, 92).

title: BENGAL INDIGO CONTRACTS ACT, 1836
purpose: To repeal a specific clause of a previous regulation and to provide for the security of advances made under indigo cultivation contracts, the protection of such contracts from interference by third parties, and the examination of parties in related legal proceedings.
scope: Applies to the Bengal Presidency. Specifically concerns disputes over the right to indigo plant, contracts between ryots and other parties for indigo cultivation and delivery, and civil actions arising from breaches of these contracts. Also covers the jurisdiction of Zillah and City Judges in suits related to these matters.

main_sections.section_title: Repeal of Clause Third, Section V., Regulation VI., 1823
main_sections.description: This section formally repeals a specific clause of a previous Bengal Code regulation.

When the right to indigo plant is contested and an order is made for its delivery to a claimant, the claimant must provide sufficient security to cover any ultimately established claims before they can cut or remove the plant. These claims could arise from prior land produce rights or rent arrears.

main_sections.section_title: Protection of Indigo Contracts and Advances
main_sections.description: If a ryot has a lawful contract to cultivate or deliver indigo, and has received an advance for this purpose, any other person knowingly inducing the ryot to break the contract is liable, along with the ryot, to civil action for damages and costs sustained by the party who made the advance. However, this does not apply to actions taken to procure payment of a debt or performance of a lawful contract.

Courts hearing suits under Regulation VI., 1823, or this Act are authorized to examine plaintiffs and defendants if deemed necessary for justice. If the award favors the defendant, they may be compensated for expenses and loss of time.

main_sections.section_title: Referral of Suits to Sudder Ameens
main_sections.description: Zillah or City Judges are empowered to refer suits, regular or summary, instituted under Regulation VI., 1823, or this Act, to Principal Sudder Ameens or Sudder Ameens for inquiry and decision, according to their respective jurisdictions.

important_rules: Rule 1: A party to whom indigo plant is ordered to be delivered under contested right must give security before cutting or removing the plant.
Rule 2: Individuals interfering with existing indigo contracts, where advances have been made, are liable to civil action for damages.
Rule 3: Courts can examine parties in suits under this Act or Regulation VI., 1823, to ensure justice.
Rule 4: Defendants who prevail in suits may be awarded compensation for costs and time lost.

penalties: Damages to the extent of the injury sustained, together with costs of suit, for persons who prevail upon a ryot to break an indigo contract after an advance has been made.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Civil Courts trying the relevant suits.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through civil actions for damages and costs.

rights: Right of the party who made an advance under an indigo contract to proceed by civil action against intermeddlers and the ryot for breach of contract.
Right of a defendant to compensation for expenses and loss of time if an award is in their favor in suits under this Act.
duties: Duty of a party claiming indigo plant, after an order for delivery, to provide sufficient security before cutting or removing the plant.
Duty of a ryot to fulfill their indigo cultivation or delivery contract.

key_procedures: Procedure 1: When indigo plant right is contested, and an order for delivery is made, the claimant must furnish security to the satisfaction of the Court before cutting or removing the plant.

Procedure 2: If a third party knowingly induces a ryot to break an indigo contract after an advance has been made, the aggrieved party can file a civil action against both the third party and the ryot.
Procedure 3: Courts may examine plaintiffs and defendants in suits under this Act or Regulation VI., 1823.
Procedure 4: Zillah or City Judges can refer suits related to indigo contracts or rights to Principal Sudder Ameens or Sudder Ameens for decision.
administration: Implied to be the judicial system responsible for trying suits under the Regulation and the Act, including Zillah Judges, City Judges, Principal Sudder Ameens, and Sudder Ameens.
important_notes: The provisions of Section III do not give a right of action against persons procuring payment of a debt or performance of a lawful contract.
The powers of examination of parties and referral of suits extend to cases instituted under both Regulation VI., 1823, and this Act.

title: The Coasting-Vessels Act, 1838
purpose: To regulate the use and registration of coasting and other vessels, including fishing vessels and harbour craft, belonging to citizens of India, employed on the coasts or trading coastwise within specified territories.
scope: The Act initially extended to the territories of Bombay, Saurashtra, and Kutch. The Central Government can extend it to other Indian states or parts of states with a sea-coast. It applies to vessels belonging to any citizen of India employed on the coasts or trading coastwise, as well as fishing vessels and harbour craft belonging to such citizens.

key_definitions.coasting vessel: A vessel employed on the coasts of any State or part of a State to which the Act extends, or in trading coastwise.
key_definitions.harbour-craft: A vessel used within a harbour.

main_sections.description: Specifies the geographical territories to which the Act applies, with provisions for extension by the Central Government.

main_sections.section_title: Rules as to coasting and other vessels belonging to any citizen of India
main_sections.description: Outlines the general applicability of the Act's rules to specified types of vessels owned by Indian citizens operating on the coast or trading coastwise.

main_sections.section_title: Marking or branding vessels with name of place and number
main_sections.description: Requires vessels to be marked or branded with the name of their home port and an assigned number. Owners must paint this name and number on each quarter of the vessel in black paint on a white ground, with figures and letters six inches in length.

main_sections.section_title: Registry of name, number and burthen
main_sections.description: Mandates the registration of the vessel's name, number, burden, and owner's name. Registry is to be made by designated officers (Principal Officer, Mercantile Marine Department at Bombay; Commissioner of Customs at other places). Fresh registration is required upon changes in burden or owner.
Owners are required to apply for registry. Information of registry at subordinate ports must be sent to the Principal Officer, Mercantile Marine Department at Bombay.

main_sections.section_title: Officers to perform duty of marking and branding
main_sections.description: Details the officers responsible for marking, branding, and ascertaining the burden of vessels, similar to those responsible for registry.

main_sections.section_title: Owner to obtain certificate of registry
main_sections.description: Owners must obtain a certificate of registry in the form specified in the Schedule. Renewed certificates can be obtained for lost or destroyed ones.
Certificates of registry are to be sealed with the seal of the Government of India and signed by the registering officer.
Prescribes the fees for certificates of registry based on the tonnage of the vessel.

main_sections.section_title: Fees to be credited to Government
main_sections.description: Fees collected for registry are to be paid to the Central Government. Fees that were previously credited to the Provincial Government shall now be paid to an officer appointed by the State Government and credited to that Government.
Owners or commanders must produce the certificate of registry upon demand by Customs officers or naval officers.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for neglect to comply with rules
main_sections.description: Imposes penalties for non-compliance with marking, branding, painting, or certificate production rules. Fines are ten times the certificate fee for vessels where fees are payable, and ten rupees for fishing vessels and harbour craft. Penalties are recoverable by sale of the vessel and are payable for each subsequent default made after one month from the last conviction.

main_sections.section_title: Power to direct compensation for trouble in seizing
main_sections.description: The Central Government can direct compensation for the trouble and diligence involved in seizing vessels, out of the proceeds of such seizure.

important_rules: Every relevant vessel, fishing-vessel, and harbour-craft must be marked or branded with the name of its home port and an assigned number.
Owners must paint the name and number on each quarter of the vessel in black paint on a white ground, with English figures and letters six inches in length.
Owners must apply for and obtain a certificate of registry for their vessels.
The certificate of registry must be produced on demand by Customs or naval officers.

penalties: For vessels subject to registry fees: a fine of ten times the amount of the fees payable for the certificate of registry.
For fishing-vessels and harbour-craft: a fine of ten rupees.
Penalties are payable as often as default is made, provided a subsequent default occurs more than one month after the last conviction.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Customs officers, naval officers, and Magistrates having jurisdiction.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Penalties can be recovered on conviction before a Magistrate by the sale of the vessel, her furniture, ammunition, tackle, and apparel.

rights: Right to a certificate of registry upon proper application and payment of fees.
Right to compensation for trouble in seizing vessels, as directed by the Central Government.
duties: Duty of owners to ensure vessels are marked, branded, and painted according to regulations.
Duty of owners to apply for and obtain a certificate of registry.
Duty of owners or commanders to produce the certificate of registry on demand.
Duty of registering officers to perform marking, branding, and registration tasks.
Duty of registering officers to remit fees to the Government.
obligations: Obligation to register vessels, including their name, number, burden, and owner's details.
Obligation to maintain the painted name and number on the vessel.
Obligation to adhere to the specific forms and procedures outlined in the Act and its Schedule.

key_procedures: Applying for registry: Owners must apply to the authorized officer.
Marking and Branding: Vessels are to be marked or branded with the name of the place and an assigned number.
Painting: Owners must paint the name and number on each quarter of the vessel.
Obtaining Certificate: Owners must apply for and obtain a certificate of registry.
Renewal of Certificate: A renewed certificate may be obtained in case of loss or destruction.
Production of Certificate: The certificate must be produced on demand by authorized officers.
Recovery of Penalties: Fines are recovered on conviction before a Magistrate by sale of the vessel.
administration: Principal Officer, Mercantile Marine Department (at Bombay); Commissioner of Customs (at other places); or other persons appointed by the Central Government.
important_notes: The Act has been subject to repeals and adaptations over time, particularly concerning its application to sea-going ships fitted with mechanical propulsion and sailing vessels by the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
The fees for certificates vary based on the tonnage of the vessel.
The purpose of the Act is to regulate vessels engaged in coastal trade, distinct from larger maritime shipping regulations.

title: THE BENGAL BONDED WAREHOUSE ASSOCIATION ACT, 1838
purpose: To incorporate persons for the warehousing of goods, either in bond or otherwise, and to establish a corporate body for this purpose, managing its affairs through Directors and a Capital Stock.
scope: Applies to the warehousing of goods in Bengal Presidency, managed by the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association. It details the incorporation, capital, shareholding, directorate, meetings, voting, calls for share money, transfer of shares, and the extension of existing warehousing laws to the Association's warehouses.

key_definitions.Capital Stock: The sum of Rs. 10,00,000 subscribed for the purpose of the Association, divided into 2,000 shares of 500 Rupees each.
key_definitions.Proprietor of Shares: Any person who holds shares in the Capital Stock of the Association and is therefore a member of the corporation.

main_sections.description: Establishes the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association as a corporate body for the warehousing of goods, naming the initial incorporators as listed in Schedule No. 1.

main_sections.section_title: Power to sue and be sued, and to acquire, hold and transfer property
main_sections.description: Grants the Association the power to sue and be sued in its corporate name, to use a common seal, and to acquire, hold, and transfer any description of property.
Defines the Capital Stock at Rs. 10,00,000, divided into 2,000 shares of Rs. 500 each, with each subscriber receiving one share for every Rs. 500 subscribed.

Mandates the Directors to maintain a register of proprietors' names, additions, residences, and the number of shares held. This register is to be numbered and open for public inspection during business hours.

Outlines the powers of the Directors, including expending Association funds for purchasing and erecting warehouses, warehousing and bonding goods, making contracts, appointing and removing servants, managing the Association's concerns, and using the common seal in the presence of three Directors.

main_sections.section_title: Power to refuse to register transfer by defaulting proprietor
main_sections.description: Allows Directors to refuse registration of share transfers for proprietors who have not paid their instalments and interest. If payment is not made within two months, Directors can sell the shares to recover dues and issue new certificates.

main_sections.section_title: Extension of Act 25 of 1836 to warehouses of Association
main_sections.description: Declares that the provisions of Act 25 of 1836, relating to private licensed warehouses, will apply to all warehouses where the Association receives bonded goods.

main_sections.section_title: Power to give general security for payment of import and export duties
main_sections.description: Empowers the Association to provide a general security bond for the payment of import duties on goods lodged in its warehouses or for their due exportation, thereby exempting other parties from providing similar security.

main_sections.section_title: Individual members not to be liable
main_sections.description: Specifies that individual members of the Association shall not be held liable for the debts or engagements of the Association.

important_rules: Rule on Share Transfer Registration: A share transfer is only effectual after it has been registered at the Association's office and a note of registration and date is made on the back of the indorsed certificate by an appointed officer.

Rule on Director Rotation: Two Directors shall go out of office annually on the Monday following May 15th. A general meeting will be held on the same day to elect two new Directors. Directors going out by rotation cannot be re-elected until the following year.
Rule on Director Qualifications: Directors must be residents within the Territories subject to the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal.
Rule on Voting Qualification: A proprietor must possess at least two shares, registered in their name for not less than three calendar months prior, to be allowed to vote at general meetings.
Rule on Maximum Votes: No proprietor shall have more than eight votes at general meetings, with the number of votes scaled according to the number of shares held.
Rule on Seal Affixing: The Association's seal shall only be affixed to an instrument in the presence and by the consent of three Directors, who must sign the instrument.

Rule on Calls for Share Money: Directors can call for instalments up to 50% of each share. Further calls require a vote of a general meeting. Proprietors must be called upon proportionally to their share in the Capital Stock.
Rule on Interest on Unpaid Calls: If an instalment is not paid on the due date, the Association can claim interest at 10% per annum on the deficient sum.
Rule on Application of Dividend for Unpaid Calls: Directors may apply any dividend due to a proprietor towards satisfaction of unpaid instalments and interest.

penalties: Interest on unpaid calls at 10% per annum (Section 23).
Refusal to register transfer of shares for defaulting proprietors (Section 24).
Sale of shares by public auction to satisfy unpaid calls and interest (Section 24).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Directors of the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through refusal to register share transfers, selling shares of defaulting proprietors, applying dividends towards unpaid dues, and enforcing interest on overdue payments.

rights: Right to sue and be sued by the Association's corporate name (Section 2).
Right to acquire, hold, and transfer property (Section 2).
Right to receive share certificates (Section 5).
Right to transfer shares by endorsement (Section 6).
Right to vote at general meetings (subject to qualifications) (Section 17).
Right to vote by proxy (Section 20).
Right to receive dividends on shares (Section 23).
Right to demand any surplus after sale of defaulting proprietor's shares (Section 24).
Right of original proprietors to subscribe to increased Capital Stock first (Section 34).
duties: Duty to pay subscribed share money (Sections 3, 22).
Duty to register name and details in the proprietors' book (Section 4).
Duty to comply with calls for share money (Section 22).
Duty to pay interest on unpaid calls (Section 23).
Duty to adhere to the rules and bye-laws of the Association.
Duty of Directors to manage affairs, use the common seal appropriately, and ensure proper accounting.
obligations: Original proprietors are obligated to subscribe to the Capital Stock as specified.
All proprietors are obligated to pay instalments when called upon by the Directors.
Any person becoming a proprietor of the Capital Stock is under the same liabilities as an original proprietor.

key_procedures: Share Transfer Procedure: A share can be transferred by endorsement on the certificate. This endorsement must specify the transferee's name. The transfer is only effective after registration at the Association's office and a note of registration on the back of the certificate.

Director Election and Rotation Procedure: Directors serve on a rotation basis, with two retiring annually. A general meeting on the Monday following May 15th elects two Directors to replace those retiring. If a Director ceases to be so otherwise than by rotation, an extraordinary general meeting is called to elect a successor.
Procedure for Extraordinary General Meetings: Such meetings are held according to bye-laws and require at least fourteen days' prior notice, published in at least two Calcutta newspapers.
Procedure for Collecting Share Money Calls: Directors can call for instalments up to 50% of each share. Further calls require a general meeting vote. Proprietors must pay by the appointed date.

Procedure for Defaulting Proprietors: If an instalment and interest are unpaid for two months after notice, Directors can sell the defaulting proprietor's shares by public sale to recover dues and issue new certificates to the purchaser.
administration: The Directors of the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association are responsible for managing the Association's affairs.
important_notes: Repealed Sections: Sections 12 (Qualifications of Directors) and 14 (Ordinary meetings) were repealed by Act 5 of 1854, Section 1.
Association's Property: The Association can acquire, hold, and transfer any description of property. Upon dissolution, the property will be divided amongst the proprietors (Section 39).
Liability Limitation: Individual members are not liable for the Association's debts (Section 31).
East India Company's Pre-emption Right: The East India Company has the right of pre-emption when the Capital Stock is increased (Section 36).

title: THE MADRAS RENT AND REVENUE SALES ACT, 1839
purpose: To empower Tahsildars within the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort St. George with the powers of Commissioners for the sale of property distrained for arrears of rent or revenue, and to outline the control and fees associated with such sales.
scope: Applies to all Tahsildars within the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort St. George. Subject matter scope is the sale of property distrained for arrears of rent or revenue.

main_sections.description: This section, concerning the repeal of Regulation XXVIII of 1802, s. 23, has been repealed by Act XIV of 1874.

main_sections.section_title: Tahsildars empowered to sell property distrained.
main_sections.description: Vests Tahsildars within the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort St. George with the powers of Commissioners for the sale of property distrained for arrears of rent or revenue, making them subject to all relevant rules and provisions.

main_sections.section_title: Control of tahsildars in exercise of such power.
main_sections.description: Establishes that Tahsildars, in exercising their powers of selling distrained property, are subject to the control and superintendence of the Collector and not the Zila Judge, except in cases of judicial proceedings.

main_sections.section_title: [Their liabilities in exercise of same power.]
main_sections.description: This section concerning their liabilities in the exercise of the same power has been repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1891 (XII of 1891).

main_sections.section_title: Fees for selling property to be credited to Government.
main_sections.description: Stipulates that Tahsildars are not entitled to any fee or commission for selling distrained property. Instead, all fees or commissions lawfully taken by Commissioners for such sales shall be credited to the account of the Government.

Grants Tahsildars the authority, under the orders of the Collector, to delegate their powers vested by section 2 of this Act to any public servants under their authority. The provisions of sections 3 and 5 of this Act apply to such delegated public servants as they do to Tahsildars.

important_rules: Tahsildars in the Madras Presidency are empowered to sell property distrained for rent or revenue arrears.
Tahsildars are subject to the control of the Collector in exercising these powers, not the Zila Judge (except in judicial proceedings).
No fees or commissions are payable to Tahsildars for selling distrained property; all such fees go to the Government.
Tahsildars can delegate these sale powers to subordinate public servants, who will then be subject to sections 3 and 5 of the Act.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector (for control and superintendence), Tahsildars (for executing sales), and delegated public servants.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the established legal framework for distraint and sale of property for arrears of rent or revenue, overseen by the Collector.

rights: Tahsildars have the right to sell property distrained for rent or revenue arrears.
Public servants delegated powers by Tahsildars have the right to exercise those powers.
Government has the right to all fees/commissions collected from the sale of distrained property.
duties: Tahsildars have a duty to exercise their powers of sale subject to the Collector's control.
Tahsildars have a duty to ensure that no fees are charged by them for selling distrained property.
Delegated public servants have a duty to exercise their delegated powers in accordance with the Act.
Collectors have a duty to control and superintend Tahsildars in their exercise of these powers.
obligations: Tahsildars are obligated to operate within the framework of the Act and Collector's orders.
All fees collected are obligated to be credited to the Government.

key_procedures: Distraint of property for arrears of rent or revenue.
Sale of distrained property by empowered Tahsildars or delegated public servants.
Collection of all sale fees and commissions for Government credit.
administration: The Act is administered under the overall superintendence of the Collector and the Presidency of Fort St. George government.
important_notes: Sections 1 and 4 of the Act have been repealed.
The Act was declared to be in force in the whole of the Madras Presidency, except the Scheduled Districts, by the Laws Local Extent Act, 1874.
It was later extended to Scheduled Districts in Ganjam and Vizagapatam, and Godavari.

title: An Act to enable the holders of Revenue which has been alienated to them by the State, to collect that Revenue within the Presidency of Bombay.
purpose: To authorize the Governor in Council of Bombay to grant commissions to certain Jageerdars and others, conferring increased powers for collecting revenue alienated to them by the State.
scope: This act applies within the Presidency of Bombay to Jageerdars, Surinjamdars, Inamdars, and other persons holding lands or villages where the revenue has been alienated to them by the State. It grants these individuals, or their agents, specific powers for revenue collection.

main_sections.description: Empowers the Governor in Council of Bombay to grant commissions to holders of alienated revenue, conferring additional powers for collection beyond those already exercisable by law. These powers can be specified in the commission.

States that commissions shall be drawn according to Schedule A, can be granted or withheld at the pleasure of the Government, and may be withdrawn. Commissions can also be issued to agents of the revenue holder.

Grants commission holders the authority to demand security for revenue payment. If security is not furnished, they can take precautions as authorized for a Collector under Section XI, Regulation XVII of 1827, Bombay Code.

Authorizes commission holders to send Mohussuls (enforcement officers) on defaulters under specific clauses of Regulation XVII of 1827, Bombay Code. Limitations include using only one Mohussul per case and cessation of Mohussulee upon enforcement of other remedies, except for taking security.

Empowers commission holders to attach the property of persons defaulting on revenue payments. An immediate report must be made to the Collector or his Assistant. If the demand is deemed just, the Collector or Assistant will order the sale of the property, conducted according to Regulation XVII of 1827, Bombay Code. Exception: Jageerdars, Surinjamdars, or Inamdars with civil jurisdiction and decree execution powers under Regulation XIII of 1830 will conduct the sale themselves.

main_sections.section_title: Cessation of Compulsory Process and Forfeiture
main_sections.description: All compulsory process ceases if the alleged defaulter furnishes security to institute a suit within 15 days to try the demand and pay any decreed amount. Suits involving privileged classes under Regulation XXIX of 1827 and Regulation VII of 1830 will be tried by the Collector. Holders proceeding with compulsory process after security is furnished or duly tendered forfeit three times the amount of revenue sought.

Demanding excess rent or revenue beyond the amount fixed by a Government Officer, or the usual rate according to custom, is deemed extortion. The victim can obtain three times the excessive demand as damages. However, this does not prevent suits to establish claims for re-assessment or re-settlement of revenue if a Ryut is paying less than justly liable.
The powers conferred by the commission extend only to enforcing payment of revenue for the current season and the immediately preceding season, not for former years.

important_rules: Holders of a commission have the authority to demand security for the payment of revenue from specified lands or villages.
If security is not provided, commission holders can take precautions similar to those authorized for a Collector.
Mohussuls can be sent on defaulters, but only one per case, and their deployment ceases if other remedies are enforced (except for taking security).
Property of defaulters can be attached, with immediate reporting to the Collector. Sales are generally conducted by the Collector, unless the commission holder has specific civil jurisdiction powers.
Compulsory process stops if the defaulter provides security to file a suit and pay any decreed amount.
Demanding revenue exceeding the legally fixed or customary rate is considered extortion and incurs penalties.
Commission powers are limited to the current and previous season's revenue, not older arrears.

penalties: Forfeiture of three times the amount of revenue sought if compulsory process is continued after security has been furnished or duly tendered.
Damages of three times the excessive demand awarded to individuals against whom extortionate demands have been enforced.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Governor in Council of Bombay, Collectors and their Assistants, and commission holders (Jageerdars, Surinjamdars, Inamdars with specific jurisdiction).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the issuance and withdrawal of commissions, demanding security, deploying Mohussuls, attaching and selling property, and instituting legal proceedings. Enforcement of certain demands can be tried by the Collector and his Assistants.

rights: Right to grant or withhold commissions.
Right to withdraw commissions.
Right to demand security for revenue.
Right to take precautionary measures if security is not furnished.
Right to attach property of defaulters.
Right to have property of defaulters sold (under specific conditions).
Right to institute suits to re-assess or re-settle revenue.
Right to recover current and preceding season's revenue.
duties: Duty to report attachments to the Collector or Assistant Collector.
Duty to conduct sales of attached property according to prescribed regulations (unless exempt).
obligations: Obligation to cease compulsory process upon furnishing of security to institute a suit.
Obligation to conform to legally established revenue rates.
Obligation to not engage in extortionate demands.

key_procedures: Granting of Commission: Governor in Council of Bombay considers and issues a commission to a holder of alienated revenue or their agent, specifying the powers and lands/villages involved. The commission is subject to withdrawal at Government's pleasure.
Demand and Security: Commission holder demands revenue and may require security for its payment. If security is not provided, precautionary measures can be taken.

Enforcement on Defaulters: If revenue is not paid, commission holders can deploy Mohussuls (with limitations). Property of defaulters can be attached and, if deemed just by the Collector, sold according to regulations.

Challenging Demands: A defaulter can furnish security to file a suit within 15 days to contest the demand. If security is provided, compulsory process ceases. Failure to comply with such suits leads to decree payment.
Addressing Extortion: Individuals subjected to excessive demands can seek damages up to three times the amount of the extortionate demand.
administration: The Governor in Council of Bombay is responsible for granting, withholding, and withdrawing commissions. Collectors and their Assistants are involved in overseeing property attachments and sales, and in trying certain legal cases.
important_notes: The powers conferred by the commission are limited to the revenue of the current season and the immediately preceding season.
Special provisions exist for the trial of suits involving privileged classes and for the conduct of sales by Jageerdars, Surinjamdars, or Inamdars vested with civil jurisdiction.
Holding or enforcing compulsory process after security has been furnished or tendered for a suit can lead to significant financial penalties for the commission holder.

title: THE REVENUE COMMISSIONERS, BOMBAY ACT, 1842
purpose: To repeal and re-enact provisions regarding the number and powers of Revenue Commissioners under the Presidency of Bombay, allowing for one or more commissioners and their deputies/assistants.
scope: Applies to the Territory composing the Presidency of Bombay. Specifically repeals parts of Regulation V, 1830, concerning the appointment and jurisdiction of Revenue Commissioners. Empowers the Governor in Council of Bombay to define the jurisdiction of each Revenue Commissioner.

main_sections.description: Repeals so much of Regulation V, of 180, of the Bombay Code, as provided for a single Revenue Commissioner for the Territory subordinate to Bombay and excluded the Southern Maharatta Country from his jurisdiction.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment and powers of Revenue Commissioners
main_sections.description: Enacts that one or more Revenue Commissioners shall be appointed for the entire Presidency of Bombay. Each commissioner will have all the powers of the single Revenue Commissioner under Regulation V, 1830, and will operate within the Presidency of Bombay or as prescribed by the Governor in Council of Bombay.
Enacts that each Revenue Commissioner shall have such number of Deputies and Assistants as the Governor in Council deems expedient to appoint.

important_rules: One or more Revenue Commissioners shall be appointed for the whole Presidency of Bombay.
Each Revenue Commissioner shall be vested with all powers possessed by the single Revenue Commissioner under Regulation V, 1830.
Revenue Commissioners can act within the Presidency of Bombay or over such portion as the Governor in Council prescribes.
The Governor in Council can appoint the necessary number of Deputies and Assistants for each Revenue Commissioner.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Governor in Council of Bombay, and by extension, the Revenue Commissioners.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the powers vested in the Revenue Commissioners and the orders of the Governor in Council.

rights: Revenue Commissioners have the power to act within their prescribed jurisdiction.
The Governor in Council has the power to prescribe jurisdiction and appoint deputies/assistants.
duties: Revenue Commissioners are responsible for carrying out duties under Regulation V, 1830.

administration: Governor in Council of Bombay
important_notes: The act repeals specific provisions of Regulation V, 1830.
The jurisdiction of Revenue Commissioners can be altered by the Governor in Council via an order published in the Gazette.

title: An Act for the establishment and maintenance of field boundary marks in the Presidency of Bombay
purpose: To provide for the establishment and maintenance of permanent marks to distinguish the boundaries of fields, with a view to the better definition and security of landed property, the prevention of encroachments and disputes, and the identification of lands assessed to, or exempted from, public revenue.
scope: Applies within the territories subject to the Presidency of Bombay. It concerns the boundaries of fields and the rights and responsibilities of their owners or occupants.

main_sections.section_title: Authority to require erection and maintenance of boundary marks
main_sections.description: Empowers Revenue Officers, authorized by the Governor in Council, to require owners or occupants to erect and maintain field boundary marks. The marks should be of sufficient material and number to permanently distinguish field limits.

Specifies how the requisition to erect or maintain boundary marks shall be served on owners or occupants. If persons are not found in the village, the requisition will be posted at the Village Chowree or other conspicuous place, which will be considered sufficient service.

If owners or occupants fail to comply with the requisition, Revenue Officers are authorized to direct the erection and repair of the marks. The cost will be apportioned among the fields they distinguish and charged to the owners/occupants, or to the village revenues if no such persons are forthcoming.

main_sections.section_title: Claims of persons out of possession
main_sections.description: Individuals out of possession but claiming ownership or occupancy, whose boundary mark costs were charged to village revenues due to their neglect, cannot have their claims allowed until they settle these charges.

Establishes a penalty of a fine not exceeding Fifty Rupees for each boundary mark wilfully erased, removed, or injured. Half of the fine can be awarded to the informer, and the other half is for restoring the mark.

main_sections.section_title: Assessment and realization of sums due
main_sections.description: Grants authority to Revenue Officers for the assessment and realization of sums due under the Act, including costs for erection and maintenance of boundary marks. This authority is to be exercised in conformity with general revenue demand rules. Proceedings are to be recorded and are subject to appeal to subordinate Revenue Authorities.

important_rules: Owners or Occupants of fields are required to erect and maintain boundary marks as directed by Revenue Officers.
If owners or occupants default, the Revenue Officers will arrange for the work, and the cost will be recovered from them or charged to village revenues.
Persons claiming ownership or occupancy, whose boundary mark costs were charged to village revenues due to neglect, must pay these costs before their claims are allowed.
Wilfully erasing, removing, or injuring field boundary marks is punishable by a fine.

penalties: Fine not exceeding Fifty Rupees for each boundary mark wilfully erased, removed, or injured.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Revenue Officers authorized by the Governor in Council.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through requisitions served on owners/occupants, direct action by officers upon default, and recovery of costs. Appeals are to subordinate Revenue Authorities.

rights: Right to appeal decisions of Revenue Officers regarding boundary marks to subordinate Revenue Authorities.
duties: Duty of owners or occupants to erect and maintain field boundary marks as required.
Duty to pay for the erection or maintenance of boundary marks if defaulted.
Duty to settle outstanding charges for boundary marks if out of possession but claiming rights.
obligations: Obligation to comply with requisitions from Revenue Officers regarding boundary marks.
Obligation to refrain from wilfully erasing, removing, or injuring field boundary marks.

key_procedures: Service of requisition on owners/occupants for boundary mark erection/maintenance, with provisions for posting if individuals are absent.
Revenue Officers undertaking the erection/repair of boundary marks upon default and apportioning costs.
Recovery of costs from owners/occupants or village revenues.
Assessment and realization of sums due, following general revenue demand rules.
Appeals process to subordinate Revenue Authorities for decisions made by Revenue Officers.
administration: Revenue Officers acting under the authority of the Governor in Council and the general supervision of Revenue Authorities.
important_notes: The specific mode of boundary marks (e.g., ridging or raising mounds of earth) can be determined by the Revenue Officers.
The Act aims to improve land security, prevent disputes, and facilitate identification of lands for revenue purposes.
Half of the fine for damaging boundary marks can be awarded to the informer.

title: THE BENGAL LAND HOLDER’ ATTENDANCE ACT, 1848
purpose: To provide summary power to Collectors to impose and levy reasonable daily fines on land proprietors or farmers who omit or refuse to attend when summoned or to furnish required accounts and documents, subject to review by superior authorities. This is intended to expedite the process and prevent the burden of penalties from increasing due to delays.
scope: Applies to proprietors or farmers of land subject to sundry Regulations of the Bengal Code. Geographically, it applies to the Presidency of Bengal, with an explicit exclusion for the North West Provinces.

key_definitions.Collector: Any person lawfully exercising the powers of a Collector.

main_sections.section_title: Imposition and Levy of Daily Fines
main_sections.description: Empowers the Collector to impose a daily fine, not exceeding fifty Rupees, on proprietors or farmers of land who fail to attend when summoned or to furnish required accounts/documents without sufficient cause. The fine is payable daily until compliance and can be levied like arrears of revenue without further confirmation.

Requires the Collector to forthwith report the imposition and amount of every fine, and subsequently the amount levied, to the Commissioner of Revenue, who will then report it to the local Government.

States that orders passed by a Collector under this Act are appealable to the Commissioner of Revenue and other superior authorities, but an appeal will not prevent the levy of the fine pending the appeal.

Mandates that if the amount levied under a Collector's order exceeds five hundred Rupees, the Collector must specially report the case to the Commissioner of Revenue. No further levy for such a default can be made without the Commissioner's authority.
Clarifies that this Act does not repeal the existing power of imposing and levying daily fines as prescribed by the said several Regulations.
Defines the term 'Collector' for the purposes of this Act.
Specifies that the Act does not extend to the North West Provinces of the Presidency of Bengal.

important_rules: If a proprietor or farmer of land is duly summoned by the Collector and fails to attend, or fails to cause their Officer or Agent to attend, or fails to furnish required accounts or documents without sufficient cause, the Collector can impose a daily fine.
The daily fine imposed by the Collector shall not exceed fifty Rupees.
The daily fine is payable until compliance with the Collector's requisition.
Fines can be levied by the same process as prescribed for the recovery of arrears of revenue, without further confirmation.
The Collector must report the imposition and levy of fines to the Commissioner of Revenue.
Appeals against Collector's orders are permitted, but do not stay the levy of the fine.
Levies exceeding five hundred Rupees require special reporting to the Commissioner of Revenue and their authority for further action.

penalties: Daily fine, payable daily until compliance, not exceeding fifty Rupees.
Levy of fines by the same process as for recovery of arrears of revenue.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Levied by the same process as prescribed for the recovery of arrears of revenue.

rights: Proprietors and farmers of land have the right to appeal orders passed by a Collector under this Act to the Commissioner of Revenue and other superior authorities.
duties: Proprietors or farmers of land have a duty to attend when duly summoned by the Collector, or to cause their Officer or Agent to attend.
Proprietors or farmers of land have a duty to furnish the accounts or documents required by the Collector.
Proprietors or farmers of land must show sufficient cause for omission or refusal to attend or furnish documents.
obligations: Landholders are obligated to comply with the requisitions of the Collector, which may include attendance or providing documents, failing which daily fines will accrue.

key_procedures: Summoning of Landholder: The Collector issues a notice to the proprietor or farmer of land requiring attendance or submission of documents.
Imposition of Fine: If the landholder fails to comply without sufficient cause, the Collector imposes a daily fine.
Levy of Fine: The fine is levied through the process for recovering arrears of revenue.
Reporting to Commissioner: The Collector reports the fine imposition and levy to the Commissioner of Revenue.
Appeal: The landholder can appeal the Collector's order, but this does not stop the fine collection.
Special Reporting for large amounts: If the levied amount exceeds 500 Rupees, the Collector reports specially to the Commissioner, and further levy requires the Commissioner's authority.
administration: The Act is administered by Collectors, with oversight by Commissioners of Revenue and the local Government.
important_notes: Existing powers under other Regulations for imposing and levying daily fines are not repealed by this Act.
The Act does not apply to the North West Provinces of the Presidency of Bengal.

title: An Act for appointing a Commissioner of Revenue at Madras
purpose: To empower the Governor of Fort St. George in Council to depute a Member of the Board of Revenue to perform collectively held duties of the Board within any district of the Presidency.
scope: Applies to the Presidency of Fort St. George (Madras). Specifically, it concerns the performance of duties by a deputed Member of the Board of Revenue within designated districts and the powers granted to such a Commissioner.

key_definitions.Governor of Fort St. George in Council: The governing authority in Fort St. George (Madras) responsible for enacting and implementing the act.
key_definitions.Member of the Board of Revenue: An individual serving on the Board of Revenue who may be deputed under this Act.
key_definitions.Commissioner: A Member of the Board of Revenue who has been specially commissioned under this Act to perform specific duties.

main_sections.section_title: Deputation of a Member of the Board of Revenue
main_sections.description: Authorizes the Governor of Fort St. George in Council to depute a Member of the Board of Revenue to perform, either fully or partially, the collective duties of the Board within any district of the Presidency.

main_sections.section_title: Powers and Duties of the Commissioned Member
main_sections.description: Grants the deputed Member, through a special commission, the authority to exercise all powers and duties vested in the Board of Revenue collectively, subject to any exceptions or restrictions outlined in the commission. It also states that regulations and acts concerning the Board of Revenue will apply to the Commissioner within their limits.

Mandates that every commission issued under this Act must be published in the Fort St. George Gazette. The Commissioner assumes office from the date of publication. Revocation or termination of the commission also requires publication in the Gazette.
Stipulates that all correspondence and documents related to a commission, upon its determination, shall be deposited in the Office of the Board of Revenue and considered as records of the Board.

important_rules: Rule 1: The Governor of Fort St. George in Council has the authority to depute a Member of the Board of Revenue to perform specific duties in any district.
Rule 2: A commissioned Member of the Board of Revenue can exercise all powers of the Board of Revenue collectively, as per their commission.
Rule 3: All commissions and their revocations must be published in the Fort St. George Gazette.
Rule 4: Documents related to a commission are to be retained as records of the Board of Revenue.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Governor of Fort St. George in Council, and by extension, the appointed Commissioner of Revenue.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the issuance and publication of special commissions, and the subsequent exercise of powers by the deputed Commissioner, with the oversight and administrative support of the Board of Revenue.

rights: Right of the Governor of Fort St. George in Council to depute a Member of the Board of Revenue.
Right of the deputed Member (Commissioner) to exercise the powers of the Board of Revenue collectively within the limits of their commission.
duties: Duty of the Governor to see fit to depute a Member.
Duty of the Commissioner to exercise powers as per the commission.
Duty to publish commissions and their revocations in the Gazette.
Duty to deposit commission-related documents as records of the Board of Revenue.

key_procedures: Procedure 1: Issuance of a special commission by the Governor of Fort St. George in Council to a Member of the Board of Revenue.
Procedure 2: Publication of the commission in the Fort St. George Gazette, upon which the Commissioner assumes office.
Procedure 3: Exercise of powers by the Commissioner within the scope of their commission and applicable regulations.
Procedure 4: Deposit of all commission-related correspondence and documents with the Board of Revenue upon the determination of the commission.
Procedure 5: Publication of revocation or termination of any commission in the Fort St. George Gazette.
administration: Board of Revenue, under the authority of the Governor of Fort St. George in Council.
important_notes: The act grants specific powers to a single member of the Board of Revenue, allowing for more efficient administrative functioning within districts.
The powers of the Commissioner can be subject to exceptions or restrictions as prescribed in their commission.

title: THE IMPROVEMENTS IN TOWNS ACT, 1850
purpose: To enable improvements to be made in Towns, including better provision for making, repairing, cleaning, lighting, or watching any public streets, roads, drains, or tanks, and for the prevention of nuisances, or for improving the said Town or Suburb in any other manner.
scope: Applies to Towns or Suburbs within the Territories under the Government of the East India Company, excluding Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay. It can be put into force in a specific Town or Suburb upon application and declaration of desire by its inhabitants.

main_sections.description: Repeals the previous Act X. 1842, which was enacted for similar purposes but proved ineffectual.

main_sections.section_title: Enabling Act to be put in force
main_sections.description: Empowers the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, to order this Act to be put in force in any Town or Suburb if the inhabitants express a desire for improvements related to public health and convenience.

Requires public notice in the Government Gazette and by proclamation within the Town or Suburb when an application is made to put the Act into force, allowing inhabitants to declare their wishes for or against its adoption.

Mandates that the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, will consider all declarations and make a final order, published and notified, determining whether the application aligns with the inhabitants' wishes and for which purposes the Act will be in force.

States that the Act comes into force upon the publication of the order and that the making and publication of such an order is conclusive evidence of compliance and the Act being in force for specified purposes.

When the Act comes into force, the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, will appoint Commissioners (including the Magistrate and selected inhabitants) to implement the Act and authorize them to prepare Rules for its effective execution. The Government can also remove or replace Commissioners.

main_sections.section_title: Rules to be prepared by Commissioners
main_sections.description: Details the essential provisions that the Commissioners' Rules must cover, including appointment of officers, definition of taxable persons and methods, amendment of rules, prohibition of nuisances, and imposition of penalties.
Grants Commissioners the power to make necessary contracts, apply collected taxes for necessary works, payment of officers and servants, and other incidental expenses.

Exempts Commissioners from personal liability on contracts made on behalf of inhabitants but holds them liable for misapplication of monies they knowingly participated in or for gross neglect of duty.

Applies the powers of Act II. 1839 for the recovery of fines to the recovery of all arrears of taxes and penalties under this Act. Magistrates are required to enforce these powers when requested by the Commissioners.
Ensures that no rate or assessment made under this Act will be invalid due to a defect in form. Property only needs to be described generally to be known for rating or assessment purposes.

main_sections.section_title: Liability of moveable property for taxes
main_sections.description: States that all moveable property found on assessed premises can be seized and sold by warrant of a Magistrate to pay any arrears of tax levied on that property.
Requires Commissioners to submit an annual account of works executed and sums received and spent to the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, by April 30th each year.

Empowers the Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor, to suspend the operation of the Act in any town or suburb and to appoint persons to investigate the conduct of Commissioners or their officers.

important_rules: Rules must provide for the appointment and management of necessary officers and servants and their salaries.
Rules must define who is to be taxed (by House Assessment or Town Duties), the amount of tax, how it's raised and collected, and ensure its safety and due application.
Rules must outline the process for amending, rescinding, or making new rules, subject to Government approval.
Rules must define and prohibit nuisances within the Town or Suburb.
Rules can impose penalties for breach, not exceeding Fifty Rupees, or Five Rupees per day for continuing nuisances.

penalties: For breach of any Rule made by the Commissioners, not exceeding Fifty Rupees.
For continuing nuisance, not exceeding Five Rupees for every day such nuisance is continued.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Commissioners appointed under the Act, and Magistrates when requested for recovery of fines and penalties.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the application of powers from Act II. 1839 for the recovery of fines, including seizure and sale of moveable property for tax arrears.

rights: Inhabitants have the right to declare their wishes for or against the adoption of the Act in their Town or Suburb.
Inhabitants have the right to have public streets, roads, drains, or tanks made, repaired, cleaned, lit, or watched, and nuisances prevented, if the Act is put in force.
duties: Inhabitants have a duty to pay taxes and assessments levied under the Act.
Commissioners have a duty to faithfully execute the Act and manage collected monies, facing liability for misapplication or gross neglect.
obligations: The Local Government has an obligation to consider inhabitants' wishes when deciding to put the Act into force.
The Local Government has an obligation to ensure accounts of receipts and disbursements are submitted annually.

key_procedures: Application to Local Government for putting the Act into force.
Public notification of application and a period for inhabitants to declare their wishes.
Consideration of declarations and a final order by the Local Government.
Publication of the final order and commencement of the Act in the specified Town or Suburb.
Appointment of Commissioners by the Local Government.
Preparation and approval of Rules by the Commissioners and the Local Government.
Collection and application of taxes for town improvements.
Submission of annual accounts by Commissioners to the Local Government.
administration: Local Government (Governor or Governor in Council, or Lieutenant Governor) and appointed Commissioners.
important_notes: The Act is an amendment and extension of previous legislation (Act X. 1842) which was found ineffectual.
The Act cannot be applied within the towns of Calcutta, Madras, or Bombay.
The decision of the Local Government regarding the adoption of the Act is final.
The publication of the order putting the Act into force is conclusive evidence of compliance.

title: THE MADRAS CITY LAND REVENUE ACT, 1851
purpose: To ascertain and collect land revenue accruing due to the East India Company at Madras in a summary manner.
scope: Applies to all assessable lands within the limits of the Town of Madras, as defined in Section XII., Regulation II. of 1802 of the Madras Code. It covers lands not owned by the East India Company, lakiraj tenures, and land revenue collection.

key_definitions.Collector: Any person or persons lawfully appointed to exercise the powers vested in the Collector under this Act.
key_definitions.Board of Revenue: Any person or persons lawfully appointed to exercise the powers vested in the Board of Revenue under this Act.

main_sections.description: Lands within the Town of Madras, not owned by the East India Company, which are assessable but have not been assessed or their assessment rate is unknown, shall be assessed at customary rates for similar lands in the vicinity, considering their location inside or outside the walls of Black Town.

Lakhiraj tenures in Madras with uninterrupted possession for sixty years under alleged grants exempting or partially exempting from assessment are valid. Other lakiraj tenures are only valid if held under an unexpired grant from the British Government.

main_sections.section_title: Determination of Assessment Rate and Appeal
main_sections.description: The Collector of Madras will determine the assessment rate for assessable land based on similar lands nearby. An appeal can be made to the Board of Revenue within six months of the Collector's notification, and the Board's decision will be final.

The Collector can order the measurement of assessable or already assessed lands to determine the assessment amount or to verify if actual dimensions match the dimensions used for calculating assessment or rent.
If measurement reveals that the actual dimensions of land are less than those used for calculating assessment or rent, a proportionate abatement will be made upon demand.

If actual dimensions exceed those used for calculation, the excess will be charged at the same rate. An appeal lies to the Board of Revenue against such extra assessment if preferred within six months, and the Board's decision is final. This provision does not prejudice the holder of land from which ground was usurped.

main_sections.section_title: Recovery of Rent by Distress and Sale
main_sections.description: If an owner or holder of assessed land neglects to pay the assessed sum or rent after written demand, the Collector can recover it by distress and sale of goods and chattels. The Collector has powers similar to a Judge of the Court of Small Causes for this purpose and can appoint officers as bailiffs and appraisers.
An under-tenant who pays rent directly to the East India Company or whose property is seized and sold may deduct the amount from the next rent payment to their landlord.

main_sections.section_title: Priority of East India Company's Claim
main_sections.description: The claim of the East India Company for land revenue or rent has priority over all other claims on the land or to which distrained property may be liable.
If the Collector's claim for rent arrears is disputed, the distress and sale process will not be stayed unless the claimed amount is deposited with the Collector.
Arrears of rent or revenue due to the East India Company are recoverable within six years from the date they are due or from the date of a written acknowledgment of the debt.

Claims to hold land lakiraj or free of assessment will be investigated by the Collector, who will report to the Board of Revenue. If the Board is satisfied, their order is final. If not, the Collector will assess the land, and the claimant can contest it in the Civil Courts.

Obstructing or molesting the Collector or subordinate officers in their duty is punishable by a fine not exceeding five hundred rupees, or imprisonment for up to six months in default of payment, upon conviction before a Magistrate of the Town of Madras.

The Collector can punish contempts in his presence by fine not exceeding two hundred rupees, or imprisonment for up to one month in default of payment. An appeal lies to the Board of Revenue, whose decision is final.
The Collector shall execute this Act under the usual control of the superior revenue authorities.

Ground rents payable to the East India Company in Madras are considered revenue under 21 Geo. 3 Cap. 70. The Supreme Court of Judicature has no civil jurisdiction over these ground rents or their assessment/collection.

Actions concerning trespass or injury by revenue officers acting under this Act, claims regarding goods taken or monies paid to revenue officers, or claims of rent/revenue by the East India Company under this Act, shall be tried in the Civil Courts in the Zillah of Chingleput. Such actions must be brought within six months of the cause of action.
Defines 'Collector' and 'Board of Revenue' as persons lawfully appointed to exercise their respective powers under the Act.

important_rules: Rule 1: Assessable lands not assessed or with unknown rates in Madras City shall be assessed at customary rates for similar lands nearby.
Rule 2: Lakhiraj tenures with sixty years of uninterrupted possession under alleged grants are valid; others are valid only if under a British Government grant.
Rule 3: Rent may be recovered by distress and sale of goods and chattels after a written demand for payment, with powers similar to those for distresses for small rents.
Rule 4: The East India Company's claim for land revenue or rent has priority over all other claims on the property.
Rule 5: Arrears of rent are recoverable within six years of becoming due or after a written acknowledgment of the debt.
Rule 6: Obstructing revenue officers in their duty is punishable by fine and/or imprisonment.
Rule 7: Contempts before the Collector can be punished by fine and/or imprisonment, with an appeal to the Board of Revenue.

penalties: Fine not exceeding five hundred rupees and/or imprisonment up to six months for obstructing revenue officers.
Fine not exceeding two hundred rupees and/or imprisonment up to one month for contempt before the Collector.
Recovery of rent by distress and sale of goods and chattels.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector of Madras, under the control of superior revenue authorities.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through measurement of lands, determination of assessment rates, written demands, and by distress and sale of goods and chattels. Appeals can be made to the Board of Revenue. Criminal offenses are dealt with by the Magistrate of the Town of Madras.

rights: Right to claim proportionate abatement of assessment if actual land dimensions are less than those used for calculation.
Right to appeal against assessed rates to the Board of Revenue.
Right of an under-tenant to deduct rent payments.
Right to contest assessment of land claimed as rent-free in Civil Courts.
duties: Duty to pay assessed land revenue or rent.
Duty to allow measurement of land.
Duty to allow distress and sale of goods for non-payment of rent.
Duty not to obstruct revenue officers.
obligations: Obligation to comply with the assessment and collection of land revenue as determined by the Collector and Board of Revenue.
Obligation to provide evidence for claims of rent-free land.

key_procedures: Procedure for assessing unassessed lands: Collector determines rate based on customary rates of similar lands in the vicinity.

Procedure for handling lakiraj claims: Collector investigates, reports to Board of Revenue, whose decision is final. If claim is invalid, Collector assesses the land, and claimant can sue in Civil Court.
Procedure for recovery of rent arrears: Written demand by Collector, followed by distress and sale of goods and chattels if payment is refused, or distress and sale of goods found on the land.
Procedure for appeals against assessment: Appeal to the Board of Revenue within six months of the Collector's order; Board's decision is final.
administration: Superior revenue authorities, with the Collector of Madras as the primary enforcer.
important_notes: The Act refers to and extends provisions of other Acts, including Act VII. of 1847 (regulating distresses for small rents in Calcutta) and Act IX. of 1850.

Actions concerning trespass or injury by revenue officers, or claims related to goods taken or monies paid under the Act, must be brought within six months of the cause of action and are tried in the Civil Courts of Chingleput Zillah.
The Supreme Court of Judicature has no civil jurisdiction over ground rents payable to the East India Company in Madras.

title: THE INDIAN TOLLS ACT, 1851
purpose: To enable the Government to levy tolls on public roads and bridges.
scope: This Act extends to the territories administered by the Governor of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal, the Lieutenant-Governor of North-Western Provinces of Bengal and the Governor of the Presidency of Fort St. George in Council as of July 4, 1851. State amendments extend its application to various other regions and government bodies.

main_sections.description: Defines the geographical scope of the Act as of its enactment.

main_sections.section_title: Power to cause levy of tolls on roads and bridges within certain rates, and to appoint collectors. Collectors’ responsibilities.
main_sections.description: Grants the State Government the power to levy tolls on roads and bridges constructed or repaired at the expense of the Central or any State Government, and to appoint collectors.
