Collectors are made liable to the same responsibilities as those employed in land revenue collection.

main_sections.section_title: Their powers for recovery of toll. Release of seized property on tender of dues.
main_sections.description: Outlines the powers of toll collectors for recovering unpaid tolls, including seizing property. It also details the process for selling seized property and the provision for releasing seized property upon tender of dues and double the toll.
Specifies exemptions from paying tolls, primarily for police officers on duty and property in their custody. State amendments have introduced further exemptions.
Mandates Police-officers to assist toll collectors in the execution of the Act, granting them the same powers as in their regular police duties.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for offences under Act. Compensation to person aggrieved. Saving of his right to sue.
main_sections.description: Defines penalties for individuals who illegally levy or demand tolls, or extort money under the color of the Act. It also provides for compensation to aggrieved persons and clarifies that this does not bar civil suits.

main_sections.section_title: Exhibition of table of tolls, and statement of penalties.
main_sections.description: Requires the display of a table of authorized tolls and a statement of penalties at toll gates or stations in both English and the vernacular language of the district.
States that tolls levied under this Act are deemed public revenue.

important_rules: Tolls can be levied on roads and bridges made or repaired at government expense.
Toll collectors have the power to seize property for non-payment of tolls.
Seized property can be sold after 24 hours if the toll remains undischarged.
Seized property can be released if the tender of all incurred expenses and double the toll is made before the sale begins.
Only police officers on duty and property in their custody are exempt from paying tolls.
A table of tolls and penalties must be displayed at toll gates.
Tolls levied are considered public revenue.

penalties: Imprisonment for any term not exceeding six calendar months for illegally levying or demanding tolls, or for unlawful extortion.
Fine not exceeding two hundred rupees for illegally levying or demanding tolls, or for unlawful extortion.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Magistrates, and implicitly, toll collectors and Police-officers.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Conviction before a Magistrate for illegal toll collection or extortion. Police-officers are mandated to assist toll collectors.

rights: Right to sue in Civil Court for redress, in addition to compensation awarded by a Magistrate for illegal exactions.
duties: Duty of Police-officers to assist toll collectors when required.
Duty of toll collectors to adhere to responsibilities similar to land revenue collectors.
obligations: Obligation to pay tolls on roads and bridges.
Obligation to display tables of tolls and penalties.
Obligation to return any balance remaining after the sale of seized property to the owner.
Obligation of collectors to follow procedures for seizure and sale of property.

key_procedures: Procedure for levying tolls on roads and bridges.
Procedure for appointing toll collectors and defining their responsibilities.
Procedure for recovery of tolls through seizure and sale of property, including notice and auction.
Procedure for releasing seized property upon payment of dues and penalties.
Procedure for displaying toll rates and penalties.
Procedure for enforcement of penalties through Magisterial conviction.
administration: The State Government (or its equivalent administrative body at the time of enactment) is responsible for appointing collectors and establishing toll rates. The net proceeds of tolls were intended for the construction, repair, and maintenance of roads and bridges, though this specific application detail was omitted.
important_notes: Section 1 of the Act was repealed by the Repealing Act, 1870.
The Schedule was repealed by the Devolution Act, 1920.
The words 'not exceeding the rates mentioned in the Schedule annexed to this Act' were omitted by Act 38 of 1920.

The original provision that the net proceeds of tolls shall be applied wholly to the construction, repair and maintenance of roads and bridges within the presidency in which they are levied, has been omitted by the A.O. 1937.
The Act has been subject to numerous amendments and extensions across various regions of India over time.
State amendments have introduced new exemptions and expanded the scope of entities that can be authorized to maintain roads and bridges for toll collection purposes.

title: The Bombay Rent-Free Estates Act, 1852
purpose: To provide for the adjudication of titles to certain estates claimed to be wholly or partially rent-free in the Presidency of Bombay, particularly in districts not under general government regulations.
scope: Applies to the territories of the Deccan, Kandeish, and Southern Mahratta Country, and other districts recently annexed to the Bombay Presidency, which were not brought under the General Regulations of Government by Regulation XXVIII of 1827. Specifically addresses claims against the Government related to Inams and other estates exempt from land revenue.

key_definitions.Inam: Estates wholly or partially exempt from payment of Land Revenue.
key_definitions.Non-regulation districts: Districts not brought under the General Regulations of Government by Regulation XXVIII of 1827.

main_sections.section_title: Inapplicability of existing regulations and finality of past orders
main_sections.description: Declares that existing rules regarding determination of titles and procedure in Chapters IX and X of Regulation XVII of 1827 and Clause 1 of Regulation VI of 1833 do not apply to non-regulation districts. It also states that past orders regarding land continuance or resumption in these districts shall not be questioned in any court of law.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment of Inam Commissioner and Assistants
main_sections.description: Empowers the Governor of Bombay in Council to appoint an Inam Commissioner with necessary assistants and subordinate establishment in any zillah or division of the territories not under general regulations.

main_sections.section_title: Duties of Inam Commissioner and Assistants
main_sections.description: States that the duties of the Inam Commissioner and his Assistants shall be discharged according to the Rules in Schedule A.
Specifies that titles of claimants to exempt lands or interests therein shall be determined by the Rules in Schedule B.

main_sections.section_title: Authority of Inam Commissioner and Assistants
main_sections.description: Grants Inam Commissioners and their Assistants the same authority as Civil Courts for procuring witnesses, taking evidence, and inflicting penalties for non-compliance, false testimony, resistance of process, contempt, etc. Their office is deemed a Court of Civil Jurisdiction. Appeals from their proceedings are governed by Rule 2 of Schedule A.

Prescribes punishment for bribery, extortion, abuse of authority, or other misconduct by officers of the Inam Commission as criminal offenses, with fines and imprisonment. Receipt of a present is considered extortion. This does not preclude civil prosecution.

Ensures that no decision or order of the Inam Commissioner, his Assistants, or the Governor in Council under this Act shall be questioned or avoided in any Court of Law. Officers acting bona fide in pursuance of the Act are protected from being sued in Civil Courts.

important_rules: Rule 1 (Schedule A): Defines the core duty of the Inam Commissioner and Assistants as investigating titles to Inams, Jagheers, or claims for exemption from land revenue, and acting on Government instructions.

Rule 2 (Schedule A): Establishes an appeal process: Assistant Commissioner's orders are appealable to the Inam Commissioner, whose orders are appealable to the Governor of Bombay in Council, whose decision is final.
Rule 3 (Schedule A): Dictates that claimants must provide statements of their title and supporting evidence.
Rule 4 (Schedule A): Allows for receipt of statements and evidence directly or through local Revenue Authorities.

Rule 5 (Schedule A): If general invitations are not heeded, specific notices can be issued to claimants to show their title within a specified period (at least two months), with failure leading to attachment of land.
Rule 6 (Schedule A): Details the procedure for serving notices.
Rule 7 (Schedule A): Outlines the procedure for public notice if claimants cannot be found, with a six-month period for appearance, failing which land may be attached.
Rule 8 (Schedule A): Specifies that attachment is enforced by the Collector at the written requisition of the Inam Commissioner or Assistant.
Rule 9 (Schedule A): Requires testing of statements and evidence against Government accounts and records before passing decisions on land continuance, resumption, or assessment.
Rule 10 (Schedule A): If notices fail to procure attendance, the Commissioner shall ascertain facts and pass a just decision based on procurable evidence.
Rule 11 (Schedule A): Attachment is removed upon the Commissioner's certification, but rents collected during attachment are not restored without Government instructions.
Rule 12 (Schedule A): Certified copies of decisions are to be delivered to claimants or posted publicly if claimants are undiscoverable.
Rule 13 (Schedule A): Decisions are to be executed by the Collector at the requisition of the Inam Commissioner or Assistant, as prescribed by the Governor in Council.
Rule 14 (Schedule A): Sets a 100-day limit for appeals against Inam Commissioner's decisions, requiring a copy of the decree and proof of just cause for late filing.
Rule 1 (Schedule B): Confines claims to Inams already declared permanent by competent authority.
Rule 2 (Schedule B): Land is hereditary if expressly made so by Sunnud from a competent authority, without illegal conditions, and not revoked.
Rule 3 (Schedule B): Uninterrupted holding for 60 years before heir's introduction, with heir in possession, grants hereditary right, but not to adopted heirs or female heirs.

Rule 4 (Schedule B): Lands held for 40 years in the male line continue for one more generation, not to adopted heirs. It also defines proof of authorized possession, allows claims unless disproved, and defines the introduction of British Government.
Rule 6 (Schedule B): Exemptions not protected by rules are abolished on incumbent's demise, unless held by fraud. Bona fide holders are considered incumbents.
Rule 7 (Schedule B): Lands held for support of Mosques, etc., enjoyed for 40 years are not resumed, but this doesn't apply to private holdings.
Rule 8 (Schedule B): Lands held under official tenure intended to be permanent are not resumed, subject to complicated provisions.
Rule 9 (Schedule B): A moiety of resumed lands may be continued to widows of the last incumbent in cases of destitution.
Rule 10 (Schedule B): Makes it discretionary for Government to apply these rules to certain specified kinds of lands.
Rule 11 (Schedule B): Empowers the Governor in Council to relax and interpret the rules.

penalties: Bribery, extortion, abuse of authority, or other misconduct by Inam Commission officers are punishable as criminal offenses with fine and imprisonment up to five years.
Receipt of a present by an officer is considered extortion.
Failure to comply with notices requiring the production of title can lead to attachment of land.
Failure of a claimant to appear and prove title after public notice can lead to attachment of land.
Penalties adjudicated under this Act do not preclude other Civil prosecutions.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Inam Commissioner, his Assistants, Governor of Bombay in Council, and Collectors (for attachment and rent collection).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through investigation of titles, examination of witnesses, taking evidence, issuing notices, attachment of lands, collection of rents, and execution of decisions by Collectors as prescribed by the Governor of Bombay in Council. Criminal offenses are prosecuted as per law.

rights: Right to have claims to rent-free estates adjudicated under specific rules.
Right to appeal Assistant Commissioner's orders to the Inam Commissioner, and Inam Commissioner's orders to the Governor in Council.
Right to present statements and evidence supporting title claims.
Right to receive certified copies of decisions.
Potential right to a moiety of resumed land for widows of last incumbent in cases of destitution.
Hereditary rights to land under certain conditions (Sunnud, 60-year holding, etc.).
duties: Duty of claimants to provide statements of title and supporting evidence.
Duty to comply with notices issued by the Inam Commission.
Duty of Inam Commissioner and Assistants to investigate claims, take evidence, and pass decisions.
Duty of Collectors to enforce attachment and collect rents upon requisition.
Duty of the Governor in Council to interpret and relax rules.
Duty of officers to conduct investigations and proceedings impartially and without misconduct.
obligations: Claimants are obligated to appear personally or by agent, explain their title, and produce evidence as required by notices.
Officers of the Inam Commission are obligated to act according to the Act and instructions of Government, and to discharge their duties without misconduct.

key_procedures: Investigation of rent-free estate claims by Inam Commissioner and Assistants.
Receipt of title statements and evidence from claimants.
Issuance of notices to claimants to prove their title.
Attachment of land if claimants fail to appear or provide proof.
Testing of evidence against government records.
Passing of decisions on continuance, resumption, or assessment of lands.
Appeals process from Assistant Commissioner to Inam Commissioner, and to the Governor in Council.
Execution of decisions by the Collector.
Public posting of decisions if claimants are undiscoverable.
administration: The Governor of Bombay in Council, through the appointed Inam Commissioner and his Assistants, with the assistance of Collectors and Revenue Authorities.
important_notes: The Act explicitly states that existing regulations do not apply to non-regulation districts and that past orders in these districts shall not be questioned.
Decisions of the Inam Commissioner and Governor in Council under this Act are final and cannot be questioned in any Court of Law.
Officers acting bona fide under the Act are protected from civil lawsuits.
The Act provides for the hereditary descent of land under specific historical conditions, but not to adopted heirs or female heirs in certain cases.
Lands held for the support of Mosques, etc., are protected if enjoyed for 40 years, provided they are not private holdings.

title: An Act for extending the provisions of Acts XXIV. of 1841. and XVII. of 1843, to the Straits Settlement.
purpose: To remove doubts regarding the applicability of Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843 to the Straits Settlements, and to extend their provisions to the Court of Judicature of the Straits Settlements.
scope: Geographical: The Straits Settlement, specifically Prince of Wales’ Islands, Singapore and Malacca. Subject Matter: Extends the provisions of Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843. Applies to the Supreme Courts' provisions to the Court of Judicature of the Straits Settlements.

main_sections.section_title: Extension of Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843
main_sections.description: States that the provisions of Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843 shall be applicable and in force in the Straits Settlement.

main_sections.section_title: Applicability of Supreme Court provisions to the Court of Judicature of Straits Settlements
main_sections.description: Specifies that all provisions in Act XXIV. of 1841 and Act XVII. of 1843 relating to Her Majesty's Supreme Courts shall apply to the Court of Judicature of the Straits Settlements. It further instructs that wherever the terms 'Her Majesty’s Supreme Courts' or similar are used, they should be interpreted as 'the Court of Judicature of Prince of Wales’ Island, Singapore and Malacca'.

important_rules: The provisions of Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843 are now applicable and in force in the Straits Settlement.
Provisions concerning Her Majesty's Supreme Courts in Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843 are to be applied to the Court of Judicature of the Straits Settlements.
References to 'Her Majesty's Supreme Courts' in the aforementioned Acts should be read as 'the Court of Judicature of Prince of Wales’ Island, Singapore and Malacca'.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Court of Judicature of Prince of Wales’ Island, Singapore and Malacca.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: By applying the provisions of Acts XXIV. of 1841 and XVII. of 1843 to this court as if it were the Supreme Court.

administration: Likely administered by the judicial authorities in the Straits Settlements, specifically the Court of Judicature.
important_notes: This act aims to clarify and confirm the legal status of two prior acts within the Straits Settlements, which had previously been subject to doubt.
The act is essentially an extension act, not introducing new substantive law but rather applying existing law to a new jurisdiction.

title: The Rent Recovery Act, 1853
purpose: To resolve doubts regarding the jurisdiction of Collectors and Deputy Collectors in cases involving the sale of lands and summary suits for rent recovery, especially when lands are situated in multiple collectorates. It also aims to validate past decisions and sales made by officers of improper districts, provided no proceedings were initiated to dispute them before the Act's passage. Furthermore, it extends existing acts and regulations concerning rent recovery and sales of tenures to sales conducted under Act VIII of 1835.
scope: This Act applies to lands that are the subject of sale for recovery of rent or are related to summary suits for rent. It covers situations where lands are situated within one or more Collectorates, and it addresses the jurisdiction of Collectors and independent Deputy Collectors. The scope includes sales of Putnee Talooks and other saleable tenures, as well as sales of land in satisfaction of Summary Decrees for rent.

key_definitions.Collectorate: The zillah or other district to which a Collector is appointed. Lands situated beyond these limits are not considered within the Collectorate, even if they form part of an estate paying revenue to that Collector.
key_definitions.Independent Deputy Collector: An Officer appointed by Government to act as a Deputy Collector, independently of a Collector, irrespective of whether their office is for revenue receipt. A Deputy Collectorate is the district within which such an officer is directed by Government to act.

main_sections.section_title: Jurisdiction in cases of lands in multiple Collectorates
main_sections.description: Defines which Collector has jurisdiction for sales or suits when lands are in multiple Collectorates. If all lands are in one Collectorate, the Collector of that Collectorate presides. If a Talook or tenure comprises lands in two or more Collectorates, or if lands in multiple Collectorates are under one lease or engagement at one entire rent, the Collector in whose Collectorate the greater part of such lands is situated will have jurisdiction.

main_sections.section_title: Determination of jurisdiction by the Board of Revenue
main_sections.description: If a Collector is uncertain about the location of lands or the greater part thereof within their Collectorate, they must report the case to the Board of Revenue to which they are subordinate. The Board's order in such matters will be conclusive regarding the Collector's jurisdiction.

Clarifies that 'Collectorate' refers to the zillah or district to which a Collector is appointed. Lands outside this defined area are not considered part of the Collectorate, even if they contribute revenue to it.

States that an independent Deputy Collector can exercise all the powers and jurisdictions of a Collector within their Deputy Collectorate, to the same extent as a Collector can within their Collectorate. Their Deputy Collectorate is considered a Collectorate for the purposes of this Act, and they are considered a Collector.

main_sections.section_title: Definition of Independent Deputy Collector and Deputy Collectorate
main_sections.description: Defines an independent Deputy Collector as an officer appointed by the Government to act independently of a Collector. It also defines a Deputy Collectorate as the district where such an officer is directed to act.

main_sections.section_title: Notices of sale by Independent Deputy Collector
main_sections.description: Specifies that any notice required to be posted at the Collector's Cutcherry for sales conducted by an independent Deputy Collector can instead be posted at the Deputy Collector's Cutcherry.

main_sections.section_title: Location of public Cutcherry for Independent Deputy Collector
main_sections.description: Allows an independent Deputy Collector to exercise their assigned powers in any part of their Deputy Collectorate, as long as the public Cutcherry where these powers are exercised is located within that Deputy Collectorate.

Requires that any notice to be posted at the Zillah Court or local Adawlut be displayed within the jurisdiction of the Zillah Court or local Adawlut where the lands to be sold, or the greater portion thereof, are situated.

main_sections.section_title: Validation of past orders, decisions, and sales
main_sections.description: Grants validity to any order, decision, or sale made before the Act's passage by a Collector, Deputy Collector, or other Officer, even if they were from the improper district or if the notice was posted at an improper Cutcherry, unless proceedings to invalidate such action were initiated before the Act was passed.

main_sections.section_title: Extension of existing Acts and Regulations
main_sections.description: Extends Act XXV of 1850 and Section IX of Regulation VIII of 1819 (as modified by Clause I, Section XVI of Regulation VII of 1832, and as altered by Act XXV of 1850) to all sales conducted under Act VIII of 1835.

important_rules: When lands are subject to sale or a summary suit for rent, and they are situated in one Collectorate, the Collector of that Collectorate has jurisdiction.

If lands subject to sale or suit are in multiple Collectorates, and they are held under one lease or at one entire rent, the Collector in whose Collectorate the greater part of the lands lies has jurisdiction.
A Collector uncertain about jurisdiction must refer the matter to the Board of Revenue, whose order will be conclusive.
Independent Deputy Collectors can exercise the powers of Collectors within their designated Deputy Collectorates.
Notices for sales conducted by Independent Deputy Collectors can be posted at their Cutcherry.
Notices to be posted at the Zillah Court or local Adawlut must be placed within the jurisdiction where the lands to be sold are situated.
Past orders, decisions, and sales are deemed valid unless their invalidity was challenged before the Act's enactment.
Act XXV of 1850 and specific parts of Regulation VIII of 1819 are extended to sales under Act VIII of 1835.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collectors, Deputy Collectors, and potentially the Board of Revenue for jurisdictional disputes.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the exercise of powers by Collectors and Deputy Collectors in conducting sales and hearing summary suits for rent. The Act also provides for the validation of past actions, implying enforcement through official recognition and continuation of proceedings.

rights: Landholders have the right to have their rent recovery and sale matters heard by the legally designated Collector.
Parties involved in rent recovery and sale proceedings have the right to proper notice.
Individuals can seek to invalidate past decisions or sales if proceedings were initiated before this Act.
duties: Collectors are obligated to conduct sales and hear summary suits according to the provisions of this Act, particularly concerning jurisdiction.
Independent Deputy Collectors have a duty to exercise their entrusted powers within their Deputy Collectorates.
Officers are required to provide notices of sale at the designated locations.
obligations: Collectors have an obligation to seek clarification from the Board of Revenue when jurisdictional doubts arise.
The Board of Revenue has an obligation to provide conclusive orders on Collectorate jurisdiction when referred.
All parties are implicitly obligated to comply with the decisions and sales made under this Act, unless previously challenged.

key_procedures: Procedure for determining jurisdiction when lands are in multiple Collectorates: If all lands are in one Collectorate, that Collector handles the matter. If lands are in multiple Collectorates, the Collector where the greater part of the land lies handles it. If a Collector doubts jurisdiction, they must report to the Board of Revenue for a conclusive order.

Procedure for posting notices: Notices of sale are to be stuck up at the Cutcherry of the relevant Collector or Independent Deputy Collector, and at the Adawlut of the Zillah where the lands are situated.
Procedure for validation of past acts: If no proceedings were commenced to dispute an order, decision, or sale made before this Act on grounds of improper jurisdiction or notice, it is deemed valid.
administration: Collectors and Deputy Collectors of Land Revenue, overseen by the Board of Revenue.
important_notes: The Act specifically addresses and resolves doubts that may have arisen due to the transfer of powers related to rent recovery and sales from Judges to Collectors, and when lands span multiple administrative districts.
The Act aims to prevent past sales and decisions from being invalidated due to technical errors in jurisdiction or notice posting, provided no legal challenge was made prior to the Act's enactment.

title: THE SHORE NUISANCES (BOMBAY AND KOTABA) ACT, 1853
purpose: To facilitate the removal of nuisances, obstructions, and encroachments below high-water mark in the Islands of Bombay and Colaba, with a view to the safe navigation of the Harbour of Bombay and public interests generally.
scope: Applies to the sea-shore and harbor of the Islands of Bombay and Colaba, specifically to nuisances, obstructions, and encroachments located below the high-water mark.

key_definitions.high_water_mark: The ordinary line of high-water at monsoon tides.

main_sections.section_title: Empowers the Collector to require removal of Nuisances, &c. and to abate them himself.
main_sections.description: The Collector of Land Revenue at Bombay is empowered to issue a notice requiring the removal of any nuisance, obstruction, or encroachment below high-water mark in the Harbour of Bombay or on the shores of the Islands. The notice must be affixed near the offending item and published in the Bombay Government Gazette, stating that it will be removed by the Collector if not abated within one month.

main_sections.section_title: Authorizes proprietor to apply to Supreme Court to stop proceedings.
main_sections.description: If a person denies the Collector's right to abate or remove, they can petition the Supreme Court of Judicature at Bombay within one month of receiving notice. The petition must state the grounds of their alleged right and pray for the Collector to be restrained. The Court may fix a hearing, make orders, and potentially restrain further extension or abatement until adjudication.

main_sections.section_title: Onus of proof lies on petitioner.
main_sections.description: Upon the hearing of any petition filed under this Act, the burden of proving the alleged right rests with the petitioner.

main_sections.section_title: Petition to be presented within a month, except under special circumstances.
main_sections.description: No petition can be presented to the Court after the one-month period specified, unless the petitioner provides satisfactory accounting for the delay to the Court.

main_sections.section_title: Prescribes mode of proceeding in case of no petition or adverse decision.
main_sections.description: If no petition is presented within the month, or if a petition is presented and decided against the petitioner, or dismissed for want of prosecution, the Collector can authorize the abatement or removal of the nuisance. This is done through a warrant under his hand. The Collector and those acting under his warrant are not answerable for any unavoidable damage caused during the removal.

main_sections.section_title: Collector may sell materials of encroachment.
main_sections.description: The Collector is empowered to sell the materials of any encroachment or obstruction removed under this Act. The proceeds from the sale are to be applied towards the expenses of the removal. Any surplus remaining will be forfeited and paid as directed by the Governor of Bombay in Council.

main_sections.section_title: Save rights of E.I. Co. as trustees for the Crown, &c.
main_sections.description: This Act does not prejudice or affect the rights of the East India Company as trustees for the Crown in the Harbour or sea-shore of the Islands. It also does not interfere with any civil or criminal proceedings that could have been taken if the Act had not been passed.
Defines 'high-water mark' as the ordinary line of high-water at monsoon tides.

important_rules: A notice must be given by the Collector requiring the removal of a nuisance, obstruction, or encroachment below high-water mark.
The notice must be affixed conspicuously on or near the nuisance and published in the Bombay Government Gazette.
The notice must state that if the nuisance is not removed within one month, the Collector will abate it.
If a person disputes the Collector's right, they must petition the Supreme Court within one month of the notice.
The onus of proving a right lies with the petitioner in court.
No petition can be filed after one month without a satisfactory explanation for the delay.
If no petition is filed, or if the petition is lost, the Collector can issue a warrant for removal.
The Collector can sell materials of removed encroachments to cover removal costs; surplus goes to the Governor of Bombay in Council.

penalties: No explicit monetary penalties are detailed in the provided text. The primary enforcement mechanism is the abatement and removal of the nuisance/encroachment by the Collector.
Any surplus from the sale of materials of an encroachment or obstruction, after covering removal expenses, is forfeited and applied as directed by the Governor of Bombay in Council.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Collector of Land Revenue at Bombay, and persons authorized by his warrant.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through issuing notices requiring removal, and subsequently by authorizing abatement and removal of nuisances, obstructions, or encroachments either by the Collector's own agents or by persons acting under his warrant. This can also be enforced through Supreme Court proceedings if challenged.

rights: Right to petition the Supreme Court to stop proceedings if one's right is denied.
Right of the East India Company as trustees for the Crown to their existing rights.
Right to bring civil or criminal proceedings as if the Act had not been passed.
duties: Duty to remove a nuisance, obstruction, or encroachment within one month of receiving notice from the Collector.
Duty of the petitioner to prove their alleged right upon hearing of the petition.
obligations: Obligation to present a petition to the Supreme Court within one month if challenging the Collector's actions.
Obligation for the petitioner to provide sufficient security for costs when petitioning the Supreme Court.

key_procedures: Notice and Abatement: Collector issues notice (Form 1) requiring removal of nuisance/encroachment within one month. If not abated, Collector abates it.
Challenging the Collector: If a person denies the Collector's right, they must petition the Supreme Court within one month, detailing their grounds. Court may restrain actions and fix a hearing.
Court Proceedings: Onus of proof is on the petitioner. No petitions after one month without good cause.
Warrant for Removal: If no petition or if petition fails, Collector issues a warrant (Form 2) to authorize removal. Damaged caused unavoidably during removal does not make the Collector liable.
Sale of Materials: Collector can sell removed materials to cover expenses. Surplus is forfeited.
administration: Collector of Land Revenue at Bombay, and the Governor of Bombay in Council for directing the application of surplus sale proceeds.
important_notes: The Collector and those acting under his warrant are not liable for any damage unavoidably occasioned in the removal of any nuisance, obstruction, or encroachment.
The Act explicitly saves the rights of the East India Company as trustees for the Crown and does not preclude existing civil or criminal proceedings.

title: THE BENGAL BONDED WAREHOUSE ASSOCIATION ACT, 1854
purpose: To amend Act No. V. of 1838, relating to the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association, by altering certain provisions regarding its management and dissolution.
scope: This act applies to the Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association and its proprietors within the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal.

main_sections.description: Repeals Sections XII, XIV, XXXII, and XXXVII of Act No. V of 1838.
Specifies that the business of the Association shall be managed by six Directors, with three forming a quorum.

Details the rotation of Directors, with two going out of office in May each year before the ordinary General Meeting. Two Directors are to be chosen at this meeting, and retiring Directors are eligible for re-election.
Stipulates that a person must own at least five shares of the Capital Stock of the Association in their own right to be eligible to be a Director.

Requires Ordinary General Meetings to be held at least twice a year (second Wednesday in May and November). Directors must present a written report and balance sheet. Dividends may be declared from profits but must not diminish the capital.

Empowers the Association to make By-laws for regulating its proceedings. These By-laws are binding on Members and Officers but require approval from a specially convened extraordinary General Meeting and confirmation by the Governor of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal.

Allows the Governor-General of India in Council to order the dissolution of the Association after March 14, 1860. Dissolution will occur five years from the date of the order, except for purposes outlined in Section XXXIX of Act No. V of 1838.

important_rules: Rule 1: The business of the Association is to be managed by six Directors, with a quorum of three.
Rule 2: Directors are subject to rotation, with elections held annually in May.
Rule 3: A Director must own at least five shares of the Association's capital stock.
Rule 4: Ordinary General Meetings must be held twice a year, in May and November.
Rule 5: Dividends can only be declared from profits and must not reduce the Association's capital.
Rule 6: By-laws need approval from an extraordinary General Meeting and the Governor of Bengal.
Rule 7: The Corporation can be dissolved by order of the Governor-General in Council after March 14, 1860, with dissolution taking effect five years after the order.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Governor-General of India in Council (for dissolution), and potentially the Governor of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal (for By-law confirmation).
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through orders in council for dissolution, and confirmation for by-laws. Enforcement of other provisions would likely fall under general corporate governance mechanisms for the Association.

rights: Proprietors have the right to elect Directors.
Proprietors have the right to receive dividends from profits (provided capital is not diminished).
The Association has the right to make By-laws.
The Association has the right to be dissolved under specific conditions after a set period.
duties: Directors have a duty to manage the business of the Association.
Directors have a duty to present a report and balance sheet at General Meetings.
The Association has a duty to adhere to its approved By-laws.
The Association must ensure no dividend diminishes its capital.
obligations: Individuals must meet the share qualification to be a Director.
The Association must convene General Meetings as specified.
The Association must obtain necessary approvals for its By-laws.

key_procedures: Election of Directors: Two Directors go out of office in May annually. Two Directors are chosen at the Ordinary General Meeting held in May.
Declaration of Dividends: May be declared at Ordinary General Meetings from profits, but not if it diminishes capital.
Making of By-laws: Must be approved by an extraordinary General Meeting and confirmed by the Governor of Bengal.
Dissolution of the Association: Can be initiated by the Governor-General in Council after March 14, 1860, with dissolution occurring five years after the order.
administration: The Bengal Bonded Warehouse Association itself, overseen by its Directors and proprietors, with ultimate governmental oversight for dissolution.
important_notes: Sections of Act No. V of 1838 have been repealed, indicating this act is an amendment.
The dissolution of the corporation is a significant provision, indicating a potential end-of-life or restructuring possibility.
By-laws are only binding on members and officers and require significant external approval.
The provisions for dividend declaration emphasize capital preservation.

title: The Legal Representatives’ Suits Act, 1855
purpose: To enable executors, administrators, or representatives to sue and be sued in certain cases for wrongs which, according to the existing law, do not survive to or against them.
scope: Applies to legal representatives (executors, administrators, heirs) of deceased persons. It covers wrongs committed by or against the deceased in their lifetime, provided such wrongs occurred within one year before death and have occasioned pecuniary loss to the estate or are actionable by the deceased. The act's territorial scope has been extended over time to various parts of India, including specific districts and union territories.

main_sections.section_title: Executors may sue and be sued in certain cases for wrongs committed in lifetime of deceased.
main_sections.description: This section allows actions to be maintained by the executor, administrator, or representative of a deceased person for wrongs committed during the deceased's lifetime that caused pecuniary loss to the estate, provided the wrong was committed within one year before death. It also allows actions to be maintained against such representatives for wrongs committed by the deceased in their lifetime, provided the wrong was committed within one year before death. Damages recovered against representatives who administer according to English law are payable in the same order as simple contract debts.

main_sections.section_title: Death of either party not to abate suit. Proviso.
main_sections.description: This section states that a suit commenced under this Act will not abate due to the death of either party. Such a suit can be continued by or against the executors, administrators, or representatives of the deceased party. A proviso allows these representatives to set up a want of assets as a defense, either wholly or in part, as if the action had been originally commenced against them.

important_rules: An action can be maintained by legal representatives for wrongs committed by the deceased in their lifetime, if such wrongs caused pecuniary loss to the estate and were committed within one year before death.

An action can be maintained against legal representatives for wrongs committed by the deceased in their lifetime, if such wrongs were actionable by the deceased and were committed within one year before death.
Suits under this Act do not abate upon the death of a party and can be continued by or against their legal representatives.
Legal representatives can plead want of assets as a defense when a suit is continued against them.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be the courts of law.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through civil suits and legal proceedings initiated by or against the legal representatives of the deceased.

rights: Right of executors, administrators, or representatives to sue for wrongs that caused pecuniary loss to the deceased's estate.
Right of plaintiffs to continue actions against the legal representatives of a deceased defendant.
Right of defendants (legal representatives) to plead want of assets as a defense.
obligations: Obligation of legal representatives to administer damages recovered in accordance with the order of administration for simple contract debts, if they administer according to English law.
The original wrongdoer's obligation to have committed the wrong within one year before their death for the action to be maintainable by or against their representatives.

key_procedures: Initiation of an action by the legal representatives of a deceased person for wrongs committed by the deceased that resulted in pecuniary loss to the estate, provided the wrong occurred within one year of death.
Initiation of an action against the legal representatives of a deceased person for wrongs committed by the deceased, provided the wrong occurred within one year of death.
Continuation of an action by or against the legal representatives of a party who dies during the pendency of a suit commenced under this Act.
Pleading want of assets as a defense by the legal representatives when a suit is continued against them.
administration: Not explicitly stated, but the administration of justice and enforcement of such acts fall under the purview of the judicial system.
important_notes: The time limit for bringing an action under this Act was originally set, but has since been superseded by the Indian Limitation Act, 1963.
The territorial application of the act has been extended to numerous regions and states through various notifications and amendments over time.

title: THE BENGAL EMBANKMENT ACT, 1855
purpose: To provide for the better supervision and protection of embankments in the Territories under the Government of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, as existing regulations were found ineffectual.
scope: Applies to embankments within the Territories under the Government of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal. It covers public embankments and private embankments that affect public ones or drainage. It also applies to proprietors bound to maintain embankments.

key_definitions.embankment: An embankment for the purpose of excluding or retaining water. Every embankment kept up by government officers, at the expense of the government or any private person, is considered a public embankment.

main_sections.description: Repeals Bengal Regulation VI of 1806 and Regulation XI of 1829 concerning embankments, except for their own repeal clauses and acts done before the current Act.

main_sections.section_title: What is a public embankment within this Act
main_sections.description: Defines 'embankment' for the purpose of the Act and clarifies what constitutes a 'public embankment'.

main_sections.section_title: Who to have superintendence of public embankments
main_sections.description: Establishes the 'Superintendent of Embankments' as the officer responsible for the superintendence of public embankments, under the general orders of the Government.

Details the Superintendent's authority to take charge of connecting or crucial embankments, remove private embankments endangering public ones, change the line of public embankments, make new ones, and enlarge existing ones.

main_sections.section_title: Procedure for taking charge of private embankments and modifications
main_sections.description: Outlines the process: Superintendent gives notice to the Collector, Collector issues a proclamation, parties show cause, Collector hears objections and refers to the Superintendent, with further appeals to Commissioner of Revenue and Board of Revenue. Orders are final and not open to revision by Civil Courts, except for the stated appeals.

main_sections.section_title: Maintenance of private embankments taken charge of by Government Officers
main_sections.description: States that the expense of maintaining private embankments taken charge of by government officers is to be charged to the person bound to maintain it, not exceeding reasonable expenses for its original size and description.

main_sections.section_title: Compensation for damages sustained under this Act
main_sections.description: Provides a mechanism for compensation to persons sustaining damages from alterations to embankments. It details the process of claiming compensation from the Collector, arbitration for settling disputed amounts, and the appointment and functions of arbitrators and umpires. It also specifies conditions for appealing arbitration awards and the timeframe for civil actions.
Authorizes the making of sluices for landholders in embankments, with a requirement for an officer's report and the applicant to pay the expense.
Specifies that sluices are to be opened only by public officers or authorized individuals.
Authorizes the making of temporary water-courses through embankments.
Provides for specifications of works whose expenses belong to Zemindars, etc., and for keeping accounts of these works.
Empowers the Superintendent to report necessary removals of houses, etc., to the Collector, who then notifies interested parties. A jury is to ascertain value and make an award.

main_sections.section_title: Notice and Removal of Houses, etc.
main_sections.description: After an award, the Collector gives notice to concerned parties. If they default, the Collector may remove the houses, etc.
Establishes penalties for obstructing the removal of houses, for cutting embankments, and for damaging embankments by other means.
Grants jurisdiction under the Act to Deputy and Assistant Magistrates.
Empowers Darogahs to inquire into matters under the Act.
Orders of Magistrates, etc., are appealable.
Provides for the interpretation of terms used in the Act.

important_rules: Proprietors are bound to maintain embankments and pay for their maintenance when required.
The Superintendent of Embankments must give notice to the Collector before removing, changing, or enlarging any embankment.
The Collector shall issue a proclamation and hear objections before works on embankments proceed.
Damaged parties are entitled to compensation, with arbitration as the primary method for settling amounts if not agreed upon.
Sluices are to be opened only by public officers.
Temporary water-courses can be made through embankments.
Penalties are established for obstructing removals, cutting, or damaging embankments.

penalties: Penalty for obstructing the removal of houses, etc.
Penalty for cutting embankments.
Penalty for damaging embankments by other means.
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Superintendent of Embankments, Collector of the district, Commissioner of Revenue, Board of Revenue, Deputy Magistrates, Assistant Magistrates, and Darogahs.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through notices, proclamations, hearings of objections, appeals to higher revenue authorities, arbitration for compensation, removal of structures, and imposition of penalties by magistrates.

rights: Right to compensation for damages sustained from embankment alterations.
Right to appeal orders of the Superintendent, Commissioner, and Magistrate.
Right to a copy of the arbitration award.
Right to appeal to the Commissioner of Revenue from orders of the Superintendent.
Right to appeal to the Board of Revenue from orders of the Commissioner.
duties: Duty of proprietors to maintain embankments and pay for maintenance.
Duty of Superintendent to provide notice to the Collector before making changes.
Duty of the Collector to issue proclamations and hear objections.
Duty of arbitrators to deliver a full and complete award.
Duty of parties to appear and provide evidence when summoned.
Duty of claimants to prefer claims for compensation within the prescribed period.
obligations: Obligation to pay for the expense of sluices for landholders.
Obligation to cooperate with the arbitration process.
Obligation to cease actions that obstruct or damage embankments.

key_procedures: Procedure for taking charge of and modifying embankments: Superintendent's notice to Collector, Collector's proclamation and hearing of objections, referral to Superintendent/Commissioner/Board of Revenue.
Procedure for compensation claims: Presenting claim to Collector, reporting to superior authorities, arbitration for amount settlement, appeal of awards.
Procedure for removal of houses: Superintendent's report, Collector's notice, jury assessment, award, and removal upon default.
Arbitration process: Appointment of arbitrators, nomination of a third arbitrator, conduct of inquiry, delivery of award, and deposit of proceedings.
administration: Government of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, through the Superintendent of Embankments, Collector, Commissioner of Revenue, and Board of Revenue.
important_notes: Existing Regulations VI of 1806 and XI of 1829 are repealed, except as to prior acts, offenses, and liabilities.
Orders passed under Section V are final and not open to revision by any Civil Court, except for specified appeals.
Compensation awards can only be set aside by a Civil Court on grounds of corruption or misconduct of arbitrators, and suits must be instituted within three months.
Payment of compensation may be deferred if the right is doubtful or payment is deemed improper, with funds invested in government securities.

title: The Bengal Ghatwali Land Act, 1859
purpose: To empower the holders of Ghatwalee lands in the District of Beerbhoom to grant leases extending beyond the period of their own possession, for the development of mineral resources and improvement of the lands.
scope: This act applies to Ghatwalee lands in the District of Beerbhoom. It affects the Ghatwals (holders of these lands), proprietors of other lands, the Court of Wards, and Revenue authorities.

main_sections.section_title: Ghatwals of Beerbhoom to have the same right of granting leases as is allowed to other proprietors of lands.
main_sections.description: Grants Ghatwals of Beerbhoom holding lands under Regulation XXIX of 1814 the same power to grant leases for any period they deem conducive to land improvement, as is allowed to proprietors of other lands. A proviso outlines conditions for leases extending beyond the grantor's lifetime/incumbency, requiring them to be for specific purposes (mining, clearing jungle, building, tanks, canals) and approved by the Commissioner.

main_sections.section_title: Court of Wards and Revenue authorities to have the like power in certain cases.
main_sections.description: Empowers the Court of Wards or the Commissioner to grant leases for the specified purposes if the Ghatwalee lands are under their superintendence or control. Such leases are valid and binding on future possessors.

important_rules: Leases granted by Ghatwals for their lands in Beerbhoom are valid for any period conducive to land improvement.
Leases extending beyond the grantor's lifetime or incumbency are only valid if granted for mining, jungle clearing, building dwelling houses or manufactories, or for tanks, canals, and similar works.
Leases extending beyond the grantor's lifetime or incumbency require the approval of the Commissioner of the Division, certified by an endorsement.

penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Commissioner of the Division, Court of Wards, and Revenue authorities.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the approval and endorsement of leases by the Commissioner, and the direct granting of leases by the Court of Wards or Commissioner.

rights: Ghatwals of Beerbhoom have the right to grant leases for their lands.
Court of Wards and Revenue authorities have the right to grant leases for Ghatwalee lands under their control.
obligations: Leases extending beyond the grantor's life must be for specified improvement purposes.
Leases extending beyond the grantor's life require Commissioner's approval.

key_procedures: Granting a lease by a Ghatwal: Ghatwal deems a lease period conducive to improvement and grants it.
Granting a lease by Court of Wards/Revenue authorities: If lands are under their control, the Court of Wards or Commissioner can grant leases for specified purposes.
Obtaining Commissioner's approval for extended leases: Lease document must be presented to the Commissioner, who certifies approval with an endorsement and signature.
administration: The act is administered by Revenue authorities, specifically mentioning the Commissioner of the Division and the Court of Wards.
important_notes: Regulation XXIX of 1814 of the Bengal Code is referenced as the basis for how Ghatwals pay revenue directly to the Government.
The act aims to overcome the previous legal interpretation that Ghatwals did not have the power to alienate their lands.
The act specifies certain purposes for which leases exceeding the grantor's tenure can be granted, emphasizing development and improvement.

title: THE BENGAL LAND REVENUE SALES ACT, 1859
purpose: To improve the law relating to sales of Land for arrears of Revenue in the Lower Provinces under the Bengal Presidency, to discontinue the practice of obtaining the previous sanction of the Board of Revenue to sales of estates for arrears of revenue, to secure persons having a lien upon an estate who pay money to protect it from sale, to provide easy means for sharers to protect their shares from sale due to co-sharers' default, to facilitate landholders in guarding against accidental sale of their estates due to agents' neglect or fraud, to provide for voluntary registration of dependent talooks, and to protect holders of registered under-tenures from loss upon sale of the superior estate.
scope: The Act applies to the Provinces of Bengal, Behar, and Orissa, specifically dealing with the sale of land for arrears of revenue and related matters. It covers estates, shares of estates, and under-tenures within these provinces.

key_definitions.arrear of revenue: If the whole or a portion of a kist or instalment of any month of the era according to which the settlement and kistbundee of any mehal have been regulated, be unpaid on the first of the following month of such era, the sum so remaining unpaid shall be considered an arrear of revenue.

main_sections.description: Repeals Regulation VII. 1822 and IX. 1825 and Act I of 1845 (except for existing provisions and actions taken thereunder) in the Lower Provinces of Bengal.

main_sections.section_title: What is an arrear of revenue
main_sections.description: Defines an arrear of revenue as any portion of a kist or instalment remaining unpaid on the first of the following month according to the settlement era.

Empowers the Board of Revenue to fix dates for payment of revenue and other demands, after which estates in arrear will be sold at public auction. Requires notification of these dates in the official Gazette and local publications.

main_sections.section_title: In Sylhet, personal property of defaulters may in the first instance be distrained and sold
main_sections.description: Allows for the distress and sale of personal property of defaulters in Sylhet, instead of estate sales, as a first instance measure, if authorized by the Board of Revenue.

main_sections.section_title: Proviso in the case of certain descriptions of arrears
main_sections.description: Specifies conditions for selling estates or shares for specific types of arrears, including those other than the current or preceding year, arrears from other estates, estates under attachment, or arrears of tuccavee, poolbundee, or similar demands. Requires a detailed notification to be affixed for at least fifteen clear days.

main_sections.section_title: Notifications of sale to be issued, and no tender after latest day of payment to stop the sale
main_sections.description: Mandates the issuance of sale notifications by the Collector after the latest payment day, specifying estates or shares to be sold and the sale commencement date (15-30 days after notification). Requires official Gazette publication for estates with revenue exceeding five hundred Rupees. States that no payment or tender after sunset of the latest payment day will stop the sale.

Requires the Collector to affix proclamations forbidding ryots and under-tenants from paying rent due after the latest payment day to the defaulting proprietor, on pain of not receiving credit for such payments from the purchaser.

main_sections.section_title: Claims against Government held by a defaulter not to invalidate a sale
main_sections.description: States that claims against the Government or private demands held by a defaulter, or the presence of the defaulter's money in the Collector's hands, will not invalidate a sale, unless specific conditions regarding the money and the Collector's refusal to apply it are met.

main_sections.section_title: Deposits receivable from persons not proprietors
main_sections.description: Allows persons not proprietors to pay arrears as a deposit to protect an estate. Outlines provisions for courts to order temporary possession to such depositors if they are parties in a suit, and for recovery of the deposit amount from the defaulting proprietor if it was made to protect an interest.

main_sections.section_title: Separation of shares held in common, by the opening of a separate account
main_sections.description: Permits a recorded sharer of a joint estate to apply for a separate account to pay their share of government revenue individually.

important_rules: Rule 1: If any portion of a kist or instalment of revenue remains unpaid on the first of the following month, it is considered an arrear of revenue.
Rule 2: The Board of Revenue will fix the latest dates for payment of revenue and other demands; failure to pay by these dates will result in the sale of estates at public auction.
Rule 3: Sales notifications must be issued and published, and no payment made after sunset on the latest payment day will prevent a sale.
Rule 4: Ryots and under-tenants are forbidden from paying rent due after the latest payment day to defaulting proprietors, as such payments will not be credited by the purchaser.
Rule 5: Claims against the government or private demands held by a defaulter do not invalidate a sale unless specific conditions are met regarding the Collector's actions.
Rule 6: Persons who are not proprietors can deposit the arrear amount to protect an estate, and may have legal recourse to recover the deposit.
Rule 7: A sharer in a joint estate can apply to open a separate account for paying their revenue share.

penalties: Punishment for contempt of court or revenue authorities, including for default in making deposits (Section 56 & 57).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: Collector or other Officer duly authorized to hold sales under this Act, Board of Revenue, Civil Courts, Judge, Magistrate, Moonsiff.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Distress and sale of property (in Sylhet), public auction of estates or shares, affixing of notifications and proclamations, court orders for possession, suits to annul sales, recovery of arrears.

rights: Right of a person having a lien to protect an estate from sale by paying arrears.
Right of a sharer to protect their share from sale due to co-sharers' default.
Right of landholders to guard against accidental sale of their estates.
Right of holders of registered under-tenures to protection from loss upon sale of the superior estate.
Right of a purchaser to receive a certificate of sale and delivery of possession.
Right of a purchaser of a permanently settled estate sold for its own arrears to specific rights (Section 37).
Right of a purchaser of an estate not permanently settled sold for its own arrears to specific rights (Section 52).
duties: Duty of defaulting proprietors to pay revenue by the latest day of payment.
Duty of the Collector to issue sale notifications and conduct sales.
Duty of the Collector to affix proclamations to notify ryots and under-tenants.
Duty of ryots and under-tenants to pay rent to the purchaser for periods after the latest payment day.
obligations: Obligation to pay land revenue and other government demands by the prescribed dates.
Obligation to register certain tenures and farms.
Obligation of the purchaser to pay the full purchase money and comply with the Act's provisions.

key_procedures: Procedure for determining the latest day of payment and its notification.
Procedure for issuing and affixing sale notifications.
Procedure for conducting public auctions of estates or shares.
Procedure for receiving deposits from non-proprietors to protect estates.
Procedure for applying for and obtaining separate accounts for shares in joint estates.
Procedure for registration of talookdaree tenures and other under-tenures.
Procedure for appeals against sales.
Procedure for annulment of sales in special cases.
Procedure for obtaining a certificate of sale and delivery of possession.
Procedure for suits to annul sales and the effects of annulment.
administration: Board of Revenue, Collector or other Officer duly authorized to hold sales under this Act.
important_notes: Sales may be adjourned under certain conditions (Section 20).
The Government may purchase at a sale (Section 58).
Fees and charges may be demanded by the Collector (Section 59).
Certain regulations remain in force in specific estates (Section 60).
The Act applies from the date of its commencement (Section 62).

title: THE MADRAS DISTRICT POLICE ACT, 1859
purpose: To make the Police Force throughout the Madras Presidency a more efficient instrument for the prevention and detection of crime, and to re-organize the Police Force and improve the condition of the Village Police.
scope: Applies to the territories subject to the Presidency of Fort St. George (Madras Presidency). Covers both General and Village Police, including specific roles like Cuttoobadies and Kavilgars.

key_definitions.Magistrate: Includes all persons, within their respective jurisdictions, exercising all or any of the powers of a Magistrate.
key_definitions.Subordinate: As applied to Police functionaries, means District Superintendents and their Assistants.
key_definitions.Police: Includes General and Village Police, Cuttoobadies, Kavilgars, and all other persons, by whatever name known, who exercise any Police functions throughout the Madras Presidency.
key_definitions.General Police District: Embraces all districts to which the operation of this Act shall be extended.
key_definitions.Property: Includes any movable property, money or valuable security.
key_definitions.Number: Words importing the singular number shall include the plural number, and vice versa.
key_definitions.Gender: Words importing the masculine gender shall include females.
key_definitions.Cattle: Besides horned cattle, includes elephants, camels, horses, asses, mules, sheep, goats and swine.

main_sections.description: Defines key terms used in the Act.
Repeals and amends certain Regulations and Acts mentioned in a schedule, except for ongoing proceedings or incurred penalties.

main_sections.section_title: Jurisdiction of Officers appointed under Regulation XI, 1816
main_sections.description: Clarifies that the Act does not affect powers of appointment given to Magistrates under Regulation XI, 1816, but limits these officers from exercising Executive Police Officer functions.

main_sections.section_title: Superintendence vested in Governor in Council
main_sections.description: Vests the superintendence of the police in the Governor in Council and prohibits appointment, supersession, or control of police functionaries by others, notwithstanding any contrary regulation, act, or usage.
Vests the administration of the police in an Inspector-General of Police for Madras Presidency and such subordinates as appointed by the Governor in Council.
Confers all existing police powers, not inconsistent with this Act, to the police authorities appointed under this Act, but prohibits them from exercising judicial or revenue authority.

main_sections.section_title: Inspector-General to be appointed a Justice of the Peace. To have the powers of a Magistrate but to exercise such powers under the orders of Government. District Superintendent may be appointed a Magistrate. In what cases he may act in that capacity.
main_sections.description: Appoints the Inspector-General as a Justice of the Peace with Magistrate powers under Government orders. Allows the Governor in Council to vest District Superintendents with Magistrate powers for specific purposes like peace, crime prevention, and offender apprehension.

Declares the entire Police establishment of Madras Presidency as one Police Force, to be enrolled and constituted as ordered by the Governor in Council with the sanction of the Governor General in Council.

main_sections.section_title: Inspector-General to control Force and make rules
main_sections.description: Empowers the Inspector-General, subject to Governor in Council's approval, to frame rules for the government, distribution, classification, inspection, arms, and overall efficiency of the Police Force.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment and dismissal of Police Officers
main_sections.description: Assigns the appointment of all Police Officers to the Inspector-General and Deputy Superintendents, who can dismiss, suspend, or fine officers deemed remiss, negligent, or unfit.

main_sections.section_title: Police Officers to receive certificates of Office
main_sections.description: Mandates that appointed Police Officers receive a certificate of office, which vests them with police powers and privileges. This certificate ceases upon suspension, dismissal, or removal and must be surrendered.

Establishes a 'Police Superannuation Fund' funded by deductions from pay, stoppages, fines, and sales of old equipment, to be used for superannuation or retiring allowances under rules passed by the Governor in Council. Excludes entitlement to the fund or refunds for dismissed officers.

main_sections.section_title: Additional Police Officers employed at the cost of individuals
main_sections.description: Allows the Inspector-General or District Superintendent to depute additional Police Officers at the charge of an applicant for keeping the peace, subject to their orders and for a specified time. The applicant can terminate this deputation with one month's notice.

main_sections.section_title: Appointment of additional Force in the neighbourhood of Railway and other works
main_sections.description: Authorizes the Inspector-General, with consent of the Governor in Council, to direct the employment of an additional Police Force near Railway, Canal, or other Public works if deemed necessary due to the behaviour or apprehended behaviour of workers. Payment is to be made by the company carrying out the works.

main_sections.section_title: Payment of money for support of additional Police Force
main_sections.description: States that monies paid for additional Police Forces as per Sections XIII and XIV shall be paid into 'The General Police Fund' and applied to the maintenance of the Police Force as per Governor in Council's orders.

important_rules: Police officers must receive a certificate of office upon enrollment, which vests them with police powers and must be surrendered upon removal from service (Section XI).
Deductions from police pay, fines, and other sources are to be invested to form a Police Superannuation Fund for retiring allowances (Section XII).

Additional police officers can be deputed at the cost of individuals requiring peace-keeping services, with the option for the individual to discontinue the force with one month's notice (Section XIII).
Additional police forces can be appointed near public works if necessary due to worker behaviour, with costs borne by the company undertaking the work (Section XIV).
All fines collected from individuals and police officers for offences are to be paid into 'The General Police Fund' (Section XV).

penalties: Fines for neglect of duty (Section 44).
Penalties for receiving unauthorized fees (Section 45).
Penalties for extortion (Section 46).
Penalties for obstructing a Police Officer in the execution of duty (Section 47).
Penalties for refusal to assist a Police Officer when required (Section 43).
penalties_and_enforcement.enforcement_authority: The Police Force itself, under the superintendence of the Governor in Council, and with specific powers vested in the Inspector-General and District Superintendents.
penalties_and_enforcement.how_enforced: Through the powers granted to Police Officers, including arrest without warrant, execution of warrants and summonses, and laying of informations. Enforcement is also managed through the framework of rules and regulations set by the Inspector-General and approved by the Governor in Council.

rights: Police officers have the right to arrest without warrant (Section 22).
Police officers have the right to require assistance from the public (Section 43).
Police officers are vested with the powers, functions, and privileges of Police Officers by virtue of their certificate of office (Section 11).
District Superintendents may be vested with Magistrate powers for specific purposes (Section VII).
duties: Duties of Police Officers are outlined in Section 21.
Police officers are responsible for preventing and detecting crime.
Police officers must execute all warrants and summonses (Section 32).
Police officers must ensure no unnecessary restraint is used during arrests (Section 38).
Police officers must bring arrested persons immediately before the authority mentioned in the warrant (Section 41).
Police officers must not make threats or promises to compel disclosure from an arrested person (Section 42).
Police officers have specific duties within the limits of towns, including addressing obstructions and nuisances in roads (Section 48).
obligations: Police officers not to resign without leave or two months' notice (Section 19).
Every person appointed as a police officer must receive a certificate of office and surrender it upon dismissal or removal (Section 11).
The Inspector-General is obligated to control the Force and make rules for its efficiency (Section IX).

key_procedures: Arrest without warrant and subsequent procedure: A Police Officer may arrest without warrant and the person arrested must be taken to a Station House until brought before a Magistrate or bailed (Sections 22, 23).
Release on bail: Persons arrested without warrant may be released on bail (Section 24).
Recognizance for appearance: Superior Officers may take recognizance for the appearance of a prosecutor or witness, with specific conditions (Sections 25, 26).

Execution of warrants: All warrants are to be executed by Officers of the Police Force, with provisions for endorsement, service, and execution methods, including notification of the warrant's substance and breaking of doors/windows if necessary (Sections 32-40).

Deputation of additional police officers at individual cost: An individual can apply for additional police officers, and can later request their discontinuation with one month's notice (Section XIII).

Appointment of additional force near public works: The Inspector-General can direct the employment of additional forces near public works, with payment to be arranged from the company's funds (Section XIV).
administration: The Governor in Council, through the Inspector-General of Police and their subordinates.
important_notes: The Act repeals and amends existing laws but preserves their effect on past actions, offences, and proceedings commenced before its operation (Section II).
Judicial functions or jurisdiction previously exercised by officers under repealed enactments are not affected (Section II).
The Inspector-General, while having Magistrate powers, must exercise them under the orders of the Governor in Council (Section VII).
Police officers appointed under this Act are not to possess or exercise any judicial or revenue authority (Section VI).
No police officer is entitled to a superannuation allowance or a refund of deductions made from their pay (Section XII Proviso).

title: THE STAGE-CARRIAGES ACT, 1861
purpose: To license and regulate stage-carriages.
scope: Applies to every carriage drawn by one or more horses, ordinarily used for conveying passengers for hire to or from any place. The act's extent is clarified to apply to all States of India, not superseding local laws on the same subject.

key_definitions.stage-carriage: Every carriage drawn by one or more horses which shall ordinarily be used for the purpose of conveying passengers for hire to or from any place.

main_sections.description: Defines what constitutes a stage-carriage under the Act.
Requires all stage-carriages to be licensed by a Magistrate or the Commissioner of Police of a Presidency-town.

main_sections.section_title: Power to refuse license. Particulars of license.
main_sections.description: Grants the licensing authority the power to refuse a license if the stage-carriage is deemed unserviceable, unsafe, or unfit for public accommodation. It also specifies the details to be included in a license if granted.

main_sections.section_title: Charge for and duration of license.
main_sections.description: Prescribes the fee for a license (five rupees or as fixed by the State Government) and states that the license is valid for one year. It also outlines the process for substituting a new proprietor's name in the license.

main_sections.section_title: Particulars to be painted on conspicuous part of carriage.
main_sections.description: Mandates that license particulars be distinctly painted in English on a conspicuous part of the licensed stage-carriage.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for letting carriage without having particulars painted.
main_sections.description: Penalizes proprietors who let a stage-carriage for hire without the required particulars painted on it.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for letting for hire unlicensed carriage.
main_sections.description: Imposes penalties for letting a stage-carriage for hire without a valid license, with increased penalties for subsequent convictions.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for allowing carriage to be drawn by fewer animals or more passengers, etc., to be carried than provided by license.
main_sections.description: Penalizes proprietors or drivers who permit a licensed carriage to be drawn by fewer animals or to carry more passengers/luggage than specified in the license. It also establishes a presumption of guilt for the proprietor unless they can prove reasonable precautions were taken.
Punishes any person who cruelly ill-treats or over-drives any horse used for drawing a stage-carriage, or who uses an unfit horse.
Empowers the Magistrate or Commissioner of Police to cancel a license if the stage-carriage, horse, or harness is found to be unserviceable, unsafe, or unfit for public use.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for not conforming to provisions of section 5.
main_sections.description: Details the procedure for seizure and penalty imposition if a stage-carriage does not have the required license particulars painted on it. It includes provisions for detention, sale, and forfeiture of the carriage and horse.

main_sections.section_title: Penalty for misconduct on part of drivers.
main_sections.description: Penalizes drivers or persons in charge of stage-carriages for endangering safety through intoxication, neglect, furious driving, or other misconduct.

Makes proprietors liable for penalties incurred by drivers or horse owners if the offender is unknown or cannot be found. It includes a proviso allowing proprietors to be discharged if they prove the offense was committed without their knowledge or profit, and they took reasonable steps to prevent it.
Describes the process for issuing summons to proprietors or their agents, including transmission by registered post and reasonable time for appearance.
States that penalties are to be adjudicated by a Magistrate or Commissioner of Police, and their orders are final.
Outlines the procedure for levying penalties and outstanding balances by distress and sale of the offender's movable property through a warrant issued by the Magistrate.

main_sections.section_title: Offender may be apprehended and detained in custody until return of warrant of distress.
main_sections.description: Allows for the apprehension and detention of an offender until a warrant of distress can be returned, unless security is provided for appearance.

main_sections.section_title: Imprisonment of offender if distress not sufficient.
main_sections.description: Specifies that if no sufficient distress can be found to levy the penalty, or if the offender has no sufficient goods, imprisonment may follow.
Defines the jurisdiction for enforcing the Act.
Grants the power to make rules.
Provides definitions for terms used in the Act, including 'Magistrate' and clarifies that the Act applies to all animals used for drawing carriages.
Specifies the territorial extent of the Act, which has been declared to apply to all States of India.

main_sections.section_title: Power to State Government to exempt.
main_sections.description: Gives the State Government the power to exempt certain entities or carriages from the provisions of the Act.

important_rules: All stage-carriages used for conveying passengers for hire must be licensed by a Magistrate or Commissioner of Police.
License particulars, including carriage number, proprietor's details, passenger capacity, and horse number, must be painted on the carriage.
Proprietors are responsible for ensuring their stage-carriages comply with the license conditions regarding the number of animals, passengers, and luggage weight.
Cruel treatment of animals used for drawing stage-carriages is prohibited.
Drivers and persons in charge must not endanger passengers or property through misconduct, intoxication, or furious driving.

penalties: Fine not exceeding one hundred rupees for letting a carriage for hire without particulars painted (Section 6).
First conviction: fine not exceeding one hundred rupees; subsequent conviction: fine up to five hundred rupees for letting an unlicensed carriage (Section 7).
First conviction: fine not exceeding one hundred rupees; subsequent conviction: fine up to five hundred rupees for allowing fewer animals or more passengers/luggage than licensed (Section 8).
Fine not exceeding one hundred rupees for ill-treating animals (Section 9).
Fine not exceeding one hundred rupees for misconduct by drivers endangering safety or property (Section 12).
